Based on clinical record reviews, review of agency policies and interview with agency personnel for one of two patients (Patients #1) in the survey sample, the hospice agency failed to ensure the patient's right to be free from abuse or neglect and failed to follow the agency policies. The finding includes:
 

Patient #1 elected the Hospice benefit on 12/17/2023 with diagnoses that included muscle weakness, difficulty walking, severe protein-calorie malnutrition, dysphagia, seizures, cardiac disease, and dementia. The physicians orders dated 12/17/2023 included nursing services once a week for symptom management and assessments, home health aide services once a week for assistance with activities of living, and a social worker evaluation for caregiver support.
 
Review of Patient #1s hospice start of care summary dated 12/17/2023, identified Patient #1 was hospitalized after having a seizure, admitted to a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation services and discharged to a private home to reside with a caregiver. The hospice agencys Medical Director approved end of life services related to Patient #1s severe protein-calorie malnutrition after a twenty-six-pound weight loss since 11/2023. The start of care summary further identified the home environment presented with no safety issues and the caregiver was assisting the Patient with ambulation, transfers from the chair to the bed, dressing, bathing, incontinence care, housekeeping, meal preparation, shopping, and laundry. The admitting Registered Nurse (RN) identified no signs of neglect or abuse and the caregiver had no limitations but would need respite care or sitter services to meet the Patients increasing care needs.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note dated 01/09/2024, identified an as needed visit was made related to Patient #1s increased care needs, an unclean living environment, and the caregiver leaving the Patient home alone after being advised not to by the primary case manager RN #1. Social Worker #1 offered the Patients caregiver additional support in the home, but the caregiver declined.
 
Review of RN #1s clinical notes dated 01/18/2024, 01/26/2024, and 01/30/2024 identified providing Patient #1s caregiver with education about safety concerns in the home, and the importance of not leaving the Patient alone for any period due to increased confusion and weakness.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note date 01/30/2024, identified Social Worker #1 spoke with the Patients caregiver about the Patients increased care needs, safety concerns, and the need for an additional caregiver in the home. The Patients caregiver declined assistance and indicated having people who could assist if needed.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note dated 02/15/2024, identified a joint visit was conducted with RN #1. Patient #1 was anxious, agitated and the caregiver appeared stressed, but continued to decline the need for supportive services.
 
Review of the Administrators case coordination note dated 02/21/2024, identified contacting Patient #1s caregiver on 02/21/2024 to discuss concerns for the unclean home environment, the caregivers ability to safely manage the Patients medications and leaving the Patient home alone.
 
Review of RN #2s clinical note dated 02/28/2024, identified Patient #1s caregiver contacted the hospice agencys answering service to report the Patient was confused and vomiting. Upon arrival to the Patients home, RN #2 identified the Patient was lying on the floor covered in feces and vomit. Patient #1s caregiver indicated the Patient may have eaten old food from the wastebasket which resulted in him/her vomiting. RN #2 advised the caregiver that Patient #1 needed to be transferred to the hospital bed and cleaned. The caregiver indicated the Patient sleeps on the couch, and he/she sleeps in the hospital bed provided by the hospice. RN #2 assisted the Patient to the hospital bed and attempted to clean the Patient, but the caregiver lacked necessary supplies such as washcloths, a wash basin, clean clothing, or linen. RN #2 cleaned the Patient with paper towels. RN #2 left the home and contacted SCS #1 to report the unsafe and concerning conditions in the Patients home.
 
Interview and review of Patient #1s clinical record with RN #1 on 03/11/2024 10:40 AM, identified the Patients home environment as cluttered, with unclean surfaces, a strong odor present and waste overflowing from the wastebasket. RN #1 indicated the Patient appeared disheveled and the caregiver was unable to safely manage the Patients medications. RN #1 identified the caregiver reported having weapons in the home and would become agitated toward the hospice staff and the Patient. RN #1 and Social Worker #1 reported the concerns to the Administrator and the Supervisor of Clinical Services (SCS) #1 at the beginning of February 2024. Social Worker #1 left a message for Protective Services for the Elderly on 02/21/2024 and filed a report with Protective Services for the Elderly on 02/27/2024. The Administrator and SCS #1 advised hospice clinicians to not return to Patient #1s home but did not discharge the Patient.
 
Interview and review of Patient #1s clinical record with the Administrator on 03/11/2024 at 12:00 PM, identified RN #1 and Social Worker #1 reported the Patients living conditions as unsanitary and the caregiver was unable to safely care for the Patient. The Administrator indicated the Patient was not discharged for cause from the hospice agency, but clinicians were advised not to return to Patient #1s home after Protective Service for the Elderly was contacted on 02/21/2024. The Administrator identified Patient #1 was visited by hospice clinicians on 02/15/2024 and did not receive another visit until 02/28/2024. The Administrator identified hospice services were not provided for twelve days (02/16/2024 to 02/27/2024), as the agency was waiting for directives from the Regional Managers of Clinical Services. The Administrator indicated after RN #2 reported concerns for Patient #1's safety on 02/28/2024, SCS #1 contacted the police and the Patient was removed from the home.
 
Interview with the Regional Vice President of Clinical Services on 03/11/2024 1:00 PM, identified the hospice agency failed to follow the Assessment and Reporting of Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation policy, Safety Management policy and the Discharge for Cause policy. The Regional Vice President of Clinical Service indicated the hospice agency failed to immediately report suspected abuse and/or neglect to the appropriate state agency, failed to coordinate care by having the Patient immediately removed from the unsafe situation, then discharge the Patient from the hospice agency due to compromised patient and staff safety. Additionally, the Vice President of Clinical Services identified the hospice agency staff failed to ensure the Patient's safety by not providing oversight of the Patient for twelve days. 
 
Review of the agencys Assessment and Reporting of Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation policy, identified agency staff would assess, identify, and intervene on the behalf of victims of abuse and neglect and exploitation in an appropriate and professional manner. All cases of alleged, observed, or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation would be investigated by the agency and appropriate interventions would be initiated, including mandated reported requirements in accordance with the state regulations. When abuse or neglect is suspected, the hospice staff would report the incident to the Administrator immediately and complete an incident report. If the patient is felt to be in immediate danger, the staff member would first ensure the patients personal safety and notify the Administrator. The Administrator would immediately start an investigation and notify the appropriate state agencies.
 
Review of the agencys Discharge for Cause policy, identified the agency reserved the right to discharge patients for cause if all attempts to remediate the situation failed. There may be circumstances in which a hospice would be unable to continue to provide hospice care to a patient. These situations would include issues where the patient safety or hospice staff safety was compromised. The agency must make referrals to all relevant state agencies. The hospice would assist in coordinating continued care for the patient.
 
Review of the agencys Safety Management policy, identified upon admission and at every visit, all patients would be assessed for falls and the home environment would also be evaluated for safety issues. Suspected or confirmed patient abuse or neglect would be reported to specified state agencies and living conditions which place patients in eminent danger.

Review of the agencys Assessments policy, identified the hospice conducts patient specific assessments at the time of admission, signification change and on an ongoing basis as the condition of the patient requires. The comprehensive assessment identifies the physical, psychosocial, emotional, behavioral and spiritual needs of the patient are addressed in order to promote the hospice patient's wellbeing, comfort and dignity throughout the dying process.

Based on review of the Hospice’s Standard (in lieu of Policy and Procedure), patient record review and staff interview, the Hospice provider failed to ensure 2 of 6 sampled patients (Patient #1 and #22) were free from neglect. This affected Patient #1 who expressed suicidal ideation and the Hospice failed to develop care plan with appropriate interventions and/or referrals, and failed to communicate concerns for suicidal ideation between disciplines and care settings, which ended with a family member finding Patient #1 dead by gunshot wound to the head with gunpowder residue on his hands. This affected Patient #22 for whom Hospice staff was notified by nursing home staff on 06/17/24 that she was found disoriented with pills nearby after a return from a leave of absence, but the Hospice did not implement any interventions to address the risk of patient overdose, and Patient #22 died on 06/20/24 after a suspected second overdose on 06/19/24. The findings include:

2. Review of the medical record revealed patient #22, a 78-year-old female, was admitted to the hospice agency on 7/29/23 with terminal diagnosis of atherosclerotic heart disease and secondary diagnosis of heart failure. 
Review of the medical record dated 7/31/23 revealed a Registered Nurse (RN) completed the Initial Comprehensive Assessment that noted the patient was alert and oriented to person, place, situation and time. The patient reported a pain level of ";6" with care plan goal of ";3" or less. The assessment indicated the patient was on opioid type medications for sharp/shooting pain down her left leg and across her back. The patient stated, ";I just want to feel better, I have no quality of life". The RN documented under psychosocial assessment no history of psychiatric illness/substance abuse or suicidal ideation. The RN documented the patient had history of depression since her son passed away in January from Corona Virus Disease.
The Bachelor of Social Work (BSW) completed a Psychosocial Comprehensive Assessment on 8/1/23 and documented the patient denied concerns regarding suicidal ideation or substance abuse history and currently was in acceptance of her terminal illness, had depression and was coping appropriately. The plan moving forward was for SW (Social Worker) to meet with patient twice per month to provide support and education. The plan of care included symptom management regarding ";sense of control and ability to cope" and interventions to provide reassurance, educate regarding hospice services and provide support through being present. The SW assisted patient #22 with nursing home placement per note dated 2/26/24. 
The hospice RN note dated 6/15/24 revealed the nurse visited the patient at the nursing home. During the visit the patient opened her eyes when her name was called but fell asleep while talking. She then opened her eyes and said she felt ";wiped out." The hospice RN did not collaborate with other hospice staff or with nursing home staff to determine the reason for the patient's change in condition and why she was so lethargic. 
On 6/16/24 to 6/17/24, patient #22 went on a Leave of Absence (LOA) from the nursing home and obtained unknown drugs while on leave. The hospice agency did not ensure coordination of communication and were not notified of the patient's leave.
The hospice Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) #LL visited the patient at the nursing home on 6/17/24 from 9 AM to 10:20 AM, and documented the patient was alert and calm. He wrote he was informed by nursing home staff the patient returned from LOA and was found in her room very disoriented. About 5-6 bottles of medications including Ativan and other narcotics were found in the patients room which the nursing home staff secured in a locked box. The hospice LPN did not initiate an incident report or collaborate with the nursing home staff to address why the resident brought the medications to the nursing home or which medications she may have taken.
On 6/18/24 at 11:45 PM, the Telecare Call Action Log by hospice RN #ZZ showed the nursing home LPN called to report patient #22 was found 10 minutes ago foaming at the mouth and unresponsive. The patient had a pulse of 51 bpm [beats per minute]. The nursing home LPN stated she found a cup in the patients room with Ativan, Temazepam and Potassium pills. The LPN also reported the patient had history of self-harming behavior. The patient was sent to the hospital for possible overdose. At 12:45 AM, the ";Hospital called in stated that patient overdose, reason for the visit to hospital..."
On 6/19/24 at 6:43 AM, Telecare Call note by hospice staff #BBB read, ";Facility nurse called in and stated patient came back from the hospital at 0400 (4 AM) but the patient's condition is still bad..."
On 6/19/24 hospice RN #MM visited the patient at the nursing home and documented a visit note at 10 AM. The noted indicated the patient was unresponsive, and foaming at the mouth. The patient was suctioned, and family notified of the situation. The family informed this situation has occurred many times..."
On 6/20/24 RN #MM documented a visit at the nursing home from 8:45 AM to 9:55 AM. The note showed the patient had no response to stimuli and was clammy. The patient was not able to swallow, and all medications were discontinued except for comfort. 
On 6/20/24 at 10:35 AM, the hospice chaplain visited the patient at the nursing home and documented death at this time was imminent. She had decreased response to verbal and visual stimuli. The date and time of death according to the hospice Case Sheet was on 6/20/24 at 1:30 PM. 
On 8/27/24 at 12:43 PM, interview and concurrent record review was conducted with General Manager (GM) DD in person and other staff on the phone from program #78 including Senior Patient Care Administrator (PCA) #II, Performance Improvement Specialist (PIS) #JJ, and Associate GM #KK. The staff verified they did not have a General Manager for program #78 at this time. They explained this incident was suspected suicide as the patient was found with bottles of pills nearby. Hospice staff indicated they did not know what day she went on leave and thought that a friend brought her home, and that is how she obtained pills and brought them back to the nursing home. 
The Senior Patient Care Administrator verified she was responsible to ensure a thorough investigation and root cause analysis was done post incidents. She verified that hospice staff did not talk to the nursing home staff to find out exactly what happened. She said they did identify areas of opportunity for communication and education. They needed to educate the nursing home staff that hospice should have been notified immediately after drugs were confiscated from patient #22. She stated, ";the main thing that was lacking was our communication between facility staff and hospice staff. I think mainly being aware the patient went out of the facility so that we would have known when she came back, she was having a hard time adjusting to being at the facility". The Senior Patient Care Administrator noted they needed to improve their communication with the nursing home staff and should have implemented measures to keep the patient safe. She acknowledged they had not revised the care plan after it was identified the patient brought in medications to the nursing home and was found disoriented. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 1) The hospices Standard titled VS Responding to Abuse, Neglect and Financial Exploitation and Reporting of Crimes in the Long-Term Care Facility, dated 06/15/23 documents ";Neglect means failure to provide goods and services necessary to avoid physical harm or mental anguish.
Review of the clinical record reveals Patient #1 was admitted to the Hospice for ";Routine Home Care" in February 2021 with no known history of depression or mental illness. An Interdisciplinary Plan of Care Revision/Physician Orders dated 07/01/24 documents, ";Transfer to IPU [Inpatient Unit] – [name of hospital] for SOB [shortness of breath] & cough. Pneumonia." A Psychosocial Updated Comprehensive Assessment was completed by an unlicensed and unregistered Social Worker, Staff A on 07/03/24 who documented Patient #1 was lethargic but arousable, did not want nursing home placement but wanted to go home and was receptive to seek veteran benefits for aide services. This assessment did not document any signs of suicidality. 
 
Patient #1s Focus Visit by Staff A on 07/04/24 for 3:00 PM to 4:30 PM documents the Social Worker (SW) conducted a follow up visit after report from Registered Nurse, Staff B that ";patient said he wished he had a gun, he doesn't want to live like this (bed bound)" and under interventions performed, ";SW provided PS [psychosocial] support/provide active empathetic listening/validation of feelings assess for suicidal ideation re: statements made to RN [name] when providing care SW called PCG [primary caregiver] to discuss safety re: statements of ideation + DC [discharge] planning" and Response to Care ";Patient presented AAOx2 [awake alert and oriented to person and place]; intermittent forgetfulness/confusion/receptive/engaged Pt [patient] advised ";I was just running my mouth; I would never do anythin_ I do not want to hurt my family I do not want to leave this as my legacy to my grandkids Pt denied plan/attempts of suicid_ son advise pt made similar statements since pt was 50 years old PCG advise_ gun in home in lock box away from pts reac_ PCG wants pt to return home." This Focus Visit does not document communication or collaboration with any other staff although there is a place on the form to indicate collaboration with empty checkboxes for several disciplines. 
 
Review of Patient #1s inpatient nursing notes for 07/02/24, 07/03/24, 07/04/24, and 07/05/24 reveal no documentation that Patient #1 made any statements indicating suicidal intent or ideation while in the inpatient unit. An entry on Patient #1s Addendum: VIPU Shift Care Note for 07/05/24 at 7:35 PM documents ";Pt discharged home." Review of Patient #1s physician notes for 07/02/24, 07/03/24, 07/04/24 reveal no documentation of awareness that Patient #1 made any statements indicating suicidal intent or ideation. There was no physician note for 07/05/24 and no order to send the patient home from the inpatient unit, as of the date of record review on 08/28/24. 
 
After inquiry on 08/28/24 to Patient Care Administrator, Staff C as to whether the physician ever gave an order for Patient #1 to go home from the Inpatient Unit on 07/05/24, Staff C reviewed the chart and on 08/29/24 at 10:18 AM confirmed she could not find such an order, stated she talked to the physician that morning and he confirmed he had given the order, so she wrote a late order for the discharge. Later that day, Staff C provided an Interdisciplinary Plan of Care Revision/Physician Orders documenting ";Late entry for 07/05/24 DC [discontinue] IPU Level of Care Resume Routine Home Care" with physician signature dated 08/29/24, and no evidence of any other orders or changes to the care plan. Review of Patient #1s Plan of Care Review dated 07/05/24 documents in the Psychosocial category ";S/W available" and in the Spiritual category ";Chaplain available" and gives no indication of any interventions or changes to the plan of care to address his suicidal statement in the inpatient unit.
 
Review of the Nursing-Updated Comprehensive Assessment by Registered Nurse, Staff D dated 07/06/24 for a visit at 6:25 PM to 7:25 PM reveals no documentation or evidence of awareness of Patient #1s suicidal statement in the inpatient unit and no evidence of psychosocial assessment other than the words ";SW involved c [with] care." Review of the Nursing-Updated Comprehensive Assessment dated 07/08/24 for a visit at 9:40 to 10:40 (no AM or PM) reveals no documentation or evidence of awareness of Patient #1s suicidal statement in the inpatient unit; the Psychosocial section documents a reported level of ";4", care plan outcome ";maintain psych", care plan goal ";2"; and on the next line a reported level of ";0", care plan outcome ";0", and care plan goal ";0", followed by Interventions Performed ";assessed psych" and Response to Care ";SW involved in case"; and the Location of Care (Home) Environmental Safety section indicates by a mark in a checkbox ";Cluttered or unclean living area(s), the Care Plan Outcome ";maintained safety," interventions ";assessed safety," and Response to Care ";Educated PCG to keep pt belonging in reach." 
 
A Supplemental Interdisciplinary Note for 07/08/24 by the Social Worker on the home team, Staff E documents phone contact to Patient #1s family member who reported the patient is stable and the nurse visit would be sufficient for now, Social Worker advised will be visiting the home the next day and the visit is important in case there are any needs, and the PCG asked her to call before arriving. A Supplemental Interdisciplinary Note for 07/09/24 by Staff E documents she called to confirm the visit, but the family member denied the visit and rescheduled it for 07/11/24. A Psychosocial Updated Comprehensive Assessment completed by Staff E for 07/11/24 at 12:30 PM to 1:30 PM indicates in the psychosocial section by marks in checkboxes: Emotional Affects/Behavioral Manifestations, Patient is a Veteran, and in comments that the patient was very happy with services provided, support to patient and caregiver, the caregiver confirmed patient is a veteran but wants to put benefits on hold for now. 
 
An Addendum Interdisciplinary Note dated 07/13/24 by a Chaplain documents she was notified the patient had died and visited the Patient #1s residence, that the family member stated ";I think he shot himself," that the family member reported they went into the patient's room that morning and found him in an odd position with the gun next to him, that the family called 911, and that the family member mentioned a nurse had reported to him Patient #1 had made the comment ";I wanna blow my head off" while he was at the Inpatient Unit. Review of the associated police report printed 08/27/24 at 1:00 PM revealed when police arrived to the home on 07/13/24, they found Patient #1 dead with a gunshot wound to his head, loaded firearm in his hand, and a presumptive test was positive for the presence of gunshot residue on Patient #1s right hand. The police report also documented the family member reported Patient #1 ";had made comments about shooting himself and so he hid his firearm in another drawer in the room."
 
During telephone interview on 08/27/24 at 2:35 PM, the inpatient Registered Nurse, Staff B reported Patient #1 stated to her in the hospice inpatient unit that he should have blown his brains before he came to this place, but when she asked what he meant by that, he then said it's nothing and he was just frustrated; that when she asked if he had a gun at home he denied having one and said forget it, it's nothing, that he was just frustrated and then he talked of what his life had been, his past accomplishments, and that now he's here; that Staff B then told the Social Worker, Staff A what Patient #1 had said, and Staff A said she would go talk to him; that Staff B then told the Team Manager, who said she had to ";escalate this all the way up"; that Staff B called Patient #1s family member and told them what Patient #1 had said and asked if that seemed strange, to which the family member responded Patient #1 has been saying this for 35 years and it's nothing; that Staff B asked the family member if there was a gun in the home, but the family member downplayed it, said it's nothing, and asked when they are sending the patient home.
 
During telephone interview on 08/27/24 at 2:55 PM, the inpatient Social Worker, Staff A stated she evaluated Patient #1 on 07/03/24, there were concerns for his loss of autonomy and she remembered he wanted to keep his urinary catheter in when he went home, which was an unusual request but maybe he did not want to burden the household with trips to the bathroom; that her focus was his weakness and need for support and they discussed veteran benefits to try to get him part-time help at home; that on 07/04/24 she was informed Patient #1 wanted to be discharged as soon as possible, she met with him early in the day and he talked of his life experiences and wanting to go home for the holiday with family; that after this Staff B reported he just made a statement that he wished he had a gun to make things go faster, so Staff A immediately texted the physician to put a hold on the discharge and talk when he gets in, and informing the physician the nurse verbalized Patient #1 had suicidal ideation and Staff A was going to go talk to Patient #1; that Staff A talked to Patient #1 about his statement that he wished he had a gun and he said Oh, no, it's just words, and minimized it; that Staff A immediately asked Patient #1 if he ever attempted suicide before and if he had a plan, and he said he would never do that to his children or grandchildren; that Patient #1 talked about feeling depressed and his loss of autonomy and weakness; that Staff A then talked to Staff B about symptom management for his depression and moving him closer to the nurses station; that Staff A called the family member who said Patient #1 has been saying things like that since his first cardiac event at age 50, that there was a gun in the home but it was on the other side of the house in a locked box out of reach, and the family member denied feeling concerned about Patient #1s statement; that Staff A then talked to the Team Manager and Physician about Patient #1s statements and conversations, and the discharge was held, but Patient #1 ended up being discharged the following day while Staff A was not working; Staff A denied using, or the Hospice having, any formal suicide assessment or suicide screening tool; Staff A reported they used to contract for safety when a person was a suicide risk, but they stopped doing that at this Hospice; Staff A denied having a Social Work license or being a Registered Clinical Social Work Intern but reported she has a Masters in Social Work and has worked in the Hospice as a Social Worker seeing patients for the last nine years.
 
During telephone interview on 08/28/24 at 11:31 AM, Registered Nurse, Staff D stated she remembered Patient #1 and had been seeing him weekly since January 2024 except when he was in the inpatient unit; that there was nothing concerning in her visits to indicate a Social Worker was needed; when asked about her nursing assessments in which she consistently documented for psychosocial a Reported Level of ";4" and a Care Plan Goal of ";0" and what this means, Staff D answered she was trained to put a ";4" and whether they were depressed or suicidal she would probably still put a ";4" but there are other things she would do, such as staying with them until they can find another intervention, call the doctor and social worker, start continuous care; Staff D stated since August she learned if there's nothing wrong, she could put a "0" instead of a ";4"; Staff D stated ";Psychosocial is not something I focus on. I focus on medication management and, if there is something else, I let another team member know. I have not learned how to do a psychosocial assessment"; Staff D stated she received a report from the inpatient manager when Patient #1 was coming home that he would probably need a follow up visit that night and the next day, he had a urinary catheter and wanted to keep it in, was still very weak and had issues swallowing, but no mention he had made any suicidal statements; that if there had been anything about him feeling suicidal they would probably have kept him in the inpatient unit or she could have put him on continuous care at home, and that it ";would have changed everything", but she was never informed of this; and that the Social Worker made a visit to Patient #1 right after her own on 07/11/24 to talk about veterans benefits.
 
During telephone interview on 8/28/24 at 3:34 PM, Registered Clinical Social Work Intern, Staff E stated Patient #1 was assigned to her on a Monday or a Tuesday but the family member refused a visit until she saw him later that same week on Thursday, 07/11/24; that she believed this to be a routine new patient visit and denied awareness that he was not a new patient, that there was any concern for suicidality, or that he had been in the inpatient unit; that she and Patient #1 had a really good conversation with life review and he was joking around, talked about the future and was looking forward to their next visit; that she did not ask about firearms or suicidal ideation as part of that assessment; and that if she had known of his suicidal comment she would have changed her approach, that it ";would have been a completely different thing."

Based on Medical Record (MR) review, agency policy and procedure and interviews, it was determined the agency failed to ensure:

1. Education was provided for the use of narcotics in the home

2. A count of the narcotics was completed on each Registered Nurse (RN) visit.

This deficient practice affected 2 of 11 records reviewed including MR # 2, MR # 3, and had the potential to negatively affect all patients served by this agency. 

Findings include:

Hospice Policy Number: PC.M70
Effective 10.1.17
Title: Medications-Use and Disposal of Controlled Substances

...Definitions: Controlled substances-drugs or other material that, because of their potential for abuse, are closely regulated by the Federal government...

POLICY...instructs patient/caregivers in the safe use and disposal of controlled substances...

PROCEDURES: 

1. At the time when controlled substances are ordered, the hospice nurse...

a. provides a copy of...written policies and procedures on the management and disposal of controlled drugs to the patient and...family.

b. discusses the...policies and procedures for managing the safe use and disposal of controlled drugs...

c. documents...that written...procedures for managing controlled drugs were provided and discussed.

d. discuss and document required narcotic count during each scheduled RN (Registered Nurse) visit. The name of the medication and number remaining will be documented...

1. MR # 2 was admitted to hospice on 2/9/22 with diagnoses including Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Chronic Respiratory Failure. 

Review of the Hospice Certification and Plan of Care (POC) dated 2/9/22 revealed an order for Morphine Concentrate 100 milligrams (mg)/5 milliliters (ml). Take 0.5 to 1 ml as directed/prn (as needed) for respiratory distress and severe pain. 

Further review of the POC revealed orders for SN frequency of 2 x a week for 13 weeks. 

Review of the SN Visit Note Reports (VNR) from 2/9/22 through 4/14/22 revealed no documentation of patient/caregiver teaching of the use of the Morphine Concentrate for pain. 

Review of the VNR dated 3/22/22 revealed the RN documented MR # 2 complained of aching and burning right eye pain with current pain score of 3. Further review of the 3/22/22 VNR revealed the RN documented "no" to the question "are narcotics ordered". 

Review of the VNR dated 4/7/22 revealed the RN documented MR # 2 complained of throbbing pain to the right eye at a pain level of 4. Further review of the 4/7/22 VNR revealed the RN documented "no" to the question "are narcotics ordered". 

Review of the SN VNRs dated 2/9/22, 2/10/22, 2/14/22, 2/16/22, 2/22/22, 2/24/22, 3/1/22, 3/3/22, 3/8/22, 3/10/22, 3/15/22, 3/22/22, 3/24/22, 3/29/22, 3/31/22, 4/5/22, 4/7/22, and 4/12/22 revealed no documentation of the narcotic count of the Morphine. 

In an interview conducted on 4/21/22 at 12:20 PM, Employee Identifier (EI) # 2, Director of Quality and Education, confirmed the Morphine was in the home from date of admission and no patient or caregiver education on use had been provided and counts of the narcotic had not been conducted on each visit.

Based on observation, interview and record review, the Hospice Agency (HA, agency providing care to terminally ill patients who have six months or less to live) failed to ensure that the drug profile list (a comprehensive record of a patient's entire medication regimen used by healthcare professionals to manage care and prevent errors) was reviewed for six of 19 sampled patients (Patient 3, Patient 4, Patient 6, Patient 10, Patient 11 and Patient 15) to ensure the following: 1. Two of 19 sampled patients (Patient 3 and Patient 4’s) medications were in accordance with the physician’s order as written in the drug profile list. - Patient 3 did not have melatonin (prescription medication used to help manage certain sleep problems) 5 milligram (mg, unit of measurement) tablet and morphine sulfate (a type of pain medication used to treat moderate to severe pain) 20 milligram per milliliter (mg/mL, unit of measurement) solution available on hand for administration, as ordered by the physician and as written in the patient’s drug profile list. - Patient 3 had simethicone (anti-gas medication used to relieve uncomfortable symptoms of excess gas) 80 mg chewable tablet available on hand instead of simethicone 125 mg chewable tablet as ordered by the physician and as written on the drug profile list. - Patient 3 had losartan potassium (a prescription medication primarily used to treat high blood pressure) 100 mg tablet available on hand instead of losartan potassium 25 mg tablet as ordered by the physician and as written on the drug profile list. - Patient 4 had moxifloxacin hydrochloride (antibiotic used to treat bacterial eye infections) 0.5% ophthalmic solution (eye drops) and furosemide (medication used to help the body get rid of excess salt and water by increasing urine production) 20 mg tablet, take 1 tablet by mouth every day for heart failure, were written in Patient’s 4 drug profile that Patient 4 was currently taking but Patient 4’s caregiver (CG) 2 stated moxifloxacin hydrochloride was discontinued on 9/18/2025 and furosemide was discontinued on 8/27/2025. 2. Four of 19 sampled patients (Patient 3, Patient 10, Patient 11, and Patient 15’s) controlled drugs (drugs with a potential for abuse or dependence, and their manufacture, possession, and use are heavily regulated by the government) were reviewed and counted, to ensure accuracy of administration, with each nurse visit. 3. Two of 19 sampled patients (Patient 3 and Patient 6’s) drug profile list were reviewed to identify duplicate medication orders: - Patient 3 had an order for morphine sulfate 20 mg/ml solution 0.25 ml by mouth every four hours as needed for pain ordered on 10/13/2025 and morphine sulfate 20 mg/ml solution 0.25 ml by mouth every four hours as needed for pain ordered on 12/12/2025. - Patient 6 had an order for Hydrocodone bitartrate and acetaminophen (medication for pain management) 5mg-325 mg tablet by mouth ordered on 8/29/2025 and hydrocodone bitartrate and acetaminophen 5mg-325mg tablet (via gastronomy tube [g-tube, a soft tube placed through the abdominal wall directly in the stomach used to deliver nutrition, fluids, and medication]), ordered 8/29/2025. Atorvastatin (medications to lower cholesterol and triglycerides [fats] levels to help prevent heart disease, chest pain, strokes and heart attacks) 40 mg tablet (by mouth), ordered 8/29/2025 and atorvastatin 40 mg tablet (via g-tube), ordered on 8/29/2025. These failures had the potential to result in medication administration errors and lack of controlled substance accountability, potentially resulting in unsafe medication administration, delayed or inappropriate symptom management, and drug diversion (the illegal redirection of prescription medications from their intended use or patient for abuse, addiction, or financial gain). On 12/18/2025, at 2:37 p.m., the Department called an Immediate Jeopardy (IJ, a situation in which the Hospice Agency’s noncompliance with one or more requirements of participation has caused, or is likely to cause, serious injury, harm, impairment, or death to a patient), in the presence of the agency’s Vice President of Operations (VPO) and National Patient Care Administrator (NPCA) 2, for failure to ensure that the drug profile was reviewed to ensure accuracy for six of 19 sampled patients (Patient 3, Patient 4, Patient 6, Patient 10, Patient 11 and Patient 15). These failures had the potential to result in medication administration errors and lack of controlled substance accountability, potentially resulting in unsafe medication administration, delayed or inappropriate symptom management, and drug diversion (the illegal redirection of prescription medications from their intended use or patient for abuse, addiction, or financial gain). On 12/19/2025 at 4:52 p.m. the HA was unable to submit an acceptable IJ removal plan (includes all actions the agency has taken or will take to immediately address the noncompliance that resulted in or made serious injury, serious harm, serious impairment, or death likely). On 12/19/2025, at 5:04 p.m., the Department completed the survey tasks and conducted an exit conference while onsite in the presence of the VPO, NPCA 2, Administrator and virtual attendees NPCA 1, Senior Vice President of Operations (SVPO) 1 and SVPO 2, with the IJ situations not removed. On 12/29/2025 at 1:58 PM, the agency submitted an acceptable IJ removal plan (include all actions the agency has taken or will take to immediately address the noncompliance that resulted in or made serious injury, serious harm, serious impairment or death likely) was reviewed and accepted. On 12/29/2025, the survey team conducted an onsite visit to the agency and verified the IJ implementation. The IJ was removed on 12/29/2025 at 3:45 p.m., in the presence of the Administrator. 

Findings: 1a. During a review of Patient 3’s “Case Sheet,” (page of the medical chart containing a summary of basic patient information) dated 12/11/2025, the “Case Sheet” indicated the HA admitted Patient 3 on 10/13/2025, with diagnoses that included malignant neoplasm of head of pancreas (aggressive tumor in the pancreas [organ that aides in digestion and blood sugar control] that grows uncontrollably, interfering with normal functions) and hypertension (HTN, high blood pressure) and HTN. During a review of Patient 3’s “Plan of Care (POC),” dated 12/9/2025, the “POC” indicated the following medication orders: - Simethicone 125 mg chewable tablet. Chew one tablet by mouth every 6 hours as needed for gas for abdominal distention. Start date 11/2/2025. - Losartan potassium 25 mg tablet. Take one tablet by mouth every day for high blood pressure and hold for systolic blood pressure (the top number in a blood pressure reading, showing the force in the arteries when the heart beats and pushes blood out) less than 110 for HTN. Start date 10/13/2025. - Melatonin 5 mg tablet. Take 1 tablet by mouth at bedtime for sleep for insomnia. Start date 10/14/2025. - Morphine sulfate 20 mg/mL solution. Take 0.25 mL by mouth every 4 hours as needed for pain. Start date 10/13/2025. During a concurrent observation and interview on 12/12/2025 at 11:40 a.m., Licensed Vocational Nurse (LVN) 1 was observed in Patient 3’s home conducting medication reconciliation (a formal process of creating the most accurate list of a patient's current medications and comparing it to the medications the patient is taking or should be taking to identify and resolve discrepancies). Patient 3 brought out all the medications he was taking and LVN 1 reviewed and compared Patient 3’s medication bottles to the patient’s drug profile list. Patient 3’s melatonin 5 mg tablet and morphine sulfate 20 mg/mL solution were missing from Patient 3’s medications available on hand. Patient 3 stated he brought out all the medications he was taking, and he did not have melatonin and was not using melatonin. Patient 3’s caregiver (CG) 1 stated he told the HA to stop ordering the Morphine because Patient 3 did not use it and the HA continued providing the medication. Patient 3’s CG 1 stated he had thrown Patient 3’s Morphine down the drain. During a concurrent observation at Patient 3’s home and record review on 12/12/2025 at 11:40 a.m., Patient 3’s “Plan of Care,” dated 12/9/2025 was reviewed. The “Plan of Care” indicated Patient 3 have an order for simethicone 125 mg chewable tablet and losartan potassium 25 mg tablet but observed Patient 3 medication on hand were simethicone 80 mg chewable tablet and losartan potassium 100 mg tablet. During an interview on 12/15/2025 at 2:16 p.m. with LVN 1, LVN 1 stated medication reconciliation was done by reviewing a patient’s medication list and comparing the list with the patient’s medications on hand. LVN 1 stated that any discrepancies from the medication reconciliation were reported to the Registered Nurse Case Manager (RNCM) or the physician. LVN 1 stated this process ensures the medications a patient was taking match the medications the hospice agency has on file. LVN 1 stated an accurate medication log ensures proper medication supply and keeps the patient informed on safe medication administration. During a continued interview on 12/15/2025 at 2:16 p.m. with LVN 1, LVN 1 stated that when a patient refuses medication and decides to dispose of it, it would be documented in the patient’s medical record. During an interview on 12/16/2025 at 1:27 p.m. with NPCA 1, NPCA 1 stated that the medication reconciliation process includes comparing a patient’s medication bottles with the patient's medication list to ensure the patient has all the medications listed. NPCA 1 stated that the medication reconciliation process is a review of all medications such as prescribed medication and controlled substances (a drug hose production, possession, and use are strictly monitored by the government due to high potential for abuse or addiction, classified into schedules based on risk to regulate access and prevent misuse). NPCA 1 stated that all the medications on the list must be visualized by the visiting nurse (Licensed Vocational Nurse (LVN) or Registered Nurse (RN). NPCA 1 stated the visiting nurse reviews the medication name, medication dose and the frequency of administration with the patient and then asks the patient if they were still taking the medication. NPCA 1 stated that if a medication was missing, lost, or misplaced the nurse should first clarify with the patient that they were still taking the medication and then contact the physician to verify whether the medication was required. NPCA 1 stated that if a patient’s medication list was not accurate a patient might be taking medications that were no longer necessary. During an interview on 12/16/2025 at 1:36 p.m. with NPCA 1, NPCA 1 stated that if a patient or patient family member verbalized that they do not want to receive morphine, the medication would not be prescribed or an order to discontinue the medication would be obtained from the physician. NPCA 1 stated that if an order for morphine was discontinued, the hospice nurse would provide education about safe disposal of controlled medications to the patient and/or patient family members. During a review of the Hospice Agency’s policy and procedure (P&P) titled, “Pharmacy Process,” (undated), the P&P indicated the following: “Nursing Visit Pharmacological Overview: ensure medication bottles with labels or medication list is at the location of care... Each Nursing Updated Comprehensive Assessment Visits begins with a review of the patient’s Plan of Care (POC) which included current medications... Complete and document patient assessment including... availability of medications. Monitor medication amounts every visit, and order refills to ensure adequate supply in place until next visit... Assess for medication adverse event (an undesired effect of a drug or other type of treatment,) ... Ensure that the pharmacological orders are transcribed onto all appropriate places... update the POC.” “The Chart Medication List should be reviewed during each patient visit and during Interdisciplinary Group to ensure it is up to date including active and discontinued medications.” “Pharmacy Oversight Completed by Physician: prescribed, over the counter, herbal, and alternate medications that could affect drug therapy are reviewed by the physician to include effectiveness of drug therapy, drug side effects, actual or potential drug interactions, duplicate drug therapy, drug therapy associated with laboratory monitoring... If any medication issues are identified the physician should utilize the pharmacy or pharmacist as a resource.” 1b. During a review of Patient 4’s “Case Sheet,” dated 12/11/2025, indicated the HA admitted Patient 4 on 7/2/2025 for the diagnoses including but not limited to cerebrovascular disease (a group of conditions that affect blood flow and the blood vessels in the brain), and vascular dementia (impaired supply of blood to the brain, such as may be caused by a series of small strokes). During a concurrent observation, interview and record review, on 12/12/2025 at 12:15 p.m., with Registered Nurse (RN) 3 in Patient 4’s home, Patient 4’s medication reconciliation was conducted with RN 3 during Patient 4’s home visit. Patient 4’s “Medication List,” dated 12/11/2025, indicated the following medications: Moxifloxacin Hcl 0.5%, instill 1 drop into left eye four (4) times daily for bacterial eye infection, start date of 7/2/2025. Furosemide 20mg tablet, take 1 tablet by mouth every day for heart failure, start date of 7/2/2025. Patient 4’s CG 2 brought out the medications and stated the patient’s ophthalmologist discontinued the moxifloxacin on 9/18/2025 and the patient’s cardiologist discontinued the furosemide on 8/27/2025. During a concurrent interview and record review on 12/16/2025 at 12:39 p.m. with NPCA 1, NPCA 1 stated Patient 4’s “Medication List” dated 12/11/2025, indicated the moxifloxacin (antibiotic for bacterial infection) and furosemide (medication to increase urine output) were listed as Patient 4’s active medications. NPCA 1 stated medication reconciliation should be done by license personnel with patients and family at every home visit. Based on interview and record review, the agency failed to implement the policy and procedure related to allegation of abuse for one of 20 sampled patients (Patient 13) when the patient allegation of abuse was not reported immediately by the hospice supervisor (HS B) to the hospice administrator.

This failure had the potential to cause psychological distress to the patient and family.

Findings:

Patient 13 was admitted to the agency on 7/30/2021 with diagnoses of Parkinson's disease (a progressive nervous system disorder that affects movement) and diastolic heart failure (condition where the lower left chamber of the heart (left ventricle) was not able to fill properly with blood).

Review of Patient 13's nurse's note dated 8/3/2021, indicated Patient 13 was an 88 year old female with Parkinson's disease, bed bound for three years and declined over the last several days.

Review of Patient 13's situation, background, assessment and recommendation (SBAR, a mechanism which provides a framework for communication between members of the health care team about a patient's condition) dated 10/25/2022, indicated the HS B had a home visit on 10/11/2021 for Patient 13. Patient 13's responsible party (RP, the individual who makes decisions) was suffering from caregiver burnout and Patient 13 was transferred to a skilled nursing facility (SNF, an in-patient rehabilitation and medical treatment center staffed with trained medical professionals) for respite care (temporary care provided to caregiver). The SBAR indicated the RP was unhappy regarding rough handling at the SNF which caused bruising to Patient 13. The SBAR also indicated Patient 13's RP was charged on his credit card in advance for the extra days Patient 13 planned to stay at the SNF.

Review of the complaint risk report for Patient 13 dated 10/25/21, indicated the caller stated the agency referred his wife to the skilled nursing facility (SNF). The caller stated after the first day she was maltreated and the service was really bad. Caller stated his wife had a bruise on her arm after going to the facility and the caller paid out of pocket money for an extra five days. The caller also stated the SNF did not give her medication and she had a wet diaper on for more than a day.

During an interview with HS B on 2/16/2022 at 4:40 p.m., HS B stated she went on a home visit on 10/11/2021 for Patient 13. During the home visit, the RP was angry due to the SNF staff who caused the bruising and rough handling for Patient 13. HS B stated she completed the SBAR report on 10/25/2022 and she should have reported the allegation of abuse sooner.

During an interview with the Service Director (SD) on 2/17//2022 at 4 p.m., the SD confirmed HS B should have immediately evaluated the abuse allegation for reporting.

Review of the Agency policy dated 10/29/2020, "Assessment and Reporting of Suspected Abuse/Neglect", indicated all alleged violation involving maltreatment, neglect, mental, sexual, physical abuse, including injuries of unknown source, and misappropriation of patient property by anyone furnishing services on behalf of the hospice are reported immediately by the hospice employee and the contracted staff to the hospice administrator. Reports must continue to be made by telephone immediately or as soon as practically possible. A written report must be submitted within two (2) working days to the appropriate agency.

Based on interview and record review, the agency failed to notify the Department of an allegation of mistreatment for 1 of 2 sampled patients (1). 

As a result, the Department could not verify the patient's safety. 

Findings:

Patient 1 was admitted to the agency on 1/26/22 with diagnoses which included malignant neoplasm of the biliary tract (cancer in the slender tubes that carry the digestive fluid bile through the liver) per the agency's Case Sheet.

A review of Patient 1's clinical record was conducted. Per the Home Health Aide/Homemaker Note, dated 3/29/22, Certified Home Health Aide (CHHA) 1 documented that she tried to take Patient 1's shirt off and complained of pain when CHHA 1 touched Patient 1, so CHHA 1 requested to see the bottle of medication to see if Patient 1 could take pain medication at this time, the family member got mad and asked CHHA 1 to leave [Patient 1] alone. 

On 5/11/22 at 9:55 A.M., an interview was conducted with the Patient Care Administrator (PCA) 1. PCA 1 stated on 3/29/22, when CHHA 1 was supposed to provide a bed bath, there was no allegation of abuse or mistreatment. PCA 1 said the family member requested CHHA 1 to leave their house. PCA 1 stated mid-April when Adult Protective Service called and filed a complaint against CHHA 1. PCA 1 said the investigation and in-progress. 

On 5/12/22 at 1:50 P.M., an interview was conducted with the CHHA 1. CHHA 1 stated she was unfamiliar with Patient 1, and on 3/29/22, she was supposed to provide a bed bath to Patient 1. CHHA 1 said she did not ask Patient 1 about pain before removing the clothes, and when she lifted Patient 1's arm to remove the clothing, Patient 1's complained of pain, so she inquired about giving Patient 1 pain medicine and the family member got mad. The family member asked CHHA 1 to leave the house. CHHA 1 explained herself to the family member and called PCA 1. 

On 5/12/22 at 4:43 P.M., an interview was conducted with Skilled Nurse (SN) 1. SN 1 stated she was the nurse that visited Patient 1 the next day after CHHA 1. SN 1 said the family member told her that CHHA 1 was too rough with Patient 1. SN 1 stated she listened to the family member but did not ask further questions as she did not want to be involved. SN 1 further said the family member told her the agency was aware of the incident. 

On 6/6/22 at 3 P.M., an interview was conducted with PCA 1. PCA 1 stated she did not report the allegation of abuse to the Department and should have been reported. 

On 6/14/22 at 1 P.M., an interview was conducted with the Social Worker (SW). The SW stated on 4/26/22 at 3:30 P.M., she received a report from the Adult Protective Services about CHHA 1 mishandling Patient 1 and relayed the information to PCA 1 the same day. 

There was no documented evidence that the allegation of mistreatment was reported to the Department by the agency. 

Per the agency's Management Standard, dated 2021, titled Reportable Events, "... the program senior management is responsible for ensuring suspicion is reported no later than 24 hours after notification of the suspicion. The report must be made directly to local law enforcement and the state survey agency within 24 hours..."

Based on clinical record reviews, review of agency policies and interview with agency personnel for one of two patients (Patients #1) in the survey sample, the hospice agency failed to ensure the patient's right to be free from abuse or neglect and failed to follow the agency policies. The finding includes:
 

Patient #1 elected the Hospice benefit on 12/17/2023 with diagnoses that included muscle weakness, difficulty walking, severe protein-calorie malnutrition, dysphagia, seizures, cardiac disease, and dementia. The physicians orders dated 12/17/2023 included nursing services once a week for symptom management and assessments, home health aide services once a week for assistance with activities of living, and a social worker evaluation for caregiver support.
 
Review of Patient #1s hospice start of care summary dated 12/17/2023, identified Patient #1 was hospitalized after having a seizure, admitted to a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation services and discharged to a private home to reside with a caregiver. The hospice agencys Medical Director approved end of life services related to Patient #1s severe protein-calorie malnutrition after a twenty-six-pound weight loss since 11/2023. The start of care summary further identified the home environment presented with no safety issues and the caregiver was assisting the Patient with ambulation, transfers from the chair to the bed, dressing, bathing, incontinence care, housekeeping, meal preparation, shopping, and laundry. The admitting Registered Nurse (RN) identified no signs of neglect or abuse and the caregiver had no limitations but would need respite care or sitter services to meet the Patients increasing care needs.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note dated 01/09/2024, identified an as needed visit was made related to Patient #1s increased care needs, an unclean living environment, and the caregiver leaving the Patient home alone after being advised not to by the primary case manager RN #1. Social Worker #1 offered the Patients caregiver additional support in the home, but the caregiver declined.
 
Review of RN #1s clinical notes dated 01/18/2024, 01/26/2024, and 01/30/2024 identified providing Patient #1s caregiver with education about safety concerns in the home, and the importance of not leaving the Patient alone for any period due to increased confusion and weakness.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note date 01/30/2024, identified Social Worker #1 spoke with the Patients caregiver about the Patients increased care needs, safety concerns, and the need for an additional caregiver in the home. The Patients caregiver declined assistance and indicated having people who could assist if needed.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note dated 02/15/2024, identified a joint visit was conducted with RN #1. Patient #1 was anxious, agitated and the caregiver appeared stressed, but continued to decline the need for supportive services.
 
Review of the Administrators case coordination note dated 02/21/2024, identified contacting Patient #1s caregiver on 02/21/2024 to discuss concerns for the unclean home environment, the caregivers ability to safely manage the Patients medications and leaving the Patient home alone.
 
Review of RN #2s clinical note dated 02/28/2024, identified Patient #1s caregiver contacted the hospice agencys answering service to report the Patient was confused and vomiting. Upon arrival to the Patients home, RN #2 identified the Patient was lying on the floor covered in feces and vomit. Patient #1s caregiver indicated the Patient may have eaten old food from the wastebasket which resulted in him/her vomiting. RN #2 advised the caregiver that Patient #1 needed to be transferred to the hospital bed and cleaned. The caregiver indicated the Patient sleeps on the couch, and he/she sleeps in the hospital bed provided by the hospice. RN #2 assisted the Patient to the hospital bed and attempted to clean the Patient, but the caregiver lacked necessary supplies such as washcloths, a wash basin, clean clothing, or linen. RN #2 cleaned the Patient with paper towels. RN #2 left the home and contacted SCS #1 to report the unsafe and concerning conditions in the Patients home.
 
Interview and review of Patient #1s clinical record with RN #1 on 03/11/2024 10:40 AM, identified the Patients home environment as cluttered, with unclean surfaces, a strong odor present and waste overflowing from the wastebasket. RN #1 indicated the Patient appeared disheveled and the caregiver was unable to safely manage the Patients medications. RN #1 identified the caregiver reported having weapons in the home and would become agitated toward the hospice staff and the Patient. RN #1 and Social Worker #1 reported the concerns to the Administrator and the Supervisor of Clinical Services (SCS) #1 at the beginning of February 2024. Social Worker #1 left a message for Protective Services for the Elderly on 02/21/2024 and filed a report with Protective Services for the Elderly on 02/27/2024. The Administrator and SCS #1 advised hospice clinicians to not return to Patient #1s home but did not discharge the Patient.
 
Interview and review of Patient #1s clinical record with the Administrator on 03/11/2024 at 12:00 PM, identified RN #1 and Social Worker #1 reported the Patients living conditions as unsanitary and the caregiver was unable to safely care for the Patient. The Administrator indicated the Patient was not discharged for cause from the hospice agency, but clinicians were advised not to return to Patient #1s home after Protective Service for the Elderly was contacted on 02/21/2024. The Administrator identified Patient #1 was visited by hospice clinicians on 02/15/2024 and did not receive another visit until 02/28/2024. The Administrator identified hospice services were not provided for twelve days (02/16/2024 to 02/27/2024), as the agency was waiting for directives from the Regional Managers of Clinical Services. The Administrator indicated after RN #2 reported concerns for Patient #1's safety on 02/28/2024, SCS #1 contacted the police and the Patient was removed from the home.
 
Interview with the Regional Vice President of Clinical Services on 03/11/2024 1:00 PM, identified the hospice agency failed to follow the Assessment and Reporting of Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation policy, Safety Management policy and the Discharge for Cause policy. The Regional Vice President of Clinical Service indicated the hospice agency failed to immediately report suspected abuse and/or neglect to the appropriate state agency, failed to coordinate care by having the Patient immediately removed from the unsafe situation, then discharge the Patient from the hospice agency due to compromised patient and staff safety. Additionally, the Vice President of Clinical Services identified the hospice agency staff failed to ensure the Patient's safety by not providing oversight of the Patient for twelve days. 
 
Review of the agencys Assessment and Reporting of Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation policy, identified agency staff would assess, identify, and intervene on the behalf of victims of abuse and neglect and exploitation in an appropriate and professional manner. All cases of alleged, observed, or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation would be investigated by the agency and appropriate interventions would be initiated, including mandated reported requirements in accordance with the state regulations. When abuse or neglect is suspected, the hospice staff would report the incident to the Administrator immediately and complete an incident report. If the patient is felt to be in immediate danger, the staff member would first ensure the patients personal safety and notify the Administrator. The Administrator would immediately start an investigation and notify the appropriate state agencies.
 
Review of the agencys Discharge for Cause policy, identified the agency reserved the right to discharge patients for cause if all attempts to remediate the situation failed. There may be circumstances in which a hospice would be unable to continue to provide hospice care to a patient. These situations would include issues where the patient safety or hospice staff safety was compromised. The agency must make referrals to all relevant state agencies. The hospice would assist in coordinating continued care for the patient.
 
Review of the agencys Safety Management policy, identified upon admission and at every visit, all patients would be assessed for falls and the home environment would also be evaluated for safety issues. Suspected or confirmed patient abuse or neglect would be reported to specified state agencies and living conditions which place patients in eminent danger.

Review of Patient 13's situation, background, assessment and recommendation (SBAR, a mechanism which provides a framework for communication between members of the health care team about a patient's condition) dated 10/25/2022, indicated the HS B had a home visit on 10/11/2021 for Patient 13. Patient 13's responsible party (RP, the individual who makes decisions) was suffering from caregiver burnout and Patient 13 was transferred to a skilled nursing facility (SNF, an in-patient rehabilitation and medical treatment center staffed with trained medical professionals) for respite care (temporary care provided to caregiver). The SBAR indicated the RP was unhappy regarding rough handling at the SNF which caused bruising to Patient 13. The SBAR also indicated Patient 13's RP was charged on his credit card in advance for the extra days Patient 13 planned to stay at the SNF.

Review of the complaint risk report for Patient 13 dated 10/25/21, indicated the caller stated the agency referred his wife to the skilled nursing facility (SNF). The caller stated after the first day she was maltreated and the service was really bad. Caller stated his wife had a bruise on her arm after going to the facility and the caller paid out of pocket money for an extra five days. The caller also stated the SNF did not give her medication and she had a wet diaper on for more than a day.

During an interview with HS B on 2/16/2022 at 4:40 p.m., HS B stated she went on a home visit on 10/11/2021 for Patient 13. During the home visit, the RP was angry due to the SNF staff who caused the bruising and rough handling for Patient 13. HS B stated she completed the SBAR report on 10/25/2022 and she should have reported the allegation of abuse sooner.

During an interview with the Service Director (SD) on 2/17//2022 at 4 p.m., the SD confirmed HS B should have immediately evaluated the abuse allegation for reporting.

Review of the Agency policy dated 10/29/2020, "Assessment and Reporting of Suspected Abuse/Neglect", indicated all alleged violation involving maltreatment, neglect, mental, sexual, physical abuse, including injuries of unknown source, and misappropriation of patient property by anyone furnishing services on behalf of the hospice are reported immediately by the hospice employee and the contracted staff to the hospice administrator. Reports must continue to be made by telephone immediately or as soon as practically possible. A written report must be submitted within two (2) working days to the appropriate agency.

Based on clinical record reviews, interviews with agency staff, review of the agency's complaint log, personnel record reviews and review of agency policy titled " Reporting Abuse and Neglect or Exploitation" revisited 9/21, it was determined the agency failed to report allegations of physical and verbal abuse to the State agency in a timely manner. Review of personnel records revealed two reports alleging physical and verbal abuse of three inpatient unit (IPU) patients by an Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA #AA) in three of three patient (P) (P#1, P#2 and P#3) records reviewed. 

1. Patient #1 was admitted on 2/18/21,with the hospice diagnosis of senile degeneration of the brain . P#1's clinical record was reviewed for certification period 10/16/21 to 12/14/21. P#1 was at the agency's inpatient unit (IPU) for respite care from 10/23/21 to 10/28/21. The reported documentation of alleged abuse by CNA #AA against P#1 occurred on 10/26/21, and was reported to the agency's IPU Clinical Manager Licensed Practical (LPN) #CC on 11/1/21, per an agency provided document attached to another agency document dated 11/4/21, titled "Employee Coaching/Counseling". Attached to the "Employee Coaching/Counseling" form was a handwritten statement provided by CNA #BB. The handwritten statement documents CNA #BB observed CNA #AA on 10/26/21, "grab the patient right arm and bend the patient arm back more than once. The patient yelled out while (CNA #AA) bend (sic) arm." CNA #BB's documentation also reports that CNA #AA "pinch the patient nose" and called P#1 a "bitch". 

Patient #1 did not receive a visit by a Registered Nurse (RN) to complete an assessment for possible physical or psychosocial injuries immediately after the agency having knowledge of the incident. A routine comprehensive health assessment was documented as completed on 11/4/21. The agency provided the surveyor with documentation of the agency's IPU Clinical Manager LPN #CC and the agency Director of Clinical Strategy and Compliance Registered Nurse (RN #DD) on 11/4/21, counseling and a human resources corrective action plan entitled "Employee Coaching/ Counseling" that was provided to CNA #AA on 11/4/21. However, the agency did not provide evidence of documentation to include reporting the alleged incident to P#1's family or physician. There was no documented evidence provided to the surveyor to confirm the agency conducted an investigation of the alleged incident.

2. Patient #2 was admitted on 6/28/21, with the hospice diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease . P#2's clinical record was reviewed for certification period 9/26/21 to 12/24/21. P#2 was at the agency's IPU for respite care from 10/27/21 to 11/1/21. The reported documentation of alleged abuse by CNA #AA against P#2 and was reported to the agency's IPU Clinical Manager LPN #CC on 11/1/21, per an agency provided document attached to another agency document dated 11/4/21, titled "Employee Coaching/Counseling". Attached to the "Employee Coaching/Counseling" form was a handwritten statement provided by CNA #BB. CNA #BB provided handwritten documentation in which CNA #BB documents observing CNA #AA on 10/30/21, "struck the patient on the head and patient began yelling loud." The report also documented P#2 "start swinging at us with her hands, so after that (CNA #AA) grab patient right arm and bend it back to were (sic) the patient said, 'YOU HURTING ME'." The report also documents, "Then the patient said something to were (sic) (CNA #AA) was about to get at (P#2) again so I (CNA # BB) jump in front of (CNA #AA) and said no please no just leave her. So, after that we (CNA #AA and CNA#BB) pulled the patient up in the bed and I got the heck out of the room and went to the nurse station and told the charge nurse." During the survey the agency made available to the surveyor an email dated 11/3/21, at 12:16 p.m. The email was addressed to IPU Clinical Manager LPN #CC from IPU Charge Nurse RN #EE stating: "On 10/30/21, this nurse went to administer medication to (P#2) who was displaying agitation as evidenced by continual screaming. (CNA #BB) and (CNA #AA) were already in the room. As this nurse administered said medication, patient attempted to grab at said nurse. (CNA #AA) attempted to hold (P#2) arms back, bending one in the process. Patient proceeded to state 'Ouch, you're hurting me'. CNA #AA let the patient loose."

Patient #2 did not receive a visit by a RN to complete an assessment for possible physical or psychosocial injuries immediately after the agency having knowledge of the incident. The agency provided the surveyor with documentation by the agency's IPU Clinical Manager LPN #CC and the agency Director of Clinical Strategy and Compliance RN #DD dated 11/4/21. The documentation contained counseling and a human resources corrective action plan entitled "Employee Coaching/ Counseling" that was provided to CNA #AA on 11/4/21. However, there was no documented evidence on the document of reporting the alleged incident to P#2's family or physician. No documentaton evidence was provided to the surveyor to confirm that an investigation was done regarding the alleged incident.

3. Patient #3 was admitted on 3/1/21, with the hospice diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease . P#3's clinical record was reviewed for certification period 4/30/21 to 6/28/21. The report regarding alleged physical abuse against P#3 was made by an anonymous agency staff member, who reported the incident to the hospice agency on 6/14/21. The alleges the incident took place on 6/4/21. The description of the occurrence in the agency report documented that CNA #AA was providing supervision to P#3. Based on clinical record reviews and review of agency policy titled, "Reporting Abuse and Neglect or Exploitation, the agency failed to provide nursing care and services by a Registered Nurse (RN) or under the supervision of a (RN) for three of three patients (P) (P#1, P#2, P#3) records reviewed for abuse allegations.

1. Patient #1 was admitted on 2/18/21, with the hospice diagnosis of senile degeneration of the brain . P#1's clinical record was reviewed for certification period 10/16/21 to 12/14/21. P#1 was at the agency's inpatient unit (IPU) from 10/23/21 to 10/28/21, for respite care. The agency received a handwritten document from Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA #BB) reporting physical and verbal abuse towards P#1 by CNA #AA on 11/1/21, while P#1 received care at the IPU. The handwritten document alleges the abuse occurred on 10/26/21. Although the agency received the document on 11/1/21, from CNA #BB, the agency could not provide evidence than an updated comprehensive assessment was completed by an agency RN until 11/4/21. 

2. Patient #2 was admitted on 6/28/21,with the hospice diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease . P#2's clinical record was reviewed for certification period 9/26/21 to 12/24/21. P#2 was at the agency's IPU from 10/27/21 to 11/1/21 for respite care. The agency received a handwritten document from CNA #BB reporting physical abuse towards P#2 by CNA #AA on 11/1/21, while P#2 was receiving care at the IPU. The handwritten document alleges the abuse occurred on 10/30/21. Although, the agency received the report on 11/1/21, from CNA #BB, the agency could not provide evidence that an updated comprehensive assessment was completed by an agency RN until 11/3/21. The agency's policy, entitled "Rights and Ethics 401", revised 9/21, requires that the patients's medical record will reflect the assessment, interventions and documentation of appropriate referrals. The policy also states that the abuse will be reported to the team manager and Vice President of Clinical Services immediately. CNA #BB failed to provide the report immediately per the agency's policy.

3. P#3 was admitted on 3/1/21, with the hospice diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease . P#3's clinical record was reviewed for certification period 4/30/21 to 6/28/21. P#3 was at the agency's IPU from 6/3/21 to 6/7/21, for respite care. On 6/14/21, the agency received an anonymous written report of abuse towards P#3 on the agency form entitled "Occurrence Report/Opportunity for Improvement", revised 6/21. The report alleges the abuse occurred on 6/4/21. The report was submitted to the agency by RN #FF on the agency provided form but contained documentation that the actual reporter was anonymous. 

The agency failed to follow its written policy, entitled "Rights and Ethics 401", revised 9/21, #8 which includes the patients medical record will reflect the assessement, interventions and referral. And #9, if abuse by a Hospice Savannah employee is suspected, the team manager and Vice President of Clinical Services will be notified immediately. The employee will be reassigned from direct clinical care until and internal investigation can be completed. The agency received the report on 6/14/21, and P#3 received a nursing assessment on 6/1521. However, the nursing assessment did not contain any documentation of the alleged abuse. 

The agency Administrator, Vice President of Clinical Services and the Director of Clinical Strategy and Clinical Compliance were informed of the above facts in an interview at the agency at 4:00 p.m. on 11/23/21.

Based on observation, review of policies and procedures and interview, it was determined the hospice inpatient unit staff failed to: 

1. Dispose of controlled medications for expired and discharged patients. 

2. Follow their policy for disposal of controlled substances. 

3. Ensure medications were kept secure.

4. Maintain pharmacy records and monthly reports as directed per policy. 

This deficient practice had the potential to affect all patients served by the hospice. 

Findings include:

Revised date: 2/23/21

When appropriate, (Shepherd's Cove Hospice) will provide a Comfort Kit to hospice patients. The Comfort Kit will contain medications for the management of pain and symptoms that may arise during a crisis.

Procedure:

2. The family will be instructed to pick up the sealed kit from the pharmacy once the order has been faxed and filled...

9. At the time of the patient's death or discharge, the remaining contents of the Comfort Kit will be destroyed as per agency policy. Each individual medication destroyed will be listed on the Medication Disposal/Refusal form. 

Agency policy: Drugs and Biological's
Revised date: 2/23/21

Practices: It is the policy of (Shepherd's Cove Hospice), that all necessary drugs and biological's...identified in the plan of care... are provided by the agency... and that all drugs and biological's are handled in compliance with appropriate state and federal regulations...

Inpatient Drugs and Biological's

Administration of controlled medications

"Stat" Medication Cabinet...

5. The consulting pharmacist:

1. Controlled substances and other medications unused because the medication is discontinued or because the patient is discharged, deceased, or transferred are destroyed with a reasonable period of time not to exceed 30 days...

A tour of the Hospice Inpatient Unit (HIPU) medication room was conducted on 12/7/21 at 10:35 AM to 12:15 PM and 1:00 PM to 3:30 PM with Employee Identifier (EI) # 10, Registered Nurse (RN). The surveyor observed the following:

At 10:45 AM inspection of the second locked cabinet revealed 14 Comfort Kits (CK). Each of the CK's was labeled with 13 different patient names, 2 of the CK's were labeled with the same patient's name.

The surveyor asked EI # 10, "Why are there so many CK's here? And why does 1 patient have 2 CK's in this cabinet?"

EI # 10 explained, "When a patient is admitted to Shepard's Cove Hospice, the doctor orders a Comfort Kit, the pharmacy delivers the Comfort Kit to the HIPU and then the home care nurse picks it up and takes it to the patient's home." EI # 10 added, "If there's a problem in the home like abusing medications, the home nurse will leave it here and get it when needed. And some nursing homes won't let you keep the CK at their facility." "I think (unsampled patient) has been discharged and re-admitted and discharged a couple of times, that's why he/she has 2 CK's in here."

The surveyor compared the names written on the CK's with the current patient and discharged patient list which revealed 7 current patients (1 patient had 2 CK's) and 6 patients had been discharged or expired. The discharge/expired dates ranged from 6/10/21 to 10/29/21. (All dates were greater than 30 days.)

At 2:10 PM the surveyor observed EI # 10 prepare medication for administration and observed the locked medication cabinets in the medication room were unlocked.

On 12/7/21 at 3:30 PM, in the medication room, the surveyor asked EI # 7, Chief Nursing Officer, "Are you aware there are 14 CK's housed in the HIPU? Why are the CK's at the HIPU for home care patients?" EI # 7 replied, "No, I didn't know they were there. If the patient doesn't want the CK's in the home, we keep them here. Then when needed, the home care nurse delivers it to the home." EI # 7 further confirmed CK's are ordered on admission to hospice and not "when appropriate" as directed in agency policy; there were 14 CK's (for home care patients and discharged /expired greater than 30 days) currently in the cabinet; and confirmed the doors for the controlled medications were not locked but should be locked at all times.

A telephone interview was conducted on 12/9/21 at 10:55 AM with EI # 12, Contract Pharmacist. EI # 12 was asked, "Are you aware the Inpatient Unit (IPU) has 14 CK's in the cabinet beside the STAT medication cabinet?" EI # 12 response was, "No ma'am, I did not." EI # 12 went on to say, "We do medication destruction every 3 weeks to a month. I leave it up to the them (the staff) to put medications in the box."

The surveyor asked "Who is we?" EI # 12 referred to EI # 3, IPU Clinical Director and said, "She (EI # 3) keeps up with all of the documentation of what I destroy. And I destroy it, which I disagree with, but that's the regulation. I make sure they have enough controlled medications in the STAT cabinet." 

The surveyor asked EI # 12, "Do you keep copies of what is destroyed at the HIPU? Present monthly reports for quality assurance?" EI # 12 answered, "I don't keep the records. She (EI # 3) keeps up with the destruction log for medications. I do not submit any monthly reports." 

In an interview conducted on 12/9/21 at 2:45 PM, EI # 7 confirmed the above findings. The HIPU / pharmacist failed to secure, destroy, inventory all controlled medications, prepare monthly reports and maintain records as stated per policy.
