APS report filed again yesterday due to ongoing safety concerns . . ."
Review of P15's "Client Coordination Notes Report," dated 01/14/25, written by Social Worker (SW)2 and provided by the facility, revealed, ". . . PC [phone call] to . . . APS investigator . . . we discussed difference between taking in responsibility for pt by [family member] and exploitation. We discussed solutions like private paid CGs, public fiduciary, [Arizona Medicaid]. We discussed the need to care for patients and what neglect looks like. [Social Worker] gave examples of [family member]'s behaviors, [family member] not hiring CGs, [family member] asking to not have house heated due to high cost, pt not having food at home . . ."
Review of P15's entire clinical record revealed no documented evidence APS had been notified of P15's unsafe living situation and vulnerability from 09/11/24 until 11/26/24, when contact was first made with APS. There was no documented evidence that law enforcement had been notified at any time.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 10:04 AM, RN6, the case manager for P15, stated he/she had identified "pretty quickly" that P15 was unsafe by himself/herself. RN6 stated hospice staff talked with the family member and tried to do what they could to help get more help for P15. RN6 stated he/she believed SW2 had filed a case with APS during November 2024. RN6 was asked what the agency's policy was on mandatory reporting. RN6 stated, "I'm a nurse, and it [suspicions of neglect and patients being in unsafe situations] has to be reported." RN6 was asked why P15's situation was not reported to APS until November 2024. RN6 stated P15 had caregivers and people checking in. RN6 stated he/she was "trying to give the [family member] the chance to come around." RN6 stated he/she believed law enforcement had been notified as well but could not say that for certain. RN6 stated, "We have just been kind of monitoring. I was retriggered to do it [file a case with APS] last week. I text the [family member] every week. [He/she] doesn't want to hear from me. Doesn't want to talk to us. I refiled because something needs to be done." RN6 stated P6's situation had been discussed during IDG (Interdisciplinary Group) meetings.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 11:04 AM, SW1 stated APS did not have an enforcement arm, and APS would tell a person to call local law enforcement if a patient was in immediate danger. SW1 stated calling law enforcement was a case-by-case situation, but if you could not take care of yourself, it was a "good argument" to call law enforcement at the same time you called APS. SW1 stated, "If you determine that a person is a vulnerable adult, you call [APS and law enforcement]. Whether they do anything or not." The surveyor reviewed the 09/11/24 "Visit Note" for P15 with SW1. SW1 stated, "I would consider that to be a vulnerable adult."
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 12:51 PM, SW2, who was the Social Worker assigned to P15, was asked why APS was not notified immediately when it was determined P15 was unsafe and a vulnerable adult. SW2 stated P15's family member had told the RN case manager that he/she would see if changes could be made but they never would and that the family member said that he/she would try options to help P15 qualify for long-term care placement and that never happened. SW2 stated the agency was hoping for P15 to qualify for Medicaid benefits but that would take at least 45 days to occur. SW2 was asked if law enforcement had been notified. SW2 stated law enforcement would be notified if there was an immediate danger. SW2 defined immediate danger as either a threat to a patient's own health or someone else's health and their well-being.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 1:37 PM, the Director of Clinical Services (DCS) was asked what the agency's policy was on mandatory reporting. He/she stated, "Call APS." The DCS was asked when APS should be notified, he/she stated, "When it becomes apparent that we cannot get results in a timely manner. If we think there is exploitation or neglect, it would be immediate." The DCS was asked if P15 was a vulnerable adult. He/she stated, "[He/she] has declined. In the beginning [he/she] had some odd and eccentric behaviors, and [he/she] became more vulnerable."
Review of the Arizona Adult Protective Services website, located at https://des.az.gov/services/basic-needs/adult-protective-services/report-adult-abuse, revealed, ". . . Arizona Adult Protective Services (APS) investigates reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults. APS may also become involved when there is a claim of self-neglect, which is when an adult with physical or mental impairments is not able to meet their basic needs (such as food, shelter, health care, managing money, etc.), which then impacts the adults physical health, mental health or general safety. The goal of APS is to prioritize an adults right to make their own decisions while keeping them safe.
APS tries to support the vulnerable adults in their current home, and to augment the skills they need to take care of themselves by providing services that can help with challenges the adult may be having. However, APS must always balance the need to protect the safety of the vulnerable adult with the adults right to make their own decisions.
APS does not conduct safety checks, but local law enforcement does. Law enforcement and APS work together, and if law enforcement believes an individual is a vulnerable adult, they will contact APS . . ."
Review of the Arizonia Adult Protective Services website, located at https://des.az.gov/services/basic-needs/adult-protective-services/mandated-reporters, revealed, ". . . According to A.R.S. 46-454 (A-D)(link is external), the following individuals are required to report or cause reports to be made to a peace officer or to the Adult Protective Services Central Intake Unit. The reports should be made immediately by phone or online . . . Medical personnel including a physician, physician assistant, registered nurse practitioner, licensed practical or registered nurse, certified nursing assistant, emergency medical technician, home health provider, hospital intern or resident, surgeon, dentist, psychiatrist, psychologist, pharmacist, speech, physical or occupational therapist, long-term care provider, social worker, peace officer, medical examiner, guardian, conservator, fire protection personnel, developmental disabilities provider, employee of the Department of Economic Security or other person who has responsibility for the care of a vulnerable adult . . ."
Review of the agency's policy titled, "Assessment of Possible Abuse/Neglect," dated May 2024, revealed, ". . . Neglect: Failure of a caretaker to supply the patient with the necessary food, clothing, shelter, healthcare, or supervision, or the absence or likelihood of an absence of the necessary food, clothing, shelter, health care, or supervision for a patient . . . Individual Mandated to Report: A professional or the professional's delegate who is engaged in the care of patients, or in education, social services, law enforcement, or in any of the related occupations, who had knowledge of the abuse or neglect of a patient, or who has reasonable cause to believe that a patient is being or has been abused or neglected . . . Any clinician who discovers, within the course of rendering care, any suspected abuse or neglect will immediately report such occurrences to his/her immediate supervisor . . . The clinician will submit a verbal report of the suspected abuse/neglect to the proper authorities in accordance with state law and complete a suspected abuse and/or neglect investigation report within 24 hours of the incident . . . If patient is in immediate jeopardy, the proper authorities will be contacted by the clinician immediately as required by state or local law . . ."

Based on clinical record reviews, review of agency policies and interview with agency personnel for one of two patients (Patients #1) in the survey sample, the hospice agency failed to ensure the patient's right to be free from abuse or neglect and failed to follow the agency policies. The finding includes:
 

Patient #1 elected the Hospice benefit on 12/17/2023 with diagnoses that included muscle weakness, difficulty walking, severe protein-calorie malnutrition, dysphagia, seizures, cardiac disease, and dementia. The physicians orders dated 12/17/2023 included nursing services once a week for symptom management and assessments, home health aide services once a week for assistance with activities of living, and a social worker evaluation for caregiver support.
 
Review of Patient #1s hospice start of care summary dated 12/17/2023, identified Patient #1 was hospitalized after having a seizure, admitted to a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation services and discharged to a private home to reside with a caregiver. The hospice agencys Medical Director approved end of life services related to Patient #1s severe protein-calorie malnutrition after a twenty-six-pound weight loss since 11/2023. The start of care summary further identified the home environment presented with no safety issues and the caregiver was assisting the Patient with ambulation, transfers from the chair to the bed, dressing, bathing, incontinence care, housekeeping, meal preparation, shopping, and laundry. The admitting Registered Nurse (RN) identified no signs of neglect or abuse and the caregiver had no limitations but would need respite care or sitter services to meet the Patients increasing care needs.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note dated 01/09/2024, identified an as needed visit was made related to Patient #1s increased care needs, an unclean living environment, and the caregiver leaving the Patient home alone after being advised not to by the primary case manager RN #1. Social Worker #1 offered the Patients caregiver additional support in the home, but the caregiver declined.
 
Review of RN #1s clinical notes dated 01/18/2024, 01/26/2024, and 01/30/2024 identified providing Patient #1s caregiver with education about safety concerns in the home, and the importance of not leaving the Patient alone for any period due to increased confusion and weakness.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note date 01/30/2024, identified Social Worker #1 spoke with the Patients caregiver about the Patients increased care needs, safety concerns, and the need for an additional caregiver in the home. The Patients caregiver declined assistance and indicated having people who could assist if needed.
 
Review of Social Worker #1s clinical note dated 02/15/2024, identified a joint visit was conducted with RN #1. Patient #1 was anxious, agitated and the caregiver appeared stressed, but continued to decline the need for supportive services.
 
Review of the Administrators case coordination note dated 02/21/2024, identified contacting Patient #1s caregiver on 02/21/2024 to discuss concerns for the unclean home environment, the caregivers ability to safely manage the Patients medications and leaving the Patient home alone.
 
Review of RN #2s clinical note dated 02/28/2024, identified Patient #1s caregiver contacted the hospice agencys answering service to report the Patient was confused and vomiting. Upon arrival to the Patients home, RN #2 identified the Patient was lying on the floor covered in feces and vomit. Patient #1s caregiver indicated the Patient may have eaten old food from the wastebasket which resulted in him/her vomiting. RN #2 advised the caregiver that Patient #1 needed to be transferred to the hospital bed and cleaned. The caregiver indicated the Patient sleeps on the couch, and he/she sleeps in the hospital bed provided by the hospice. RN #2 assisted the Patient to the hospital bed and attempted to clean the Patient, but the caregiver lacked necessary supplies such as washcloths, a wash basin, clean clothing, or linen. RN #2 cleaned the Patient with paper towels. RN #2 left the home and contacted SCS #1 to report the unsafe and concerning conditions in the Patients home.
 
Interview and review of Patient #1s clinical record with RN #1 on 03/11/2024 10:40 AM, identified the Patients home environment as cluttered, with unclean surfaces, a strong odor present and waste overflowing from the wastebasket. RN #1 indicated the Patient appeared disheveled and the caregiver was unable to safely manage the Patients medications. RN #1 identified the caregiver reported having weapons in the home and would become agitated toward the hospice staff and the Patient. RN #1 and Social Worker #1 reported the concerns to the Administrator and the Supervisor of Clinical Services (SCS) #1 at the beginning of February 2024. Social Worker #1 left a message for Protective Services for the Elderly on 02/21/2024 and filed a report with Protective Services for the Elderly on 02/27/2024. The Administrator and SCS #1 advised hospice clinicians to not return to Patient #1s home but did not discharge the Patient.
 
Interview and review of Patient #1s clinical record with the Administrator on 03/11/2024 at 12:00 PM, identified RN #1 and Social Worker #1 reported the Patients living conditions as unsanitary and the caregiver was unable to safely care for the Patient. The Administrator indicated the Patient was not discharged for cause from the hospice agency, but clinicians were advised not to return to Patient #1s home after Protective Service for the Elderly was contacted on 02/21/2024. The Administrator identified Patient #1 was visited by hospice clinicians on 02/15/2024 and did not receive another visit until 02/28/2024. The Administrator identified hospice services were not provided for twelve days (02/16/2024 to 02/27/2024), as the agency was waiting for directives from the Regional Managers of Clinical Services. The Administrator indicated after RN #2 reported concerns for Patient #1's safety on 02/28/2024, SCS #1 contacted the police and the Patient was removed from the home.
 
Interview with the Regional Vice President of Clinical Services on 03/11/2024 1:00 PM, identified the hospice agency failed to follow the Assessment and Reporting of Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation policy, Safety Management policy and the Discharge for Cause policy. The Regional Vice President of Clinical Service indicated the hospice agency failed to immediately report suspected abuse and/or neglect to the appropriate state agency, failed to coordinate care by having the Patient immediately removed from the unsafe situation, then discharge the Patient from the hospice agency due to compromised patient and staff safety. Additionally, the Vice President of Clinical Services identified the hospice agency staff failed to ensure the Patient's safety by not providing oversight of the Patient for twelve days. 
 
Review of the agencys Assessment and Reporting of Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation policy, identified agency staff would assess, identify, and intervene on the behalf of victims of abuse and neglect and exploitation in an appropriate and professional manner. All cases of alleged, observed, or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation would be investigated by the agency and appropriate interventions would be initiated, including mandated reported requirements in accordance with the state regulations. When abuse or neglect is suspected, the hospice staff would report the incident to the Administrator immediately and complete an incident report. If the patient is felt to be in immediate danger, the staff member would first ensure the patients personal safety and notify the Administrator. The Administrator would immediately start an investigation and notify the appropriate state agencies.
 
Review of the agencys Discharge for Cause policy, identified the agency reserved the right to discharge patients for cause if all attempts to remediate the situation failed. There may be circumstances in which a hospice would be unable to continue to provide hospice care to a patient. These situations would include issues where the patient safety or hospice staff safety was compromised. The agency must make referrals to all relevant state agencies. The hospice would assist in coordinating continued care for the patient.
 
Review of the agencys Safety Management policy, identified upon admission and at every visit, all patients would be assessed for falls and the home environment would also be evaluated for safety issues. Suspected or confirmed patient abuse or neglect would be reported to specified state agencies and living conditions which place patients in eminent danger.

Based on record review and interview, the hospice agency failed to ensure all staff recognized signs of patient neglect according to their policys definition for 1 of 1 records reviewed of a patient who exhibited signs of neglect (Patient #1), which had the potential to affect all hospice patients. 

Findings include:
Review of agency policy #9-005.1 titled ";Bill of Rights – Indiana," revised 05/15/20, indicated the hospice patient had the right to be free from neglect.
Review of agency policy #9-013.1 titled ";Assessment of Possible Abuse/Neglect," indicated the hospice agency would report ";all suspected cases" of neglect to ";appropriate protection organizations." The policy defined neglect as ";failure of a caretaker to supply the patient with the necessary food, clothing, shelter, health care, or supervision; or the absence or likelihood of an absence of the necessary food, clothing, shelter, health care, or supervision for a patient. 
Review of Patient #1s clinical record indicated the patient was admitted to hospice on 03/04/2023 with a terminal diagnosis of liver cirrhosis and secondary diagnoses including but not limited to Type 2 Diabetes and alcoholism. The patient had discharged from a local hospital to their private residence the same day of their admission to hospice. Hospice RN #1 completed Patient #1s admission assessment. The nurse documented Patient #1 had been transported via EMS to their home immediately before the nurse arrived. The EMS reported upon arrival to the home, Patient #1s caregiver was confused and was under the bed looking for the patient. The nurse assessment indicated the patients living situation had "sanitation issues," the home was "cluttered" and "unclean," and the patient's significant other was "intoxicated and confused." The patient had durable medical equipment delivered prior to returning to their home, which included a hospital bed in their kitchen and a wheelchair and oxygen supplies in the living room. The living room also contained a hospital bed for the patients significant other, a bedside commode, furniture, and ";clutter." Hospice RN #1 moved the wheelchair and oxygen into a cluttered bedroom at the patients request. Patient #1 was observed taking a drink from their significant others liquor bottle in RN #1s presence. The patient reported continuous pressure-like pain to their abdomen with a rating of an ";8" and a ";8.5" on a 0-10 numeric pain scale. The assessment indicated there was no pain medication available in the home and the patient had pain medication ordered by the hospital, but neither the patient nor caregiver could pick up the medication. Patient #1 and their significant other asked the hospice nurse to pick up food for them, but Hospice RN #1 informed the patient they could not get food for the patient. The patient and significant other then discussed options for food delivery. Patient #1s nutritional assessment indicated the patient ate fewer than 2 meals per day, did not always have the financial means to obtain food, and the patient was not always physically able to shop, cook, and/or feed themself. Patient #1 also reported a weight loss of 80 pounds in the last 1 year. The assessment also indicated the patient was incontinent of bowels, ";especially at night." RN #1 documented the patient transferred from bed to chair with ";minimal assistance" and needed assistance with bathing, dressing, grooming, and toileting. 
Review of Patient #1s hospital records prior to their 03/04/2023 discharge included a physical therapy assessment, completed on 03/02/2023, which indicated the patient was ";not safe to be home without physical assistance," required ";heavy" assistance to stand from the end of bed, could only stand for 20 seconds, and their tolerance to therapy was limited by dizziness and weakness. The hospital records also included an occupational therapy evaluation, completed on 03/02/2023, which indicated the patient had ";decreased insight/safety awareness."
During an interview with Hospice RN #1 on 03/16/2023 beginning at 5:06 PM, the nurse confirmed Patient #1s home was cluttered. The nurse reported the patient did not get out of their recliner for the length of the assessment. The nurse denied assessing for the presence of food in the home. Hospice RN #1 reported the patient had a prescription for Norco (opioid pain medication) from the hospital, but they did not have transportation to the pharmacy to pick up the medication. When queried if the nurse observed any signs of neglect or need to call Adult Protective Services, Hospice RN #1 stated ";just that [Patient #1] was unable to care of himself" and did not have a competent caregiver available. The nurse denied discussing any concerns for neglect with any hospice staff.
During a follow up interview was conducted with Hospice RN #1 on 03/17/2023 beginning at 12:03 PM, the nurse confirmed Patient #1 did not have any of their pain medication in their home at the time of admission and no pain medication was ordered for the patient by the hospice. Hospice RN #1 also confirmed they did not assess the patients ambulation status.
The clinical record indicated in the morning on 03/05/2023, Patient #1 called for EMS assistance and was found at the edge of their recliner sitting in stool. A police report from the call indicated neither the patient nor their caregiver could ";get up and around to care for themselves or each other, or even get food and water," and Patient #1 was found slumped at the side of their recliner sitting in stool. The police determined both the patient and their caregiver were severely disabled and a 24 hour Immediate Detention Order (IDO) was conducted. Patient #1 was taken to a local hospital and admitted for long term care placement. Emergency Personnel who responded to the scene referred the patient to Adult Protective Services for investigation of neglect.
During an interview conducted on 03/17/2023 at 2:08 PM with the Administrator and Corporate Regional Compliance Employee #1, the Administrator confirmed they did speak with Hospice RN #1 regarding Patient #1, but the report received did not indicate a concern for neglect.

Based on interview and document review, the hospice agency failed to ensure the Condition of Participation for Patient's Rights was met when the agency failed to protect a patient from neglect following a suicide attempt, failed to ensure the alleged neglect was investigated in accordance with established procedures, and failed to ensure a verified violation involving neglect was accurately and completely reported to the appropriate State authority.The agency's failure to protect a patient from neglect resulted in immediate jeopardy when hospice staff failed to activate emergency medical services (EMS) and failed to ensure the hospice physician received complete and accurate information necessary to direct the patient's care after staff became aware the patient intentionally ingested approximately 28 milliliters (mL), or 560 milligrams (mg), of morphine in a suicide attempt. The patient subsequently became comatose and unresponsive and developed severe respiratory depression, prolonged periods of apnea, cyanosis, and oxygen saturation as low as 35%. The patient died on 2/11/26 from the toxic effects of morphine and oxycodone.The cumulative effect of these deficient practices resulted in the hospice agency's failure to ensure patients' rights were protected and demonstrated the agency's inability to provide care and services in compliance with the Condition of Participation at 42 CFR §418.52. 

Findings include: See L509: Based on interview and document review, the hospice agency failed to provide evidence that an alleged violation involving neglect was investigated in accordance with the agency's established procedures for 1 of 1 patient (P1) reviewed who ingested a bottle of morphine sulfate solution during a reported suicide attempt and subsequently died. The agency reported an investigation was completed and identified a hospice clinical leader failed to follow the agency's established emergency response policy; however, the agency did not provide the investigative documentation necessary to verify the investigation was conducted in accordance with its established procedures. See L511: Based on interview and document review, the hospice agency failed to ensure a verified violation involving neglect was accurately and completely reported to the appropriate State and local authorities for 1 of 1 patient (P1) reviewed for neglect. The agency submitted an initial report to the Minnesota Adult Abuse Reporting Center (MAARC) that inaccurately identified the amount of morphine P1 ingested and did not include P1's documented significant clinical decline following the intentional overdose or that emergency medical services (EMS) were not activated despite the known suicide attempt. The agency subsequently verified through its internal investigation that a clinical leader failed to follow the agency's established emergency-response policy; however, the agency did not report the verified violation to the appropriate State or local authorities. See L517: Based on interview and document review, the hospice agency failed to protect 1 of 3 patients (P1) from neglect when staff failed to obtain emergency medical intervention and failed to ensure a hospice physician was provided complete and accurate information necessary to direct P1's care after staff became aware P1 intentionally ingested approximately 28 milliliters (mL), or 560 milligrams (mg), of morphine in a suicide attempt. Staff did not activate emergency medical services (EMS) despite the agency's policy requiring staff to immediately call 911 following a suicide attempt. In addition, the hospice physician was not informed P1 intentionally ingested the morphine in a suicide attempt, the amount of morphine ingested, or P1's subsequent significant change in condition. P1 became comatose and unresponsive and developed severe respiratory depression, prolonged periods of apnea, cyanosis, and oxygen saturation as low as 35%. P1 died on 2/11/26 from the toxic effects of morphine and oxycodone.The immediate jeopardy began on 2/11/26 when hospice staff failed to activate EMS after becoming aware P1 intentionally ingested approximately 28 mL, or 560 mg, of morphine in a suicide attempt and failed to ensure the hospice physician received complete and accurate information regarding P1's suicide attempt and subsequent significant change in condition. P1 became comatose and unresponsive and developed severe respiratory depression, prolonged periods of apnea, cyanosis, and oxygen saturation as low as 35%. P1 died on 2/11/26 from the toxic effects of morphine and oxycodone. The hospice agency was notified of the immediate jeopardy on 8/7/26 at 1:55 p.m. The immediate jeopardy was removed on 8/10/26 after onsite verification that the approved removal plan was implemented and the likelihood of serious injury, serious harm, serious impairment, or death no longer existed.

Upon patient record review, there was no evidence the patient has the right to be free of mistreatment, neglect, or verbal, mental, sexual and physical abuse, including injuries of unknown source, and misappropriation of patient property.
Patient #4, No evidence patient right to be free of neglect and mistreatment was prevented.

It is required that the written Patient Bill of Rights includes the right to be free from mistreatment, neglect, or verbal, mental, sexual, or physical abuse, including injuries of unknown source, and the misappropriation of patient property. 

This standard was not met as evidenced by document review, clinical record review, and interview. In 3 of 3 (100%) clinical records reviewed, the hospice did not ensure the Patient Bill of Rights form included the right to be free from mistreatment, neglect, or verbal, mental, sexual, or physical abuse, including injuries of unknown source and the misappropriation of patient property. 
 

Clinical Record 1: The patient elected the hospice benefit on 10/10/2023. The patient/representative signed a statement on admission dated 10/10/2023 confirming the patient received a copy of the "Patient Rights and Responsibilities" form. The “Patient Rights and Responsibilities” form did not include the right to be free from mistreatment, neglect, or verbal, mental, sexual, or physical abuse, including injuries of unknown source and the misappropriation of patient property. 

Clinical Record 2: The patient elected the hospice benefit on 09/19/2023. The patient/representative signed a statement on admission dated 09/19/2023 confirming the patient received a copy of the "Patient Rights and Responsibilities" form. Based on document review and staff interview, the hospice failed to ensure that allegations or suspicions of abuse and neglect were investigated and documented in accordance with hospice policy for 1 of 1 patients (Patient #3) with an allegation of abuse and neglect. This deficient practice had the potential to place all hospice patients at risk by failing to ensure that allegations of abuse or neglect were promptly investigated, addressed, and appropriate protective actions implemented.Findings include:

Review of the hospice policy, "Identifying and Reporting Possible Victims of Alleged/Suspected Abuse, Neglect or Exploitation," revised 02/2021, stated, in part, "Hospice will identify and report possible victims of neglect, exploitation, mistreatment, or verbal, mental, sexual, and physical abuse, including injuries of unknown source and misappropriation of patient property by anyone furnishing services on behalf of Hospice." The policy further stated that the Administrator will "...immediately investigate all alleged violations."The hospice failed to follow its policy. An example included:For example, Patient #3 was a 76-year-old female admitted to hospice on 04/14/2025 and expired on 05/09/2025. The primary hospice diagnosis was unspecified severe protein-calorie malnutrition with an additional documented diagnoses included a Stage IV pressure ulcer of the sacral region and pressure-induced deep tissue injury of the right heel.Review of the hospice clinical record did not identify documentation that allegations or concerns related to abuse or neglect had been assessed, investigated, or resolved.Review of the hospice incident reporting documentation identified an incident categorized as "Abuse/Neglect," with the description: "Inadequate care of patient (e.g., not providing adequate food, meds, housing, hygiene), Inadequate supervision of patient (e.g., leaving patient alone)." The incident report did not include the date of the occurrence, details describing the circumstances, findings of an investigation, actions taken, or documentation demonstrating the allegation had been reviewed and resolved.The current Hospice Administrator was interviewed on 08/04/26 beginning at 11:00 AM. The adminstrator stated they were not employed by the hospice at the time of the reported incident and were unable to provide documentation or evidence that an investigation had been completed.The absence of documentation demonstrating a timely investigation and follow-up of an allegation of abuse or neglect prevented the hospice from demonstrating compliance with its policy and had the potential to place all hospice patients at risk by failing to identify, investigate, and address allegations of abuse or neglect to protect patient health and safety. Based on record review and interview, the agency failed to notify the Indiana Department of Health of the neglect of a patient for 1 of 1 neglect incidents, with the potential to affect all patients.
Findings include:

1. Review of the policy on Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation, last reviewed 10/01/2021, identified neglect as ";... failure to provide goods and/ or services necessary to avoid physical harm, mental anguish, or mental illness." The policy evidenced instruction for the hospice to report verified violations to ";... the State Survey and Certification Agency ... within five working days of becoming aware of the verified violation ...."
2. Review of the addendum to the Abuse, Neglect, and Exploitation policy, specific to Indiana, last reviewed 11/27/2023, defined neglect as ";... fails to provide adequate food, clothing, shelter or medical care."
3. Review of video clips of Former Employee 4 with Patient #3 on 1/9/2025, evidenced Former Employee (LPN) 4 assist Patient #3 out of the recliner, then sat in a chair while the patient used a rollator to ambulate to the bathroom, where Patient #3 fell. 
4. Review of the occurrence report completed by Former Employee 4 on 1/13/2025, indicated ";Pt [patient] was standing halfway nud3 [sic] her bathroom after saying come in after writer knocked. Writer sat writer"s [sic] things and put on gloves. Pt asked writer to get [Patient #3s] baby wipes from shelf. Writer did so and whe [when] writer put down package sat down on floor on bath mat. Pt sat rather than sit down firml y [sic] against a flat surface. Pt denied dizziness or pain. No NV [nausea or vomiting]. Writer stood between Pt and wall to prevent Pt from hitting [Patient #3s] head. When staff nurse [nurse at Entity 1] arrived writer took Pts vitals which were WNL [within normal limits] for Pt..."
5. In an email exchange between Corporate Staff 6, the Human Resources Manager, and the Chief Compliance Officer, dated January 13 and 14, 2025, the Chief Compliance Officer indicated Patient #3 fell while alone in the bathroom. The email indicated the agency determined that neglect occurred by Former Employee 4.
6. The Administrator provided notes regarding the fall. The notes indicated Former Employee 4 said they escorted Patient #3 to the bathroom and remained with them. According to the notes, Former Employee 4 assisted the patient to the floor in a controlled fall. The notes indicated Former Employee 4 did not call the hospice RN, Clinical Manager, Administrator, or the Physician. The notes outlined a discussion with Person 3, from Entity 1. Person 3 indicated Former Employee 4 did not assess or provide post – fall care to Patient #3. The notes indicated the Administrator called Adult Protective Services to report neglect on 1/13/2025.
During an interview beginning at 4:35 PM on 2/26/2025, the Administrator indicated they believed they reported the neglect to Adult Protective Services and the report would then go to all required agencies. The Administrator confirmed they did not report the neglect to the Indiana Department of Health.

Based on interview and record review, the Hospice agency failed to meet the Condition of Participation (CoP) for L500 Patient's Right when they failed to 1.) comply with mandatory reporting requirements to immediately report suspicions of neglect to Adult Protective Services (APS) for one of 19 patients (Patient (P) 15) whose records were reviewed out of a total sample of 19. P15 was noted to be a vulnerable adult on 09/11/24, and the case was not filed with APS until 11/26/24. Additionally, local law enforcement was not notified. These failures had the potential to place P15 at risk of serious injury, harm, or impairment, up to and including death, and 2.) identify, document, and act upon a verbal grievance from the caregivers for one of one patient (P7) reviewed for grievances out of a total sample of 19. This had the potential to cause patient and caregiver concerns to be unaddressed.
The agency was notified of the Immediate Jeopardy (IJ) at L517which was related to the failure to comply with mandatory reporting requirements on 01/15/25 at 5:30 PM. In concurrence with Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) review, the removal plan was approved on 01/16/25 at 10:07 AM. The survey team verified implementation of the facility's IJ removal plan on 01/16/25 at 2:36 PM.
Findings include:
1. The agency failed to immediately notify APS of suspicions of neglect for one of 14 active patients (P15) when the patient was first assessed to be vulnerable and unsafe living in his home without caregivers present. (Refer to L517)
2. The agency failed to identify, document, and act upon a verbal grievance from the caregivers of P7. (Refer to L505)

Review of P15's entire clinical record revealed no documented evidence APS had been notified of P15's unsafe living situation and vulnerability from 09/11/24 until 11/26/24, when contact was first made with APS. There was no documented evidence that law enforcement had been notified at any time.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 10:04 AM, RN6, the case manager for P15, stated he/she had identified "pretty quickly" that P15 was unsafe by himself/herself. RN6 stated hospice staff talked with the family member and tried to do what they could to help get more help for P15. RN6 stated he/she believed SW2 had filed a case with APS during November 2024. RN6 was asked what the agency's policy was on mandatory reporting. RN6 stated, "I'm a nurse, and it [suspicions of neglect and patients being in unsafe situations] has to be reported." RN6 was asked why P15's situation was not reported to APS until November 2024. RN6 stated P15 had caregivers and people checking in. RN6 stated he/she was "trying to give the [family member] the chance to come around." RN6 stated he/she believed law enforcement had been notified as well but could not say that for certain. RN6 stated, "We have just been kind of monitoring. I was retriggered to do it [file a case with APS] last week. I text the [family member] every week. [He/she] doesn't want to hear from me. Doesn't want to talk to us. I refiled because something needs to be done." RN6 stated P6's situation had been discussed during IDG (Interdisciplinary Group) meetings.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 11:04 AM, SW1 stated APS did not have an enforcement arm, and APS would tell a person to call local law enforcement if a patient was in immediate danger. SW1 stated calling law enforcement was a case-by-case situation, but if you could not take care of yourself, it was a "good argument" to call law enforcement at the same time you called APS. SW1 stated, "If you determine that a person is a vulnerable adult, you call [APS and law enforcement]. Whether they do anything or not." The surveyor reviewed the 09/11/24 "Visit Note" for P15 with SW1. SW1 stated, "I would consider that to be a vulnerable adult."
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 12:51 PM, SW2, who was the Social Worker assigned to P15, was asked why APS was not notified immediately when it was determined P15 was unsafe and a vulnerable adult. SW2 stated P15's family member had told the RN case manager that he/she would see if changes could be made but they never would and that the family member said that he/she would try options to help P15 qualify for long-term care placement and that never happened. SW2 stated the agency was hoping for P15 to qualify for Medicaid benefits but that would take at least 45 days to occur. SW2 was asked if law enforcement had been notified. SW2 stated law enforcement would be notified if there was an immediate danger. SW2 defined immediate danger as either a threat to a patient's own health or someone else's health and their well-being.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 1:37 PM, the Director of Clinical Services (DCS) was asked what the agency's policy was on mandatory reporting. He/she stated, "Call APS." The DCS was asked when APS should be notified, he/she stated, "When it becomes apparent that we cannot get results in a timely manner. If we think there is exploitation or neglect, it would be immediate." The DCS was asked if P15 was a vulnerable adult. He/she stated, "[He/she] has declined. In the beginning [he/she] had some odd and eccentric behaviors, and [he/she] became more vulnerable."
Review of the Arizona Adult Protective Services website, located at https://des.az.gov/services/basic-needs/adult-protective-services/report-adult-abuse, revealed, ". . . Arizona Adult Protective Services (APS) investigates reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults. APS may also become involved when there is a claim of self-neglect, which is when an adult with physical or mental impairments is not able to meet their basic needs (such as food, shelter, health care, managing money, etc.), which then impacts the adults physical health, mental health or general safety. The goal of APS is to prioritize an adults right to make their own decisions while keeping them safe.
APS tries to support the vulnerable adults in their current home, and to augment the skills they need to take care of themselves by providing services that can help with challenges the adult may be having. However, APS must always balance the need to protect the safety of the vulnerable adult with the adults right to make their own decisions.
APS does not conduct safety checks, but local law enforcement does. Law enforcement and APS work together, and if law enforcement believes an individual is a vulnerable adult, they will contact APS . . ."
Review of the Arizonia Adult Protective Services website, located at https://des.az.gov/services/basic-needs/adult-protective-services/mandated-reporters, revealed, ". . . According to A.R.S. 46-454 (A-D)(link is external), the following individuals are required to report or cause reports to be made to a peace officer or to the Adult Protective Services Central Intake Unit. The reports should be made immediately by phone or online . . . Medical personnel including a physician, physician assistant, registered nurse practitioner, licensed practical or registered nurse, certified nursing assistant, emergency medical technician, home health provider, hospital intern or resident, surgeon, dentist, psychiatrist, psychologist, pharmacist, speech, physical or occupational therapist, long-term care provider, social worker, peace officer, medical examiner, guardian, conservator, fire protection personnel, developmental disabilities provider, employee of the Department of Economic Security or other person who has responsibility for the care of a vulnerable adult . . ."
Review of the agency's policy titled, "Assessment of Possible Abuse/Neglect," dated May 2024, revealed, ". . . Neglect: Failure of a caretaker to supply the patient with the necessary food, clothing, shelter, healthcare, or supervision, or the absence or likelihood of an absence of the necessary food, clothing, shelter, health care, or supervision for a patient . . . Individual Mandated to Report: A professional or the professional's delegate who is engaged in the care of patients, or in education, social services, law enforcement, or in any of the related occupations, who had knowledge of the abuse or neglect of a patient, or who has reasonable cause to believe that a patient is being or has been abused or neglected . . . Any clinician who discovers, within the course of rendering care, any suspected abuse or neglect will immediately report such occurrences to his/her immediate supervisor . . . The clinician will submit a verbal report of the suspected abuse/neglect to the proper authorities in accordance with state law and complete a suspected abuse and/or neglect investigation report within 24 hours of the incident . . . If patient is in immediate jeopardy, the proper authorities will be contacted by the clinician immediately as required by state or local law . . ."

It is required that each patient’s individualized written plan of care reflects patient, and family goals and identifies planned interventions based on problems identified in the initial and updated comprehensive assessments.

This standard was not met as evidenced by clinical record review, document review, and interview. On 11/27/2024, an Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Meeting was documented, and no new interventions or goals were documented. The patient is instructed to store any pill bottles found in the box designated for medications..." The plan of care for 11/10/2024 to 02/07/2025, to include the Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) plans of care updates, did not include patient-specific identified problems, goals, or interventions related to medication safety or the use of the weekly pillbox. Based on review of the agency's polices titled "Rights and Ethics 401: Reporting Abuse and Neglect or Exploitation", revised 9/21, staff interview and clinical record review, the Administrator failed to provide oversite of the agency as designated by the Governing Body. Failure of the administrative oversite was revealed upon review of three of three patients (P) (P#1, P#2 and P#3) records reviewed for abuse allegations.

1. The agency received an allegation of abuse on 11/1/21, towards P#1 by Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) #AA. P#1 was residing at the agency's inpatient unit (IPU) receiving respite care at the time of the alleged abuse. The alleged abuse was reported to have occurred on 10/26/21. 

2. The hospice agency received an allegation of abuse on 11/1/21, towards P#2 by CNA #AA. P#2 was residing at the agency's IPU receiving respite care at the time of the alleged abuse. The alleged abuse was reported to have occurred on 10/30/21. 

3. The agency received an allegation of abuse on 6/14/21, towards P#3 by CNA #AA. P#3 was residing at the agency's IPU recviing respite care at the time of the alleged abuse. The alleged abuse was reported to have occurred on 6/4/21. The administrator failed to provide oversite to the agency and follow the agency policy titled "Rights and Ethics 401", revised 9/21, by not taking the following actions immediately upon receipt of the report of the alleged abuse:

 The administrator failed to provide oversite to the agency and follow the agency policy titled "Rights and Ethics 401", revised 9/21, by not taking the following actions immediately upon receipt of the report of alleged abuse:
 
a. #6 of the policy requires a verbal report of any allegations of abuse to be made to Adult Protective Services Central Intake Division of the Georgia Department of Human Resources. The Administrator failed to provide oversite by not reporting the allegation of abuse to this entity.

b. #7 the policy requires the agency to report any allegations of abuse to be reported to Georgia Department of Community Health within 24 hours or the next business day. The Administrator failed to ensure the department was notified of the allegations of abuse.

c. #8 the policy requires the agency to document assessment, interventions and referrals in the medical record for any patient for whom there are allegations of abuse. The Administrator failed to provide oversite by not ensuring that documentation in the medical record of P#1 to reflect comprehensive physical and psychosocial assessment, interventions and referrals for the possible abuse.

d. #9 the policy requires the agency to reassign any employee suspected of abuse to nonclinical duties. The Administrator failed to provide oversite by failing to remove CNA #AA from clinical care of patients on after being notified of the possible abuse 11/1/21. CNA #AA provided direct patient care on at the agency's IPU on 11/2/21, 11/3/21 and 11/4/21.

The Administrator was made informed via email provided by the Department of Community Health, Division of Healthcare Regulation on 11/23/21 at 4:05 p.m.

Based on observation, interview, and record review, the Governing Body (GB) failed to operate and manage the agency from March 1, 2022, to June 6, 2024, in a universe of 129 Palliative Care Program patients when:
 
1. Based on interview, and record review, the agency failed to ensure the patients' initial assessment was completed within 48 hours of the physician's referral date or on the physician-ordered start of care date for three of four sampled patients (Patients 1, 2, and 3). 
 
This failure had the potential to cause a delay in the determination of Patients 1, 2, and 3s immediate care and support needs.
 
2. Based on interview and record review, the agency failed to ensure the patients' comprehensive assessments were completed within five days after the start of care for four of four sampled patients (Patient 1, 2, 3, and 4) when no spiritual or psychosocial assessments were conducted. 
 
This failure had the potential to cause the patient and familys psychosocial, emotional, and spiritual needs to go unmet.
 
3. Based on observation, interview, and record review, the agency failed to ensure the comprehensive assessment identified and addressed the physical and safety needs of two of four sampled patients (Patients 3 and 4) when:
 
a. Patient 3's left great toe wound was not identified or assessed during the admission assessment.
 
b. Patient 4's three falls in May or Patient 4s fear of falling was not identified or assessed. Patient 4's inability to raise arms past his upper chest was not identified or assessed.
 
This failure caused Patient 3 not to receive wound care for 12 days and Patient 4 not to receive care to address the inability of Patient 4 to raise his arms past his upper chest for six days. In addition, this failure had the potential to cause Patient 4 to fall again and suffer injuries. 
 
4. Based on interview, and record review, the agency failed to ensure the comprehensive assessment was updated by the agency's interdisciplinary group (in collaboration with the individuals attending physician) and considered changes that took place since the initial assessment for one of four sampled patients (Patient 1) when:
 
a. Patient 1's right great toe wound was not identified or assessed by the visiting Licensed Vocational Nurses.
 
b. No re-admission assessment was conducted after Patient 1's hospitalization from May 6, 2024, to May 8, 2024.
 
c. No discharge summary for Patient 1 was documented and no discharge order for Patient 1 was obtained.
 
This failure caused Patient 1 to suffer a delay in wound care, no re-assessment of care needs following an acute care hospital admission, caused Patient 1s attending physicians to be unaware of the medical condition and death of Patient 1 at discharge, and no physician oversight for Patient 1s discharge from the Palliative Care Program.
 
5. Based on interview and record review, the agency failed to ensure the Interdisciplinary Group (IDG - a group of health care professionals who work in a coordinated fashion toward a common goal for a patient) members supervised and provided care and services to meet the physical, medical, psychosocial, emotional, and spiritual needs for four of four sampled patients (Patients 1, 2, 3, and 4) when:
 
a. An admission order was not obtained for Patient 1.
 
b. Patient 1's gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding episode on May 5, 2024, was not discussed or addressed by the IDG.
 
c. Patient 1's hospital admission from May 6, 2024, to May 8, 2024, where Patient 1 received two units of blood was not discussed or addressed by the IDG.
 
d. Patient 1's right great toe wound identified at the hospital on May 8, 2024, was not discussed or addressed by the IDG.
 
e. Patient 1's death on May 20, 2024, and discharge on May 21, 2024, was not discussed or addressed by the IDG.
 
f. There was no documented evidence to show the IDG evaluated, discussed, or provided general oversight for Patient 2s care.
 
g. Patient 3's left great toe wound was not discussed or addressed by the IDG.
 
h. Patient 4's three falls in May or patients fear of falling was not discussed or assessed by the IDG. Patient 4's inability to raise arms past his upper chest was not discussed or assessed by the IDG.
 
This failure caused Patient 1 to be admitted to the Palliative Care Program without a physicians order, and a potential to cause Patient 1 to suffer additional GI bleeds and delayed healing or worsening of Patient 1s right great toe wound. This failure caused the IDG to be unaware of the circumstances surrounding Patient 1s death. This failure had the potential to cause Patient 2 not to achieve her desired goals of care and delayed healing or worsening of Patient 3s left great toe wound. In addition, this failure had the potential to cause Patient 4 to suffer additional falls with injuries and his arm raising restriction to worsen.
 
6. Based on interview and record review, the agency failed to develop an individualized plan of care for four of four sampled patients (Patients 1, 2, 3, and 4) when:
 
a. Patient 1's a lower gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding episode on May 5, 2024, was not care planned. 
 
b. Patient 1's hospital admission from May 6, 2024, to May 8, 2024, where Patient 1 received two units of blood was not care planned. 
 
c. Patient 1's right great toe wound identified at the hospital on May 8, 2024, was not care planned.
 
d. Patient 1's plan of care did not include discharge planning.
 
e. There was no documented evidence to show the IDG evaluated, discussed, or updated Patient 2's care plan.
 
f. Patient 3's dialysis (a process of removing excess water and cleaning the blood in people whose kidneys can no longer perform these functions naturally) and left great toe wound were not care planned.
 
g. Patient 4's three falls in May 2024, and the patient's fear of falling was not care planned. Patient 4's inability to raise arms past his upper chest was not care planned.
 
This failure had the potential to cause Patient 1 to suffer additional GI bleeds and delayed healing or worsening of Patient 1s right great toe wound. This failure caused the IDG and attending physician to be unaware of the circumstances surrounding Patient 1s death and the discharge from the program. This failure had the potential to cause Patient 2 not to achieve her desired goals of care. This failure had the potential to cause delayed healing or worsening of Patient 3s left great toe wound and unrecognized complications from dialysis treatments. In addition, this failure had the potential to cause Patient 4 to suffer additional falls with injuries and his arm raising restriction to worsen.
 
7. Based on interview and record review, the agency failed to ensure the interdisciplinary group documented the patients or representatives level of understanding, involvement, and agreement with the plan of care for one of four sampled patients (Patient 1) when Patient 1 nor Patient 1's representative consented to: treatment, a financial agreement, hospitalization, blood transfusion, or receipt of the Notice of Privacy Rights and Advance Directive information.
 
This failure had the potential to cause Patient 1 and Patient 1s representative not to know and agree or disagree with the proposed care, treatment, services, medications, interventions, or procedures. Potential benefits, risks, or side-effects, including potential problems. The likelihood of achieving the goals established. Reasonable alternatives to the proposed treatment. Relevant risks, benefits, and side effects related to alternatives. In addition, Patient 1, and Patient 1s representative had the potential not to know their Privacy Rights or Advance Directive information.
 
8a. Based on interview, and record review, the agency failed to operate and furnish services in compliance with State Law (California Code, Health, and Safety Code (HSC) § 1747.3), in a universe of 129 Palliative Care Program patients, when the agency:
a. Failed to provide the California Department of Public Health Licensing and Certification Division (CDPH L&C) the date the agency intended to begin providing a Palliative Care Program.
b. Failed to provide CDPH L&C the State form "HS 200 [a State licensing application]."
c. Failed to provide CDPH L&C the Federal form "CMS 417 [a Federal certification application]."
d. Failed to provide CDPH L&C information for the period of time in the prior calendar year during which the agency provided palliative care through the Online reporting portal, including but not limited to, all of the following:
i. The number of nonhospice patients who received palliative care.
ii. The number of patients enrolled in hospice.
iv. The primary diagnoses of the patients for which the agency provided palliative care.
v. The numbers and types of providers hired during the previous 12 months.
vi. The numbers and types of providers who left employment during the previous 12 months.
e. Complaints received by the agency during the previous 12 months that related to all the following:
i. Events that caused or were likely to cause serious injury, harm, impairment, or death.
ii. Events or incidents that negatively impacted a patient's mental, physical, or psychosocial status and were of such consequence to the patient's well-being that a rapid response was required.
iii. Delays in patient care for hospice and nonhospice patients who received palliative care pursuant to this section.
f. Failed to provide the qualifications of staff.
g. Failed to be approved by CDPH L&C to provide palliative care.
h. Failed to provide CDPH L&C all information the agency provided to the Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development.
 
8b. Based on observation, interview, and record review, the agency failed to ensure patients met the criteria to be admitted into the agencys Palliative Care Program (a program which helps patients facing chronic or quality of life-limiting illnesses, with the relief of uncontrolled symptoms, pain and stress without focusing on the patients regaining their independence, or becoming as self-sufficient as possible) instead of a Home Health Program (a program which helps patients get better from an illness or injury, regain their independence, and become as self-sufficient as possible) for three of four sampled patients (Patients 1, 2, and 3) when:
 
i. Patient 1 had been admitted to the agencys Palliative Care Program after recently starting dialysis (a process of removing excess water and cleaning the blood in people whose kidneys can no longer perform these functions naturally) treatments and had diagnoses that included end stage renal disease (a person's kidneys cease functioning on a permanent basis leading to the need for a regular course of long-term dialysis or a kidney transplant), diabetes mellitus (a disease that results in too much sugar in the blood) and congestive heart failure (a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump or fill effectively). Patient 1s wife stated Patient 1 had been on oxygen but was not short of breath and Patient 1 did not have pain. Patient 1s wife stated Patient 1 wanted to be monitored while adjusting to the new dialysis treatments and help with managing his diabetes mellitus. Patient 1s wife stated Patient 1 wanted every treatment done to help him become as functional and independent as possible.
 
ii. Patient 2 had been admitted to the agencys Palliative Care Program after right knee surgery and had a diagnosis of osteoarthritis (a degenerative joint disease, in which the tissues in the joint break down over time). Patient 2 stated she had some right knee pain due to the surgery but otherwise everything was fine. Patient 2 stated she was excited to go back to work in a few weeks.
 
iii. Patient 3 had been admitted to the agencys Palliative Care Program after a hospital stay for chest pain. Patient 3 was receiving dialysis (a process of removing excess water and cleaning the blood in people whose kidneys can no longer perform these functions naturally) treatments and had diagnoses that included chest pain, diabetes mellitus (a disease that results in too much sugar in the blood), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (a chronic inflammatory lung disease that causes obstructed airflow from the lungs). Patient 3 stated she had been receiving dialysis treatments for two years and was used to it. Patient 3 stated she did not have chest pain or any other pain. Patient 3 stated she was not on oxygen and did not have shortness of breath. Patient 3 stated she did not know what services the agency provided but she would like help with transportation to her doctors appointments, some Physical Therapy so she could walk again and someone to clean her bathroom.
 
The cumulative effect of these systemic practices resulted in the agency operating an unlicensed and unapproved Palliative Care Program without governmental oversight. In addition, the agency admitted Patients 1, 2, and 3 into a Palliative Care Program with the potential to cause Patients 1, 2, and 3 not to receive the care and services needed for them to achieve their highest level of functioning and independence.

Review of the policy titled ASSESSMENT OF POSSIBLE ABUSE/NEGLECT Policy No. 2-035, (3, 4, 5) revised 8.2023, revealed the following:
 
PURPOSE
To provide guidelines for identification of suspected abuse victims for care and referral to community resources.
POLICY
Gentiva – Hospice Division (the hospice) will report all suspected cases of abuse, neglect, or exploitation in compliance with appropriate state statutes to appropriate protection organizations.
 
3. Upon receiving a report of a potential patient violation, the hospice must:
a. Begin an immediate Investigation to verify allegation.
b. Ensure patient is protected from further potential violations during the investigational period.
c. Report any verified violations to State/Local or Accreditation bodies within 5 working days of violation verification (specific to most stringent criteria)
d. The suspected abuse/neglect investigation report with specific information relating to the occurrence is forwarded to the Clinical Supervisor, who will:
i. Notify the physician and referral source (as appropriate) or direct the clinician to do so.
 ii. Review the documentation for completeness and objectivity.
 iii. Forward the information to the Administrator and/or Executive Director
e. The Administrator and/or Executive Director will:
i. Review all reports (incident report and follow-up investigation)
 ii. Conduct any further review if necessary.
 iii. Document additional information
 iv. Submit reports to the proper authorities.
v. Reports, reviews, and investigations of suspected abuse/neglect will be held in strictest confidence.
4. The hospice will maintain evidence that all allegations of abuse, neglect, and/or mistreatment have been thoroughly investigated and that further potential abuse has been prevented while the investigation is in progress.
5. The hospice will maintain a list of private and public community agencies that provide or arrange for assessment of suspected or alleged abuse/neglect victims.

Policy:
Any difference of opinion, dispute, or controversy between a patient or family/caregiver or patient representative and Gentiva – Hospice Division (the hospice) or contracted vendor concerning any aspect of services, or the application of policies or procedures will be considered a grievance.

Based on interviews and record reviews the agency failed to protect patient rights specifically; be free from mistreatment, neglect, or verbal, mental, sexual, and physical abuse, including injuries of unknown source, and misappropriation of patient property for 2 of 2 patients (Patients #1 and #8).
 

Findings include:
 
AGENCY POLICY
 
According to the policy titled, "Rights/Responsibility," dated, 10/5/2023 (in part):
 
"The right to be free from mental, physical, sexual, and/or verbal abuse, neglect, or exploitation."
 
According to the policy titled, "Scope of Services," dated, 10/5/2023 (in part):
 
"TRU Community Care provides hospice services that are intended to meet the physical, psychosocial, practical, and spiritual needs of hospice patients and family/caregivers. The core hospice team members (registered nurse, medical social worker, physician, and Chaplain) are available to patients and family/caregivers seven (7) days a week, 24 hours a day."

1. The clinical record for Patient #1 was reviewed on 1/7/25. The patient was admitted to hospice care and services on 9/8/24, with a terminal diagnosis of Senile degeneration. The plan of care for the certification period dated 9/8/24 to 11/6/24, included orders for a skilled nurse twice a week for wound care, nurse aide twice a week for activities of daily living, medical social worker once to twice a month for psychosocial needs, and chaplain once a month for spiritual needs. He resided in an assisted living facility that was contracted with the hospice agency.
 
a. The agency failed to protect Patient #1 from neglect. 
 
Record review showed Patient #1 had three (3) wounds; one on the right foot, left heel and on the coccyx/buttocks area. On 10/22/24 the coccyx wound was described and documented by hospice skilled nurses to be yellow-green in color and to have a foul odor, which were signs and symptoms of an infection. Further record review failed to show evidence that wound care was provided by the agency's skilled nurse twice a week as ordered by the physician. The weeks of 11/4/24 through 11/30/24 and 12/4/24 through 12/16/24, no wound care was provided to the patient by the hospice staff. There were five (5) missed wound care and dressing changes the patient did not receive from the hospice agency's skilled nurse as ordered by a physician. 
 
Review of a missed visit note created by RN (Employee #4) on 11/14/24, showed RN #4 had concerns shared with her by the patient's family about wound care frequency and the patient's repositioning frequency at which the nurse advised the family member to speak to the facility. She further documented the facility staff would do the dressing change that day. There was no evidence Employee #4 did anything about the family members' concerns. 
 
Review of a missed visit note created by RN #4 on 11/28/24 revealed RN #4 wrote, "No visit made due to Thanksgiving holiday."
 
RN #4 documented on 12/5/24, dressing change completed by facility staff and that no visit was needed until next week. 
 
A review of the contract between Patient #1's hospice agency and the assisted living facility showed no evidence that skilled nurse wound care services were to be provided by the assisted living facility. 
 
On 12/17/24, RN #4 created a discharge summary for Patient #1, this summary failed to communicate the patient's wound characteristics, number of wounds, location of wounds and any wound care treatments that were given to the patient while under the hospice agency's care. Further review showed the agency failed to send the discharge summary to the home health agency that the patient was transferred to after discharge.
 
On 12/21/24, Patient #1 was admitted to the hospital with the acute medical problem of septic shock suspect bacteremia due to necrotic grade 4 pressure ulcer/buttock with suspicion of sacral osteomyelitis. In non medical terms, this is a bacterial infection in the blood from the coccyx/buttock wound with a suspicion that the patient's sacral bone is also infected by bacteria. 
 
At the entrance interview with the hospice leadership team which included, Employees #1, #3, and #8 on 1/7/25 at 10:42 a.m., they were asked the definition of patient neglect. They collectively stated the following; failure to follow the plan of care, failure to provide the patient with treatment or services, missing visits, and not responding to the patient's needs. 

An interview with the hospice leadership team which included, Employees #1, #2, #3, and #8 occurred on 1/13/25 at 4:00 p.m. They acknowledged the agency failed to provide Patient #1 with ethical care that was in the best interest of the patient which constituted patient neglect. They also acknowledged that the contract with Patient #1's assisted living facility failed to include wound care as a contracted service, and therefore wound care should have only been provided by the hospice skilled nursing staff. They further acknowledged that the discharge summary was sent to the hospice agency physicians and that they had failed to send the patient's discharge summary to the patient's new home health agency. Additionally, the discharge summary failed to mention the patient's current state or wounds that the patient had at the time of discharge while under their care. Lastly, they acknowledged that skilled nurse, Employee #4 failed to provide Patient #1 with quality nursing care or documentation and they had plans to educate and re-train her immediately. 

2. An active clinical record for Patient #8 was reviewed on 1/7/25. The patient was admitted to hospice care and services on 9/10/24, with a terminal diagnosis of Senial degeneration. The plan of care for the certification period dated 9/10/24 to 12/8/24, included orders for a skilled nurse once a week for 13 weeks, nurse aide once a week for activities of daily living, medical social worker once to twice a month for psychosocial needs, and chaplain once to twice a month for spiritual needs. He resided in an assisted living facility that was contracted with the hospice agency.
 
a. The agency failed to provide treatment or services to Patient #8 as ordered by a physician.
 
On 1/8/25 at 12:30 p.m., an observation of Patient #8 in their assisted living residence took place, RN #9 was there to assess the patient and to provide wound care to the right hip. Upon arrival, RN #9 stated the facility had already provided the patient's wound and dressing changes prior to her arrival and that Patient #8 was on a facility outing and would return shortly. She was asked how the assisted living facility was approved to provide wound care that was ordered for the hospice staff to perform. She proceeded to show an intervention in the patient's record that stated, "Facility to manage daily care needs." She also stated that she received wound updates from the facility nurse with each visit. She went on to say, with any hospice patient concerns she was called immediately by the assisted living staff or they called an afterhours hotline to get a hospice nurse. During this same discussion, RN #9 had given an introduction to the assisted living facility director of nursing (DON). The assisted living DON acknowledged that her staff had provided wound care for Patient # 8 and other hospice patients when it was needed and that the hospice agency had supplied wound care supplies. When asked about billing procedures and the facility contract with the agency she said, she was unsure how billing worked when her staff provided wound care instead of the hospice agency's skilled nurses. She did not know if the contract between the hospice agency and the assisted living facility covered wound care services.
 
A review of the contract between Patient #8's hospice agency and the assisted living facility showed no evidence that skilled nurse wound care services were to be provided by the assisted living facility.
 
Record review for Patient #8 revealed a fall on 12/29/24, resulting in a hip wound. Documentation showed the hospice agency was aware of the fall on 12/31/24 but there was no evidence of a wound assessment for infection or provision of wound care until 1/6/25. Further review showed on 1/8/25, the patient's nurse practitioner reclassified the wound as an unstageable wound with the presence of slough. 
 
At the entrance interview with the hospice leadership team which included, Employees #1, #3, and #8 on 1/7/25 at 10:42 a.m., they were asked the definition of patient neglect. They collectively stated the following; failure to follow the plan of care, failure to provide the patient with treatment or services, missing visits, and not responding to the patient's needs. 
 
An interview with the hospice leadership team which included, Employees #3 and #8 occurred on 1/14/25 at 12:00 p.m. They acknowledged that the agency delayed Patient #8 from treatment and services and that the agency should have made a visit to the patient after he had fallen to assess the patient's needs, therefore constitutes neglect. They also acknowledged that the contract with Patient #8's assisted living facility failed to include wound care as a contracted service, and therefore wound care should have only been provided by the hospice skilled nursing staff.

Based on review of Florida Statutes, the hospices Job Descriptions, observation, record review and interview, the facility failed to provide 3 of 23 sampled patients (Patient #3, 8, and 21) social services only by qualified social workers in accordance with Florida Statutes.
 

491.002 F.S. documents, part, ";The Legislature finds that as society becomes increasingly complex, emotional survival is equal in importance to physical survival. Therefore, in order to preserve the health, safety, and welfare of the public, the Legislature must provide privileged communication for members of the public or those acting on their behalf to encourage needed or desired counseling, clinical and psychotherapy services, or certain other services of a psychological nature to be sought out. The Legislature further finds that, since such services assist the public primarily with emotional survival, which in turn affects physical and psychophysical survival, the practice of clinical social work, marriage and family therapy, and mental health counseling by persons not qualified to practice such professions presents a danger to public health, safety, and welfare."
 
491.003 F.S. documents, in relevant parts, ";The ";practice of clinical social work" is defined as the use of scientific and applied knowledge, theories, and methods for the purpose of describing, preventing, evaluating, and treating individual, couple, marital, family, or group behavior, based on the person-in-situation perspective of psychosocial development, normal and abnormal behavior, psychopathology, unconscious motivation, interpersonal relationships, environmental stress, differential assessment, differential planning, and data gathering. The purpose of such services is the prevention and treatment of undesired behavior and enhancement of mental health. The practice of clinical social work includes methods of a psychological nature used to evaluate, assess, diagnose, treat, and prevent emotional and mental disorders and dysfunctions (whether cognitive, affective, or behavioral), sexual dysfunction, behavioral disorders, alcoholism, and substance abuse. The practice of clinical social work includes, but is not limited to, psychotherapy, hypnotherapy, and sex therapy. The practice of clinical social work also includes counseling, behavior modification, consultation, client-centered advocacy, crisis intervention, and the provision of needed information and education to clients, when using methods of a psychological nature to evaluate, assess, diagnose, treat, and prevent emotional and mental disorders and dysfunctions (whether cognitive, affective, or behavioral), sexual dysfunction, behavioral disorders, alcoholism, or substance abuse" and ";The definition of ";clinical social work" contained in this subsection includes all services offered directly to the general public or through organizations, whether public or private, and applies whether payment is requested or received for services rendered."
 
491.012 F.S. documents, in part ";It is unlawful and a violation of this chapter for any person to: (i) Practice clinical social work in this state for compensation, unless the person holds a valid, active license to practice clinical social work issued pursuant to this chapter or is an intern registered pursuant to s. 491.0045."
 
The Hospices Job Description for ";Social Worker I" documents in Qualifications for state specific requirements in Florida, ";must receive a Master Social Work (MSW) from a CSWE-accredited program or be verified as a Registered Clinical Social Worker Intern (RCSWI); latter preferred" and within Essential Duties and Responsibilities, ";Assess the social, spiritual, and emotional needs/factors in order to estimate the patients and involved caregivers capacity and potential to cope with the problems of daily living and with the terminal diagnosis and illness" and ";... Provide services planned to assist in achieving the optimum social, spiritual, and health adjustment within their capacity and level of health literacy" and ";ongoing evaluation of patients social determinants of health."
 
1) Review of Patient #3's record reveals she started care with the hospice in September 2024. PCG [primary caregiver] bereavement risk and provide education and psychosocial support. Will follow up with one visit monthly unless there is a change in LOC [level of care]."
 
During observation in the presence of the Director of Patient Experience on 01/29/25 beginning at 11:55 AM, Staff A was observed to talk to nursing home staff, and make the Social Work visit to Patient #3. During interview on 01/29/25 at 12:25 PM with the Director of Patient Experience, she stated all of the hospice's Social Workers are Registered Clinical Social Work Interns (RCSWIs) or licensed Social Workers and that she is Qualified Supervisor of Social Work who supervises some of their RCSWIs as they work towards obtaining their licensure in Social Work.
