Patient #21's Social Work visit note by Staff A for 10/22/24 documents he assessed Patient #21 and their caregiver for psychosocial needs, assessed Patient #21 for current degree of depression and there were no evident signs of depression, assessed the caregiver as low risk for bereavement, and attempted to contact the guardianship program regarding consent to a medical procedure.
3) Review of Patient #8's record reveals he was admitted to hospice on 01/22/25. Patient #8's Social Work Evaluation Visit dated 01/23/25 documents "low bereavement risk," "patient sees self/situation as a burden" and was completed by Staff A .
 
Review of Staff A's employee file revealed no evidence of licensure or registered internship for Social Work. A search on the Department of Health's licensure verification website for Staff A's first and last name also revealed no evidence of Social Work licensure or registered internship.

Based on record review and interview, the hospice failed to have a Social Worker available who is qualified under state law to practice clinical social work to conduct psychosocial assessments and provide counseling services as indicated to meet patients' and families' needs. 

491.002 F.S. documents, "the practice of clinical social work, marriage and family therapy, and mental health counseling by persons not qualified to practice such professions presents a danger to public health, safety, and welfare. 491.012 F.S. documents, "It is unlawful and a violation of this chapter for any person to: ...Practice clinical social work in this state for compensation, unless the person holds a valid, active license to practice clinical social work issued pursuant to this chapter or is an intern registered pursuant to s. 491.0045." 491.003 F.S. documents "The definition of ";clinical social work" contained in this subsection includes all services offered directly to the general public or through organizations, whether public or private, and applies whether payment is requested or received for services rendered." and "The ";practice of clinical social work" is defined as the use of scientific and applied knowledge, theories, and methods for the purpose of describing, preventing, evaluating, and treating individual, couple, marital, family, or group behavior, based on the person-in-situation perspective of psychosocial development, normal and abnormal behavior, psychopathology, unconscious motivation, interpersonal relationships, environmental stress, differential assessment, differential planning, and data gathering. The purpose of such services is the prevention and treatment of undesired behavior and enhancement of mental health. The practice of clinical social work includes methods of a psychological nature used to evaluate, assess, diagnose, treat, and prevent emotional and mental disorders and dysfunctions (whether cognitive, affective, or behavioral), sexual dysfunction, behavioral disorders, alcoholism, and substance abuse. The practice of clinical social work includes, but is not limited to, psychotherapy, hypnotherapy, and sex therapy. The practice of clinical social work also includes counseling, behavior modification, consultation, client-centered advocacy, crisis intervention, and the provision of needed information and education to clients, when using methods of a psychological nature to evaluate, assess, diagnose, treat, and prevent emotional and mental disorders and dysfunctions (whether cognitive, affective, or behavioral), sexual dysfunction, behavioral disorders, alcoholism, or substance abuse."
 
Review of the staff roster provided by the Administrator and form CMS-417 reveals the hospice has one Social Worker, Staff A and does not provide Social Work services by arrangements with any other providers. Search for Staff A on the Department of Health website reveals no entry for Staff A as either a licensed Social Worker or Registered Social Work Intern. Review of Staff A's employee file also revealed no evidence of a license or active Registered Social Work Internship.
 
During interview with the Administrator on 12/12/24 at 5:30 PM, she denied awareness that a Social Worker must be licensed or a registered intern in Florida in order to do psychosocial assessments and counsel patients and families and expressed her belief this applied to diagnosing and hypnotherapy.

Based on observation, record review, and interview, the hospice failed to report a verified violation of misappropriation of patient’s property to the state within 5 business days of becoming aware of the violation in 1 of 1 complaint received of a patient’s misappropriation of Patient property by a hospice employee. Findings include: 

The undated policy, titled, “Abuse, Neglect, Mistreatment and Exploitation,” indicated the hospice would follow all Federal and State requirements regarding alleged violations involving misappropriation of Patient property by anyone providing services on behalf of the hospice. The policy indicated misappropriation of patient property was the deliberate misplacement, exploitation, or wrongful, temporary of permanent use of patient’s belongings or money without the patient’s consent. The policy indicated if an alleged violation was verified the Administrator would ensure that verified violations were reported to State and local bodies having jurisdiction, including state survey and certification agency, within 5 days of becoming aware of the violation. The policy indicated all assessments, interventions, discussions and follow up with the State Agency would be documented and kept confidential. A Complaint Report, dated 07/02/2025, completed by the hospice Administrator, indicated caregiver for Patient #2 called the hospice and indicated the hospice aide was arrested at Patient’s home for taking narcotics and money and family had put in cameras the night before when the family felt the aide was acting suspiciously; the director of human resources and president of the company was informed, the aide was immediately terminated, and the president of the company called the family to ensure their wellbeing. An Email from the Administrator to the Director of Human Resources, dated 07/02/2025, indicated she spoke to FM A, indicated cameras were placed in the home the previous night because the family suspected something suspicious was happening with Hospice Aide 2; Hospice Aide 2 would immediately ask to use the bathroom upon arrival to the home, and Hospice Aide 2 would go into rooms that she didn’t need to be in. FM A informed the Administrator, Hospice Aide 2 went through FM A’s purse and took $70.00, Hospice Aide 2 took medication from a backstock of medication from a container in a cabinet and not from a container of medications in view on a counter, Hospice Aide 2 picked up a prescription on Monday and the aide immediately suggested the bottles be combined so there were not two different bottles. 8 Norco (narcotic pain medication with Hydrocodone) were found in Hospice Aide 2’s pocket on 07/02/2025, a total of 14 Norco tablets were missing from the last two days and camera footage would be sent to the hospice. An Email, dated 07/14/2025, to the Hospice Director of Human Resources from the Office of the Attorney General indicated the complaint was submitted and received by the Consumer Protection Division. An Office of the Attorney General Licensing Enforcement and HPU Complaint Form indicated the Director of Human Resources signed and submitted the complaint form on 07/14/2025 related to the 07/02/2025 misappropriation of patient’s property by Hospice Aide 2. The review failed to evidence the State Agency, The Dept. of Health [IDOH] and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services [CMS] were notified of the misappropriation of patient’s property by Hospice Aide 2 within 5 days of the violation or allegation. A Police Report from Entity C, a County Sheriff’s office, dated 07/02/2025, indicated $60.00 in cash was stolen, prescriptions stolen were recovered on 07/02/2025 at 3:20 PM at Patient #2’s private residence, and Hospice Aide 2 was transported to Entity C’s Jail and charged with theft. The Police Report indicated FM B dispatched police and had video proof of hospice stealing prescription pills that belonged to Patient #2, and indicated Hospice Aide 2 had been coming to the resident to provide care for Patient #2 for approximately 4 to 6 week. The Police Report indicated FM A indicated a Hydrocodone prescription was missing 8 tablets, FM B had installed security cameras in the home on 07/01/2025 and the video recordings evidenced Hospice Aide 2 in the kitchen retrieving Patient #2’s medication container from a cabinet, picking several pills out from a container and putting them into her pocket. The Police Report indicated Hospice Aide 2 indicated she had administered medication to Patient #2 one time due to the family had asked her to, indicated she knew where the medication was stored, and denied stealing anything. The Police Report indicated when the police officer notified Hospice Aide 2 the police officer had watched a security camera recording from 07/02/2025, of Hospice Aide 2 taking pills from Patient’s medication container and putting them into her pocket Hospice Aide 2 reached into her shirt pocket and retrieved 6 Hydrocodone pills and handed them to FM A, when asked where the other 2 outstanding pills were Hospice Aide 2 indicated she did not know, and then dug into her pocket again and was able to find the other 2 Hydrocodone pills. The Police Report indicated the police officer asked about stealing of money, to which Hospice Aide 2 denied taking money and then after further discussion Hospice Aide 2 admitted to stealing approximately $60.00 in cash and using it for gasoline for her personal vehicle. The Police Report indicated Hospice Aide 2 was placed in handcuffs and escorted to the patrol vehicle. The Police Report indicated Hospice Aide 2 was in jail and the police officer completed the remanding form and Hospice Aide 2 was charged with theft. The Police Report indicated a link was sent to FM B to upload the security camera recording, the police report was a summary of events, and the body camera footage would serve for exact dialogue and sequence of events.An observation of a video recorded by Patient #2, FM B provided by hospice, identified as person in the video by the Administrator as Hospice Aide 2, evidenced Hospice Aide 2 in Patient’s kitchen, opening a cabinet, removing a bowl with a lid with medication bottles inside. Hospice aide 2 was observed removing medication from a prescription bottle and putting medications into her scrub top pocket. During an interview on 09/02/2025, beginning at 11:45 AM, the Administrator indicated Patient #2’s family placed the cameras the night before the 07/02/2025 incident with Hospice Aide 2. The family had relayed Hospice Aide 2 was in rooms of the home where she should not have been. RN 3 as notified by Patients' family of the police being called and provided the Hospice with the home video recordings. The Administrator indicated the hospice agency was not aware of any concerns by the family about Hospice Aide 2 until RN 3 was notified that the police were called and why on 07/02/2025. The Administrator indicated there were no other patients who reported complaints related to Hospice Aide 2; Hospice Aide 2 was terminated. The Administrator indicated she had not obtained the police report. The Administrator indicated she was unaware of the timeframe required to report to the State Agency regarding allegations or actual misappropriation of patient property.

Based on review of the clinical record, hospice policy, home visit observation, hospice personnel records and a police report, and interviews with local enforcement, family members and current and former hospice staff, the hospice failed to ensure hospice staff followed written policies and procedures for the management and disposal of controlled drugs in the patient's home for 4 of 8 sampled patients (Patient #3, #6, #7 and #8).
 
Failure to ensure hospice staff followed written policies and procedures for the management and disposal of controlled drugs (a medication requiring government control for the manufacture, distribution and use) in the patient's home increased the risk for the diversion and inappropriate use of controlled medications.

Review of the hospice's policy, titled Home Use and the Disposal of Controlled Substances, dated 12/2018, revealed the following: the pharmacy will dispense medications directly to the patient and will be responsible tracking the amount of medication used and length of time between renewals; the hospice registered nurse (RN) will be responsible for providing, discussing and documenting they provided and discussed the written policies and procedures on the management and disposal of controlled drugs to the patient/family; when a hospice patient no longer needs a controlled medication, the hospice RN will instruct the patient/family in the proper disposal of the drug in accordance with federal, state and local laws; the hospice RN will provide information on drug take-back and mail back programs, as well as the drug disposal container; the hospice RN, social worker or chaplain attending the patient's death will inform the family of their responsibility to dispose all of the patient's prescribed medications and will document the instruction given in a clinical note; if a family requests assistance with the disposal, the hospice employee will instruct and facilitate them with the proper disposal of the prescribed medications in the home; hospice staff will document the disposal in the record and include the medication name, dose, amount destroyed, date, location, method of destruction, witness to the destruction and the name of the person destroying the medication.
 
On 7/10/23 at 2:00 PM, during a phone interview with the hospice's Chief Compliance Officer, she confirmed the hospice last updated their drug disposal policy in 12/2018. The Chief Compliance Officer reported all staff have access to all of the hospices policies electronically. The Director of Integration is the leader of the clinical team which is responsible for staff education. Hospice nursing staff receive training on the hospices drug disposal policy upon hire during orientation and annually through computer training. The Chief Compliance Officer reported they would provide the training records for for Staff V, Former Hospice RN. The Chief Compliance Officer denied any prior drug diversion incidents with this hospice, and reported they had no reason to suspect a drug diversion had occurred. The Chief Compliance Officer reported the hospice supplied a Drug buster (container with a chemical agent inside which makes medications unusable) to all staff. Hospice nursing staff are to destroy controlled medications with a witness in the patient's home.
 
Review of the Hospice Admission Handbook provided by hospice staff to all patients/family or patient representatives at the time of admission to hospice revealed the handbook contained directions to the patient to follow federal guidelines in the disposal of medication, to follow drug labels and any drug inserts on the specific disposal for medication, take advantage of drug take back programs. The handbook advises that if there are no instructions on the prescription label or medication insert and no drug take back programs, the patient/family should throw the medications in the household trash after removing the medication from the original container and mixing the medication with an undesirable substance such as kitty litter or used coffee grounds and placing the mixture in a sealable bag. If the medication is a controlled substance, the hospice registered nurse (RN) will be responsible for providing, discussing and documenting they provided and discussed the written policies and procedures on the management and disposal of controlled drugs to the patient/family. When a hospice patient no longer needs a controlled medication, the hospice RN will instruct the patient/family in the proper disposal of the drug. The hospice RN, social worker or chaplain attending the patient's death will inform the family of their responsibility to dispose all of the patient's prescribed medications and will document the instruction given in a clinical note. Whenever possible, the hospice RN should schedule a home visit for the witnessed destruction for any medication left in the home. Hospice personnel will witness and instruct, not dispose of any patient medications. Hospice staff are not remove prescription medications from the patient's home. If the family refuses to allow the hospice RN witness/facilitate the disposal of medications, the nurse will document this in the record and notifies the patient's physician.
 
1. Review of a police report, dated 6/27/23, revealed a local law enforcement investigator found, photographed and seized the following prescription drugs/narcotics in the vehicle and garage belonging to Staff V, Former Hospice RN: 
 
1) A red pill bottle labeled Ondansetron (a medication used to treat nausea) with the name of Patient #8 on the label and pills inside the bottle located on a shelf in the garage.
 
2) A brown pill bottle labeled Lorazepam Intensol (a controlled medication used to treat anxiety; controlled medications are drugs/substance that require government control for making, using handling and storage) with the name of Patient #6 and liquid inside the bottle on a higher shelf in the garage.
 
3) A prescription bottle labeled Protonix (a medication used to treat/prevent excess stomach acid and gastric reflux) with Patient #3's name and with pills inside the bottle located in a grocery bag on the floor of the garage.
 
4) A box containing Levemir "injectors" (a type of injectable insulin in a multi-dose injection pen used to treat high blood sugar levels) with Patient #7's name on the label located in the grocery bag.

6) One loose Humalog injector pen and one loose Levemir injector pen from the grocery bag (no patient name identified).
 
7) A pill bottle labeled Hydrocodone (a type of controlled medication used to treat pain) with Patient #3's name on the label, and with an estimated number of at least 50 white pills inside the bottle out of a total number of initially 90 pills prescribed, found in the center console of the vehicle.
 
8) A prescription bottle labeled Tramadol (a type of controlled medication used to treat pain) with Patient #3's name on the label, and white pills inside the bottle, found in the center console of the vehicle.
 
9) A prescription bottle labeled Lorazepam (a type of controlled medication used to treat anxiety) with Patient #3's name on the label, and white pills inside the bottle, found in the front passenger seat of the vehicle.

11) A prescription bottle with a handwritten label "Tramadol" in black ink with 10 unknown pills (no patient name identified and no location).
 
The local law enforcement officer documented a family member (Family Member #1) of Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported staying at Staff V's house the previous night (6/26/23) and finding the prescription medications that did not belong in the home. On 7/6/23 at 11:38 PM, during an interview, the Local Law Enforcement Officer who wrote the police report on 6/27/23 reported the officers on the scene removed medication bottles from Staff V's, Former Hospice RN, vehicle belonging to 4 different persons. On 7/12/23 at 11:55 AM, during an interview, Family Member #1 (family member of Staff V, Former Hospice RN) reported not knowing about the prescription medications the police found in Staff V's car. Based on a review of clinical records, home visits, and staff interviews, it was determined that the hospice failed to ensure the provision of adequate social work services in six (#1, #6, #7, #10, #13, and #18) of nineteen (#1-#19) clinical records reviewed. The hospice social worker provided minimal services despite identified psychosocial needs, while psychosocial interventions typically within the scope of social work practice were performed by other members of the interdisciplinary team. This failure had the potential to affect all patients currently on census and may result in unmet psychosocial needs and a lack of discipline-specific care delivery. Findings follow:

A review of Clinical Record #1, with a start-of-care date of 04/28/25, identified a patient diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. Review of the document titled “Hospice Plan of Care Update” revealed documentation by the Medical Social Worker (MSW) stating, “Visits will be done at a minimum of once a month and increase visits as needed if possible since I am presently the only Social Worker and carry the whole caseload of our hospice,” indicating that visit frequency was determined by staff availability rather than patient needs. The MSW documented an attempted visit on 04/30/25, during which he was told to “go away” through the door. A telephone call was made on 05/02/25, at which time the patient’s spouse requested that the MSW “come next week.” No further attempts to contact or visits were documented after that date.A review of Clinical Record #6, with a start-of-care date of 11/13/25, identified a patient diagnosed with lung cancer. Review of the “Plan of Care Update” dated 11/13/25 revealed no social worker frequencies of visits, interventions or goals.A review of Clinical Record #7, with a start-of-care date of 10/27/25, identified a patient diagnosed with congestive heart failure. Review of a Chaplain initial visit note dated 10/29/25 revealed psychosocial concerns including the patient had an autistic son who lived in patient's home alone while patient resided in a nursing facility. Patient's nephew helped take care of the patient's autistic son but the nephew was unsure what would happen to the son after the patient's death. Review of the Social Worker initial note dated 10/30/25 revealed no assessment, interventions, or goals relating to the psychosocial issues the chaplain had identified.A review of Clinical Record #10, with a start-of-care date of 11/16/25, identified a patient diagnosed with cerebrovascular accident. Review of a Chaplain initial visit note dated 11/19/25 identified psychosocial concerns, including the patient’s reported feelings of disconnection and lack of communication with his daughter, by the following statement, “He is married to [named person]. She has her children and he has his. His children are twins, a girl and a boy. The girl [named person] stopped talking to him when he remarried…” Review of the Medical Social Worker (MSW) initial visit note dated 12/01/25 revealed no assessment, interventions, or goals relating to the psychosocial issues the chaplain had identified. A review of Clinical Record #13, with a start-of-care date of 11/06/25, identified a patient diagnosed with lung cancer. Observation of the Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) meeting on 12/09/25 revealed the identification of multiple psychosocial concerns, including the patient’s expressed fear of her daughter and the potential for financial exploitation by the daughter. The Skilled Nurse (SN) reported that upon the daughter’s release from jail, she removed the patient from the skilled nursing facility because she could not afford rent without access to the patient’s income. Despite the complexity of these psychosocial issues, the Medical Social Worker (MSW) provided minimal input, and the plan of care reflected a visit frequency of once per month.A review of Clinical Record #18, with a start-of-care date of 08/20/25, identified a patient diagnosed with diastolic congestive heart failure. Review of the document titled “Hospice Plan of Care Update” revealed documentation indicating “MSW declined at this time.” The Medical Social Worker (MSW) documented a telephone call on 08/22/25 with the patient’s niece, during which the niece stated that a visit was not needed at that time but requested that the MSW call back in a couple of weeks. The MSW documented agreement with this plan; however, no further contact attempts or visits were documented after that date. During a home visit conducted on 12/11/25, the patient’s niece was asked whether she would be agreeable to MSW visits and stated that she would be agreeable.During an interview conducted on 12/12/25 at 9:30 a.m., Agency Personnel #1 and #2 confirmed that the agency failed to provide psychosocial assessments, interventions, or goals related the patient and family needs.

Based on record review and interview the hospice agency failed to immediately investigate allegations of misappropriation of patient funds (see tag L509), take appropriate corrective action based on the allegations (see tag L510), report the incident within 5 working days of the discovery of the violation (see tag L511), and ensure patients were free from misappropriation of funds (see tag L517).

The cumulative effect of these systemic problems resulted in the hospice agency's inability to ensure the provision of quality health care in a safe environment and resulted in the agency being found out of compliance with the condition 42 CFR 418.52 Patient Rights.

Based on record review and interview, the agency failed to immediately investigate allegations of misappropriation for 2 of 2 misappropriation allegations (Patients #1 and 2).
Findings include:

1. A review of an abuse/ neglect policy indicated exploitation by money misuse or theft required immediate action, investigation, and prevention of further exploitation. 
2. A review of the complaint process identified a purpose to ";... protect patient and family rights ...." 
3. A review of the incident reporting policy indicated a purpose of the policy was to ";... establish a foundation for early investigation of all potentially serious events." The policy indicated the person discovering the incident must follow – up with the patient and family.
4. During an interview on 6/12/2024 at 9:30 AM, the Director of Professional Services (DPS) indicated a law enforcement detective came to the office on 4/15/2024 to have the Administrator identify a picture of an employee accused of theft from Patient #2. The DPS indicated HA 1 was the employee in the picture. The DPS indicated this was the first time the agency was notified of the theft.
5. When asked during an interview on 6/13/2024 at 2:19 PM, the DPS indicated the agency had not completed an investigation into the theft allegations from Patient #2s family.
6. On 6/14/2024 the agency provided documentation of an investigation which included an undated document with a total of 9 patient names. Four patients had brief descriptions of the patient/ family experience with the agency. There were 5 patient names with a note that a message was left regarding the patient/ family experience with the agency. The document ended with ";Per [Administrator]." When asked, the DPS reported the Administrator made calls on 6/13/2024 to active patients who received care from HA 1. 
7. During an interview on 6/14/2024 at 11:50 AM, the Administrator confirmed the account of the DPS but added that the detective received another theft report against HA 1 from the family of Patient #1. When asked, the Administrator indicated they did not contact Patient #1s family as the family did not report the theft to the agency. The Administrator confirmed the detective identified Patient #1 as an alleged victim of theft by HA 1. The Administrator indicated they did not follow up with the family as the theft report was ";hearsay." When asked, the Administrator indicated they dont rely on second - hand information.
The Administrator indicated they called the active patients who received services from HA 1 to ensure they had concerns about HA 1 as part of the investigation. 
8. On 6/20/2024, the Administrator provided a list of family members of 37 active and former patients who received services from HA 1. The Administrator indicated they called them to ensure there were no concerns regarding HA 1 as part of the investigation.
The agency failed to investigate allegations of misappropriation until the survey was initiated.

Based on review of the agency's polices titled "Rights and Ethics 401: Reporting Abuse and Neglect or Exploitation", revised 9/21, staff interview and clinical record review, the Administrator failed to provide oversite of the agency as designated by the Governing Body. Failure of the administrative oversite was revealed upon review of three of three patients (P) (P#1, P#2 and P#3) records reviewed for abuse allegations.

1. The agency received an allegation of abuse on 11/1/21, towards P#1 by Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) #AA. P#1 was residing at the agency's inpatient unit (IPU) receiving respite care at the time of the alleged abuse. The alleged abuse was reported to have occurred on 10/26/21. 

2. The hospice agency received an allegation of abuse on 11/1/21, towards P#2 by CNA #AA. P#2 was residing at the agency's IPU receiving respite care at the time of the alleged abuse. The alleged abuse was reported to have occurred on 10/30/21. 

3. The agency received an allegation of abuse on 6/14/21, towards P#3 by CNA #AA. P#3 was residing at the agency's IPU recviing respite care at the time of the alleged abuse. The alleged abuse was reported to have occurred on 6/4/21. The administrator failed to provide oversite to the agency and follow the agency policy titled "Rights and Ethics 401", revised 9/21, by not taking the following actions immediately upon receipt of the report of the alleged abuse:

 The administrator failed to provide oversite to the agency and follow the agency policy titled "Rights and Ethics 401", revised 9/21, by not taking the following actions immediately upon receipt of the report of alleged abuse:
 
a. #6 of the policy requires a verbal report of any allegations of abuse to be made to Adult Protective Services Central Intake Division of the Georgia Department of Human Resources. The Administrator failed to provide oversite by not reporting the allegation of abuse to this entity.

b. #7 the policy requires the agency to report any allegations of abuse to be reported to Georgia Department of Community Health within 24 hours or the next business day. The Administrator failed to ensure the department was notified of the allegations of abuse.

c. #8 the policy requires the agency to document assessment, interventions and referrals in the medical record for any patient for whom there are allegations of abuse. The Administrator failed to provide oversite by not ensuring that documentation in the medical record of P#1 to reflect comprehensive physical and psychosocial assessment, interventions and referrals for the possible abuse.

d. #9 the policy requires the agency to reassign any employee suspected of abuse to nonclinical duties. The Administrator failed to provide oversite by failing to remove CNA #AA from clinical care of patients on after being notified of the possible abuse 11/1/21. CNA #AA provided direct patient care on at the agency's IPU on 11/2/21, 11/3/21 and 11/4/21.

The Administrator was made informed via email provided by the Department of Community Health, Division of Healthcare Regulation on 11/23/21 at 4:05 p.m.

The record contains correct clinical information that is available to the patient’s attending physician and hospice staff. The record may be maintained electronically or on paper. This standard was not met as evidenced by clinical record review and interview. In 2 of 19 (11%) clinical records reviewed. the agency did not have physician orders included in the plan of care based on the patient's individualized needs.

However, the current plan of care did not include physician orders for condom catheters or interventions of education and assessments. During a joint record review, an interview with the Director of Nursing on 4/6/2023 confirmed a physician order for the condom catheter was missing from the patient's plan of care. 

Clinical Record 13: The patient with an election of hospice benefits dated 10/12/2022 had a primary diagnosis of cerebral palsy and a PEG tube. The plan of care update order dated 2/3/2023 documented "hospice to provide instructions for performing gastrostomy feedings to include care of equipment and preparation of feedings." The plan of care update order dated 2/3/2023 documented "hospice to provide instructions for performing gastrostomy feedings to include care of equipment and preparation of feedings," however, the patient was not receiving tube feedings and was able to swallow and eat meals per the nursing assessments. Based on clinical record review, staff interview and review of the policy titled "" ASSESSMENT AND PLAN OF CARE, RESTRAINTS", it was determined the hospice agency failed to ensure the verbal order for the application of restraints was complete and not used an as needed ( PRN) order for 1 of 1 sampled patients (P) (#1).

The findings include:

Review of the clinical record for Patient #1 with an admission date of 4/20/22, and diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease revealed a verbal order dated 4/22/22, for restraints the order does not include necessary elements for the safety of the patient. The order lacks a time limit for restraints, the type of restraint used, frequency of monitoring process as well as a mandatory release at least every 30 minutes per agency policy titled, " ASSESSMENT AND PLAN OF CARE, RESTRAINTS" item B, revised December 2, 2008 page 17. 

During a telephone interview on 5/3/22, at 11:18 a.m., regarding restraints the Medical Director stated restraints were ordered for P#1 on 4/22/22, if the patient exhibited out of control and combative behavior. According to the Medical Director, P#1 had engaged in combative behaviors at home and needed to be sent to an inpatient unit for stabilization. When asked if he was aware that P#1 had been in restraints from 4/22-5/3/22, the Medical Director states he was not aware the patient had been in restraints and had not been given a report from the staff that P#1 was being restrained. The Medical Director denied giving any orders for the patient to be restrained after 4/22/22, and stated he does not want any of his patients to be restrained however, if the need for restraints is required the expectation is the restraints will be removed immediately when the patient is calm. 

During an interview on 5/5/22, at 3:00 p.m.,the Director of Clinical Services acknowledged the restraint order was incomplete.

Based on staff interview, observation and review of the agency policy titled, " ASSESSMENT AND PLAN OF CARE, RESTRAINTS" and the lack of evidence provided to the surveyor by Longleaf Hospice it was determined the hospice failed to ensure a medical and behavioral evaluation was conducted to manage the violent behaviors which resulted in the application of restraints for 1of 1 patients (P) #1. 

During observation on 5/2/22, at approximately 10:30 a.m., with the Registered Nurse (RN) AA from Longleaf Hospice, this surveyor observed an elderly gentleman laying in bed with a vest restraint applied and tied to the bed frame, hand mittens on both hands with full side rails raised on both sides of the bed. Patient #1 was lying still in bed with eyes closed and appeared to be asleep. During the visit P#1 did mumble at times but this surveyor was unable to understand what was said, RN AA assessed P#1 and completed vital signs assessment without difficulty. RN AA prompted P#1 to drink from straw but the patient was unable to follow this command. This surveyor questioned RN AA why patient was restrained and RN AA answered she did not know however, she reported P#1 had been grabbing and squeezing the staff's arms forcefully. No combative or aggressive behavior was exhibited during the visit. The patient required several prompts to awaken and appeared lethargic when awaken with eyes slightly open, mumbling and slow movement. 

During a telephone interview on 5/3/22, at 11:18 a.m. ,regarding restraints the Medical Director stated restraints were ordered for P#1 on 4/22/22, if the patient exhibited out of control and combative behavior. According to the Medical Director, P#1 had engaged in combative behaviors at home and needed to be sent to an inpatient unit for stabilization. When asked if he was aware the patient had been in restraints from 4/22-5/3/22, the Medical Director states he was not aware the patient had been in restraints and had not been given a report from the staff that the patient was being restrained. During an interview on 5/5/22, at 3:00 p.m., the Director of Clinical Services acknowledged the lack of a medical and behavioral evaluation conducted to manage the documented behaviors exhibited such as grabbing and squeezing the staff's arms forcefully, combative behavior, agitation, hallucinations and restlessness using alternatives and other less restrictive measures on 4/22, 4/23,4/24, 4/25, 4/26, 4/27, 4/28, 4/29, 4/30, 5/1, and 5/2/22.

Based on review of policy and procedures, observation, and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure patients are informed of all their rights, and the hospice must protect and promote the exercise of these rights. This deficient practice prevents patients from making informed decisions regarding their care.

Findings include:Facility policy and procedure titled, "PATIENT RIGHTS AND RESPONSIBILITIES POLICY NUMBER: AD.P15 ", revealed: "...POLICY: Dignity Hospice informs patients of their rights, and protects and promotes the exercise of these rights. Policy and Procedures: Agency policy E.87200.604, last revised on 07/03/2023, titled "Restraints, Non-Violent/Non-Self-Destructive and Violent Self Destructive" stated in part, "Restraints may only be imposed to ensure the immediate physical safety of the patient, a staff member, or others and must be discontinued at the earliest possible time.

Policy and Procedures: Agency policy E.87200.604, last revised on 07/03/2023, titled "Restraints, Non-Violent/Non-Self-Destructive and Violent Self-Destructive," stated in part, The policy requires that a physician responsible for the care of the patient order the restraint before the application of restraint.

Based on review of agency policy and procedure, the hospice's training curriculum, personnel records and interviews with agency staff, the hospice failed to ensure the hospice developed a comprehensive restraint and seclusion policy and ensured that all patient care staff working in the hospice inpatient unit receive training on the safe use of restraints and seclusion. Failure to properly train staff on the use of restraints and seclusion has the potential to put hospice patients health and welfare at risk.

Review of the agency policy and procedure entitled ";Hospice Care Center Use of Restraints Policy" dated 08/2023 revealed the policy does not include the following information to ensure the policy is written in accordance with State law:
-Restraints or seclusion are used only after less restrictive interventions have been determined to be ineffective to protect the patient, staff, or others from harm.
-The type of technique of restraint or seclusion used is the least restrictive intervention.
-The use of a restraint is in accordance with a written modification of the patients plan of care and implementation is in accordance with safe and appropriate techniques.
-Orders for the use of restraints or seclusion are never written as a standing order or on an as needed basis.
-The medical director/physician designee is consulted as soon as possible if the attending physician did not order the restraint or seclusion.
-Each order for restraint or seclusion may only be renewed in accordance with age and restraint/seclusion limitations for up to a total of 24 hours (for adults 18 years or older, the limit is 4 hours). After 24 hours, before a new order is written, a physician authorized to order restraints or seclusion must see and assess the patient.
-The restraint or seclusion must be discontinued at the earliest possible time, regardless of the length of time identified in the order.
-The condition of the restrained or secluded patient must be monitored by an appropriately trained physician or staff at an interval determined by hospice policy.
-The patients right to safe implementation of restraints or seclusion by staff who have been appropriately trained and have demonstrated competency in the application of restraints, implementation of seclusion, monitoring, assessment, and providing care for a restrained or secluded patient.
 
-Training intervals to include training and demonstration of competency as part of orientation, and subsequently on a periodic basis.
-Training content and requirement for physicians and appropriate staff to have education, training, and demonstrated knowledge based on the specific needs of the patient population to include:
-Techniques to identify staff and patient behaviors, events, and environmental factors that may trigger circumstances that require the use of a restraint or seclusion.
-The use of nonphysical intervention skills.
-Choosing the least restrictive intervention based on individualized assessment of the patients medical, or behavioral status or condition.
-The safe application and use of all types of restraints or seclusion used in the hospice, including training on how to recognize and respond to signs of physical and psychological distress (for example, positional asphyxia).
-Clinical identification of specific behavioral changes that indicate restraint or seclusion is no longer necessary.
-Monitoring the physical and psychological well- being of the patient who is restrained or secluded, including but not limited to, respiratory and circulatory status, skin integrity, vital signs, and any special requirements specified by the hospice policy associated with the one (1) hour face to face evaluation.
-The use of first aid techniques and certification in the use of cardiopulmonary resuscitation, including required periodic recertification.
-Trainer Requirements to ensure that staff who conduct the training are qualified as evidenced by education, training, and experience in techniques used to address patients behaviors.
-Training documentation. The hospice must document in the staff personnel records that the training and demonstration of competency were successfully completed."
-The requirement that the patient must be seen face-to -face within 1 hour after initiation of the intervention by an appropriately physician or Registered Nurse to evaluate the patients condition, reaction/response to the intervention, need to continue or terminate the intervention.
-Documentation requirements regarding the one-hour face to face medical and behavioral evaluation, description of the patients behavior and intervention used, alternative or less restrictive interventions attempted, and the patients condition tat warranted the use of a restraint or seclusion, the patients response to the intervention used, and the rationale for continued use of the intervention.

Based on observation, interview, and record review, the agency failed to ensure patients medication profile were being reviewed for two of 14 sampled patients (Patients 2 and 3) when:
1. For Patient 2, the agency did not develop policies and procedures in obtaining informed consent (a voluntary consent of the patient to take psychotropic medication) for psychotropic medications (medications that affect behavior, mood, thoughts, or perception) use. Four out of five of Patient 2s psychotropic medications did not have informed consent form signed by the patient/responsible party.
2. For Patient 3, the agency did not ensure a medication reconciliation was conducted during nursing and supervisory visit for Patient 3.
These failures had the potential to cause ineffective drug therapy, significant side effects and noncompliance with drug therapy, placing Patients 2 and 3s health at risk.
 

1. A review of Patient 2s ";Patient Information Report" (a document that gives a summary of patients information) and plan of care (a document that provides direction of type of nursing care a patient needs), indicated a start of care date of April 13, 2023, with a recertification period of July 12, 2023, to October 9, 2023. Further review indicated Patient 2 had a diagnosis of Alzheimers disease (a progressive disease that destroys memory and other important mental functions), anxiety (feelings of excessive, unrealistic worry and tension with little or no reason), insomnia (inability to sleep) and hypertension (elevated blood pressure).
 
During a review of facility provided document titled, ";Client Medication Report," dated September 15, 2024, it indicated the following:
 
 i. Haloperidol (antipsychotic medication) 2 milligrams tablets, 1 tablet every 3 hours for agitation, start date May 18, 2023. 
 
 ii. Lorazepam (antianxiety medication) 1 milligram tablet, 1 tablet every 3 hours for anxiety, start date September 12, 2023.
 
 iii. Risperidone (antipsychotic medication) 0.25 milligram tablet, 2 tablets, 2 times daily for agitation, start date June 28, 2023.
 
 iv. Temazepam (sedative hypnotic) 30 milligram capsules, 1 capsule at bedtime for insomnia, start date May 18, 2023.
 
 v. Trazodone (antidepressant) 50 milligram tablet, 4 tablets at bedtime for insomnia, start date June 28, 2023.
 
During a home visit on September 13, 2023, at 12:49 PM, with a Registered Nurse (RN), RN inspected Patient 2s medication bottles, which were available in the home. The medication bottles were inside the kitchens cabinet. RN compared them with Patient 2s most current medicine list. 
During further observation and interview, on September 13, 2023, at 12:51 PM, with RN, RN found the following psychotropic medications:
i. A sealed bottle containing Haloperidol (medication use to treat agitation) 2 milligrams (unit of measurement) tablets. 
ii. An opened bottle of Lorazepam (medication to treat anxiety) 1 milligram tablet.
ii. An opened bottle of Risperidone (medication to treat agitation) 0.25 milligram tablet.
iv. An opened bottle of Temazepam (medication to treat insomnia) 30 milligram capsules.
v. An opened bottle of Trazodone (medication to treat insomnia) 50 milligram tablet.
RN stated, psychotropic medications must have an informed consent. 
During a follow up interview and record review, on September 13, 2023, at 12:53 PM, with RN, RN reviewed Patient 2s ";Hospice Admissions Booklet (provided by the agency to keep at home)" and was not able to find informed consent for the psychotropic medications. RN stated, ";It must be in the patients records, at the office."
During a concurrent record review and interview, with the Administrator (Admin), on September 14, 2023, at 2:25 PM, the Admin reviewed Patient 2s document titled, ";Informed Consent for Psychotropic Medications," dated April 13, 2023, which indicated ";... A physician or NP [Nurse Practitioner] has prescribed the following psychotropic medication(s):... Lorazepam." Admin stated, Patient 2's Haloperidol, Risperidone, Temazepam and Trazodone were not included in the informed consent.
During further interview, with the Admin, on September 15, 2023, at 9:20 AM, the Admin stated, it was the nurses responsibility to obtain informed consent for all psychotropic medications, to assure families understand the mediations, side effects and potential for chemical restraint. Admin stated, it was part of the hospice admission booklet. Admin was not able to provide policies and procedures regarding obtaining informed consent for psychotropic medications.
2. A review of Patient 3s ";Patient Information Report" and plan of care, indicated a start of care date of September 9, 2023, with a recertification period of September 6, 2023, to December 4, 2023. Further review indicated Patient 3 had diagnoses of severe protein-calorie malnutrition (when patient has muscle wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat, bedridden or significantly reduced functional capacity), heart failure (when heart does not pump blood as well as it should), bed confinement (bedridden), urinary incontinence (loss of bladder control). 
During a home visit on September 13, 2023, at 1:28 PM, with a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN), LPN inspected Patient 3s medication bottles, which were available in the home. The medication bottles were on top of the kitchens table. LPN compared them with Patient 3s most current medicine list. 
During a concurrent observation and interview, on September 13, 2023, at 1:36 PM, with LPN, LPN found a small bag, which contained Bisacodyl (medication use to treat constipation) 10 milligrams (unit of measurement) suppository. LPN counted the contents of the bag and stated there were six suppositories in the bag. LPN reviewed Patient 3s ";Medicine list," dated September 13, 2023, and stated Bisacodyl suppositories medications were not included in Patient 3s medicine list. LPN stated nurses should reconcile the medicine profile with the medications on hand every home visit.
During concurrent interview and record review of Patient 3s current medicine list, on September 14, 2023, at 3:05 PM, the Director of Patient Care Services (DCPS) acknowledged Patient 3s current medicine list did not include Bisacodyl 10 milligrams. The DPCS stated medications should be reconciled by nurses every home visit and update the medicine list.
During a concurrent record review and interview, with the DCPS, on September 14, 2023, at 3:12 PM, the DCPS reviewed the agencys undated policy and procedure (P&P) titled ";Medication Reconciliation", which indicated ";... Medications ordered while the patient is receiving care will be compared to the medication list/profile. The medication list/profile will be updated with each new or changed medication." The DPCS stated the agency did not follow the policy.

Based on patient record review and staff interview, the Agency failed to ensure the hospice interdisciplinary group reviews, revises, and documents the individualized plan as frequently as the patient condition requires to ensure that care and services provided are based on all assessments of the patient and family needs. This was evident in one (1) of four (4) patient records reviewed (Patient #4).
 
Failure to ensure the hospice interdisciplinary group reviews, revises, and documents the individualized plan as frequently as the patient condition requires to ensure that care and services provided are based on all assessments of the patient and family needs has the potential for negative patient outcomes. 
 
The findings are:
 

 
Patient #4 has a start of care date of 04/20/2024 with diagnoses of Malignant Neoplasm of Pancreas, Secondary Malignant Neoplasm of Right Lung as documented on the "Physician's Plan of Care start date 04/20/2024, end date 07/18/2024".
 
The "Physician's Plan of Care start date 04/20/2024, end date 07/18/2024" documents orders for "Professional Nurse: Registered Nurse 1 -2 x week x 14 weeks (one to two visits a week for fourteen weeks), and PRN 2 (two as needed visits) for change in condition". Registered Nurse to make "assessment visit and admit to Hospice Care". Social Worker/Counselor 1-2 x month x 4 month (one to two visits a month for four months), Chaplain 1-2 x month x 4 months (one to two visits a month for four months).

This had the potential to cause patient and caregiver concerns to be unaddressed.

Review of the Arizona Adult Protective Services website, located at https://des.az.gov/services/basic-needs/adult-protective-services/report-adult-abuse, revealed, ". . . Arizona Adult Protective Services (APS) investigates reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults. APS may also become involved when there is a claim of self-neglect, which is when an adult with physical or mental impairments is not able to meet their basic needs (such as food, shelter, health care, managing money, etc.), which then impacts the adults physical health, mental health or general safety. The goal of APS is to prioritize an adults right to make their own decisions while keeping them safe.
APS tries to support the vulnerable adults in their current home, and to augment the skills they need to take care of themselves by providing services that can help with challenges the adult may be having. However, APS must always balance the need to protect the safety of the vulnerable adult with the adults right to make their own decisions.
APS does not conduct safety checks, but local law enforcement does. Law enforcement and APS work together, and if law enforcement believes an individual is a vulnerable adult, they will contact APS . . ."

Regular/short-acting insulin are usually taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal.2. Regular/short-acting insulin onset time (how quickly insulin lowers the blood sugar) is 30 minutes.3. Regular/short-acting insulin peak time (period when insulin is at maximum strength that allows adjustment of food intake or activity level to prevent severely low blood sugar) is 2-3 hours.4. Regular/short-acting insulin duration (how long insulin works to lower your blood sugar) is 3-6 hours.5. Intermediate-acting insulin “covers insulin needs for half a day or overnight” with onset of 2-4 hours, peak time of 4-12 hours, and duration of 12-18 hours.[Source: https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/about/how-to-use-insulin.html] During a review of a published journal from the American Diabetes Association (ADA), titled “Diabetes Care: 13. Older Adults: Standards of Care in Diabetes---2025,” dated 12/9/2024, the publication indicated the following:1. It is recommended that episodes of hypoglycemia at routine visits must be ascertained and addressed because older adults with diabetes have a greater risk of hypoglycemia, especially when treated with hypoglycemia agents, such as insulin.2. Older adults might be at a higher risk of hypoglycemia for many reasons, including irregular meal intake, insulin deficiency requiring insulin therapy, and worsening kidney function.3. Older adults have higher rates of unidentified cognitive impairment and dementia, leading to difficulties in performing complex self-care activities, such as blood sugar monitoring and insulin dose adjustment.4. Cognitive decline has been associated with increased risk of hypoglycemia, and severe hypoglycemia has been linked to increased risk of dementia.5. Glycemic goals (target blood sugar levels) and pharmacologic treatments might need to be adjusted to minimize the occurrence of hypoglycemic events.6. For people with diabetes receiving palliative care and end-of-life care, the focus must be to avoid hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia while reducing the burdens of glycemic management (process of regulating blood sugar levels). Thus, as organ failure develops, the treatment plan would have to be deintensified and one or more agents would need to be discontinued. At the end of life, most agents for type 2 diabetes might be removed. Based on record review and staff interviews, it was determined that the hospice failed to ensure that hospice aides receive at least l2 hours of in-service training during each 12-month period. In-service training may occur while an aide is furnishing care to a patient. This deficient practice has the potential that the personnel members are not being educated on the most current evidence-based practices that promote safe, effective patient care, posing the risk for injury to both the personnel member and patient.

Upon patient record review, 3 of 14 (Patients #1,#2,#6) did not have evidence in the patient record that the hospice has developed an individualized written plan of care for each patient. The plan of care must reflect patient/family goals and interventions based on the problems identified in the initial, comprehensive, and updated comprehensive assessments. The plan of care must include all services necessary for the palliation and management of the terminal illness and related conditions.
Patient 1: The medical record contained nursing documentation upon admission identifying patient had a history of a fall with fracture and was a high risk for falls. There was no evidence of problem, goals, and interventions related to fall safety included in the plan of care. Corrected on site. 
Patient 2: The medical record contained nursing documentation upon admission identifying patient had dyspnea and edema related to cardiac dysfunction. There were problems identified in the plan of care for altered cardiopulmonary function and respiratory dysfunction, however, there was no evidence of goals and interventions related to those issues. Corrected on site.

Based on facility policy, record review, and interview it was determined that the hospice failed to provide supervised assessment and competency based orientation. This deficiency poses a risk to the patients and the staff of injury and has a negative impact on healthcare outcome. 

Findings include:
A review of Infinite Hospice Policy No. 3-002.1, titled, ";Competency Based Orientation", revealed, ";... Policy Hospice ensures that the competency of all personnel is assessed on hire, prior to providing care to hospice patients...
A review of Employees files #4, #5, #6, #7, #8, and #9 revealed that no skills verification had been performed or documented.
Interview with Employee #1 confirmed that s/he had done a verbal skills assessment only by signing the forms. Employee #1 confirmed in interview on October 30, 2023 that s/he has no clinical experience.

It is required that if a patient revokes the election of hospice care or is discharged from hospice per hospice regulation §418.26 (i.e., no longer terminally ill), the hospice forwards to the patient’s attending physician: a copy of the hospice discharge summary and the patient's record, if requested.

This standard was not met as evidenced by a review of clinical records, document reviews, and interviews. 1 of 2 (50%) applicable clinical records of patients who revoked hospice services were reviewed and revealed the hospice did not ensure the revocation statement was signed by the patient, as required by hospice policy.. 

Record #4 was reviewed and revealed the patient elected hospice services on 5/16/22 and revoked hospice services on 6/4/22. The clinical record revealed the caregiver at the patient's group home called and stated the patient fell, had a laceration and was sent to the emergency room. In addition, the record revealed the "End of Care Summary" dated 6/4/22 included, "patient entered a facility to seek aggressive treatment and non-palliative care." The "Discharge Hospice Item Set" dated 6/4/22 documented, "patient revoked." The physician's order dated 6/4/22 documented, "discharged revoked." There was no signed revocation statement in the clinical record. 

"Revocation of Hospice Benefit" Policy No. 1-024, revised October 2019, included, "The patient will choose to revoke his/her election of hospice benefit when he/she elects active treatment inconsistent with the role of palliative care" and "A revocation of election of hospice care statement will be signed by the patient and will document the date, time and reason for the revocation". 

 During interview 7/16/22, the Executive Director/Director Clinical Services stated the group home called her to report the patient was sent to the emergency room for stitches and that she spoke to the patient's representative who stated the patient was coming off services at the hospice and would be going to a new facility after discharge from the hospital. The Executive Director/Director Clinical Services stated a revocation form was not signed.
