During the investigation of the complaint and the hospice's self-reported incident, the on-site survey team identified an Immediate Jeopardy (IJ) situation (a crisis situation that placed the health and safety of patients at risk) related to the Condition of Participation for Interdisciplinary Group (IDG), Care Planning and Coordination of Services (CFR 481.56). The hospice failed to ensure hospice nursing staff administered medications to hospice patients per the patient's Plan of Care (POC) and physician orders.
 
While on-site, the survey team identified an Immediate Jeopardy (IJ) situation and notified the administrative staff on 7/13/23 at 1:15 PM. The hospice staff acted and removed the immediacy of the situation prior to the survey team exiting the complaint investigation when the hospice administrative staff took the following steps: Provided reeducation of all hospice nursing staff on verification of physician orders, following and updating the patient's plan of care and death at home visits, as well as monitoring of all medication orders and monitoring of daily nursing visit notes by the administrative staff. 
 
The following Condition level deficiency remained for the Condition of Participation for 42 CFR 481.56 IDG, Care Planning and Coordination of Services. Based on clinical record review, hospice policy review, family interview, local law enforcement officer interview, current and former hospice staff interviews, the hospice failed to ensure nursing hospice staff provided hospice care and services based on the patient's POC and physician orders for 2 of 8 sampled patients (Patients #3 and #4).
 
Failure to ensure hospice nursing staff provide care and services in accordance with the patient's POC and physician orders resulted in the potential hastening of a patient's death and another patient not receiving treatment as ordered. 

Review of the hospice's policy, titled IDG Coordination of Care, dated 3/3/23, revealed the IDG is made up of physicians, nurses, social workers, clergy, therapists, counselors, volunteers, hospice aides and homemakers. The hospice IDG maintains professional management of the provision of services and ensures the safe and effective delivery of care and services. The registered nurse (RN) case manager is responsible for the communication of changes in the patient's status and coordination of services with the IDG and the patient's attending physician (if a patient chooses an attending physician). Hospice staff are responsible for the communication and documentation of changes in a timely manner in the clinical record. Hospice staff will document the date and time of communication and the individuals involved in the communication. The IDG will conduct assessments, develop and update the POC and review the effectiveness of the POC at a minimum of every 15 days. The IDG will consult on the selection of the most appropriate drugs to meet the patient's needs with an individual that has experience and education in the management and the use of drugs per acceptable standards of practice for hospice patients. 
 
Review of the hospice's undated policy, titled Plan of Care, revealed hospice staff are required to provide care and services to patients in accordance with an individualized POC based on the initial and ongoing assessment of the patient and family/caregiver. The POC will identify the patient's needs and services to meet those needs including the management of pain and symptom relief. 
 
Review of the hospice's policy, titled Verification of Physician Orders, dated 12/2018, revealed hospice licensed professional staff are responsible for obtaining and documenting verbal orders from a licensed physician or other authorized independent practitioner for hospice care and services provided to patients. The hospice licensed professional staff are responsible for reading back all verbal and telephone orders to the healthcare practitioner or representative issuing the order and documenting the order in the electronic medical record. Hospice staff will send a copy of the order to the healthcare practitioner for signature and retain a copy of the signed order in the patient's clinical record within 30 days of initiation of the order. 
 
1. Patient #4 had a hospice admission date of 4/14/22, received routine home care hospice services while residing in a private residence until 5/24/22, then received continuous (services provided daily, up to 8 hours per day) hospice services at home from 5/25/22 until the patient's death at the patient's home on 6/7/22.
 
a. Review of the hospice's self reported incident to the State Agency and the hospice's complaint log, dated 6/28/23, included documentation that a family member(s) of Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported Staff V informed the family members that Staff V assisted a terminally ill hospice patient to commit suicide. The hospice's Chief Compliance Officer confirmed Staff V, Former Hospice RN, had provided nursing services to this patient prior to the patient passing in June 2022.
 
b. On 7/10/23 at 2:00 PM, during a phone interview with the hospice's Chief Compliance Officer and the hospices attorney, the Chief Compliance Officer reported on 6/24/23, she received a call from a family member of Staff V's, Former Hospice RN, but had been unable to reach and speak with the family member until 6/28/23. Family Member #2 reported Staff V, Former Hospice RN, had been historically diverting drugs and had assisted a patient with hastening their death. Family Member #2 reported Staff V, Former Hospice RN, had talked about helping to hasten the death of Patient #4, a former hospice patient, and Family Member #2 thought this patient was a former physician. The Chief Compliance Officer confirmed the hospice had a patient by that name the Family Member #2 had reported and the patient had been a physician. The Chief Compliance Officer explained the hospice was still in the process of investigating the complaint, but the hospice did find concerns with a clinical narrative note written by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, on 6/7/22, the date that Patient #4 died. The clinical narrative note stated Staff V, Former Hospice RN, delivered Oxycodone (controlled medication used to treat pain/ a controlled medication is any medication that requires government regulation for the manufacture, distribution and use) and Ativan (drug trade name for Lorazepam, a controlled medication used to treat anxiety, agitation and restlessness) every 15 minutes to control pain and restlessness. The clinical record lacked an order for Ativan and Oxycodone every 15 minutes. The Chief Compliance Officer explained this was not a typical order and staff should never administer a narcotic pain medication and Ativan (the potential drug interaction between Lorazepam and Opioids such Oxycodone or Morphine can lead to slowed and difficulty breathing and possibly death) at this frequency without a physician order.
 
c. Review of a police report, dated 6/27/23, revealed a local law enforcement investigator found, photographed and seized prescription drugs/narcotics in the vehicle and garage belonging to Staff V, Former Hospice RN. The local law enforcement office identified the prescription medications belonged to former hospice patients (See L0694). On 6/27/23, according to documentation by the local law enforcement officer, Family Member #1 reported to the officer that Staff V, Former Hospice RN, bragged about assisting in the suicide of Patient #4, but had no other information.
 
d. On 7/6/23 at 11:38 PM, during an interview, the Local Law Enforcement Officer who wrote the police report on 6/27/23 reported the officers on the scene removed medication bottles from Staff V's, Former Hospice RN, vehicle belonging to 4 different persons. The Local Law Enforcement Officer reported they had been unable to obtain any information in regards to whether or not Staff V, Former Hospice RN, had assisted the patient in committing suicide or hastening their deaths. The Local Law Enforcement Officer reported he tried to contact the hospice for information, but the hospice agency would only provide a policy on the disposal of controlled drugs.
 
e. On 7/10/23 at 1:19 PM, during an interview, a Law Enforcement Officer with their agency's records department, reported their was no information regarding any possible pursuit of case concerning Staff V, Former Hospice RN, regarding the death of Patient #4. 
 
f. On 7/12/23 at 11:55 AM, during an interview, Family Member #1 (family member of Staff V, Former Hospice RN) reported not knowing any specifics about how Staff V assisted Patient #4 end the patient's life. Family Member #1 explained Staff V, Former Hospice RN, talked about Patient #4 all of the time, and Family Member #1 knew Patient #4 had been a hospice patient. Family Member #1 reported Staff V, Former Hospice RN, told the family member that Patient #4 asked Staff V to help end Patient #4's life. Staff V told Family Member #1 that Staff V did help end the patient #4's life. Family Member #1 reported Staff V, Former Hospice RN, wanted to tell Family Member #1 the details about the patient's death, but Family Member #1 would not let Staff V tell them about the specifics of patients death. According to Family Member #1, Staff V, Former Hospice RN, expressed that Staff V thought she might get money from Patient #4 when the patient passed, but Family Member #1 was not sure if this had anything to do with why Staff V helped to end the patient's life. Family Member #1 thought Staff V, Former Hospice RN, told them about ending Patient #4's life sometime this last fall in 2022. 
 
g. On 7/12/23 at 1:54 PM, during an interview, Family Member #2 (family member of Staff V, Former Hospice RN) reported Staff V told Family Member #2 that Patient #4 asked Staff V to help end the patient's life. Family Member #2 explained Staff V, Former Hospice RN, hesitated at first, but in the end, Staff V reported Staff V helped to end the patient's life. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, did not inform Family Member #2 how Staff V assisted the patient. Family Member #2 thought Staff V, Former Hospice RN, told Family Member #2 around September 2022 about assisting with ending the life of Patient #4. Family Member #2 reported knowing Patient #4's name and that the patient was a former doctor. Family Member #2 reported Staff V, Former Hospice RN, was close with family of Patient #4, and Patient #4 was Staff V's favorite patient. 
 
h. Review of Patient #4's clinical record revealed the following:
 
1) The POC, dated 4/14/22 to 7/12/22, identified the patient had a terminal diagnosis of tonsillar cancer with metastasis to the patient's bones and received medications and nutrition through a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (Peg) tube. The same POC identified Patient #4 chose the hospice Medical Director as the attending physician and included IDG orders for skilled nursing services 2 times per week. The same POC included the following medication orders: Aspirin (used as a blood thinner), Plavix (used to prevent the formation of blood clots), Calcium Citrate (vitamins used to help balance the patient's blood minerals known as electrolytes), Levothyroxine (used to treat an underactive thyroid gland), Trazadone (used to treat sleeping difficulties) and Two Cal oral liquid (liquid nutrition). The patient/family self administered medications. 
 
2) The clinical record included documentation of the following medication orders: On 4/18/22, the Medical Director ordered Hydrocodone-Acetaminophen 10 milligrams (mg)-325 mg 1 tablet every 6 hours as needed (PRN) for pain and Lorazepam 1 mg tablets 1mg every 2 hours PRN for anxiety via the Peg tube . 
 
3) The IDG meetings, dated 4/28/22, 5/12/22, 5/26/22 and 6/9/22, included documentation Staff V, Former Hospice RN, was the patient's RN Case Manager. 
 
4)The clinical record included documentation of an order from the Medical Director, dated 5/25/22, for daily RN visits per the patient's request, change in the patient's condition and (the patient's) feelings of impending doom. The hospice's orders indicated the hospice staff placed the patient on their "Voyage Program" (the hospice program for patient's in their final days of life) which included continuous care daily visits. The clinical record included an order from the Medical Director, dated 5/25/22, to give Dexamethasone 4 mg 1 tablet every day for bone pain via the Peg tube. The IDG meeting, dated 5/26/22, included documentation of the IDG's approval of the Voyage Program and medication orders.
 
5) A skilled nursing visit note, dated 5/27/22, included documentation Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported the patient had talked about possibly doing something to end his/her own life. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented she contacted the hospices Social Worker on 5/27/22 to come to assess the patient. 
 
6) A social worker visit note, dated 5/27/22, included documentation the hospice social worker assessed the patient and the patient denied that the patient would harm themselves and did not have a plan for harming themselves. 
 
7) A physician's order, dated 5/28/22, included documentation of an order given by the Medical Director for Morphine oral concentrate 20 mg/milliliters (ml), give 0.25 ml every 2 hours as needed for pain. 
 
8) The skilled nursing visits, dated 5/28/22 and 5/29/22, included documentation by Staff W, RN, that the patient's respirations were 18 breaths per minute and shallow on 5/28/22, and 20 breaths per minute and labored on 5/29/22. The hospice nurse did not document a pain level intensity, but did document liquid Morphine concentrate had been started on 5/28/22.
 
9) A skilled nursing visit, dated 5/30/22, included documentation by Staff P, RN, that the patient's respirations were in normal limit and the patient felt their pain was controlled.
 
10) A skilled nursing visit, dated 5/31/22, included documentation by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, assessed the patient's pain was at an "8" intensity level out of 10, (with 10 being the worst in the last 24 hours, and described the pain as crushing, nagging, constant and affecting all areas of the patient's life). The patient reported a pain of "10" in the last 24 hours with a goal of a pain level intensity rating of "4". Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented that the Medical Director gave Staff V an order for Hydrocodone-Acetaminophen 10 mg-325 mg 2 tabs every 4 hours for pain. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented that she helped in administering the medication. The clinical record lacked documentation of an order for Hydrocodone-Acetaminophen 10 mg-325 mg 2 tabs every 4 hours. 
 
11) A skilled nursing visit, dated 6/1/22, included documentation by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, assessed the patient's pain was at an "8" intensity level out of 10. The patient reported a pain level of 9 being the worst in the last 24 hours, and described the pain as crushing, gnawing and constant. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented the patient was resting in a chair upon arrival, the patient was oriented, confused at times and very drowsy. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, administered Lorazepam and Dexamethasone via the patient's Peg tube. 
 
12) A skilled nursing visit, dated 6/2/22, included documentation by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, assessed the patient's pain was at an "8" intensity level out of 10, with 9 being the worst in the last 24 hours, and described the pain as crushing, gnawing and constant. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented the patient was resting in a recliner, the patient's pain seemed to be under control at that time, the patient was smiling and conversing about various properties the patient owned, and the patient seemed in much better spirits today. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented "oral solutions meds ordered to avoid further hassle with Peg tube." The patient's clinical record lacked documentation of any new or changed medication orders. 
 
0n 7/11/23 at 1:43 PM, during an interview, the hospice's Director of Integration reported that Staff V, Former Hospice RN, wrote an order in the hospice's electronic script system, a system separate from the clinical records for hospice patients, on 6/2/22. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, wrote an order for liquid Lorazepam and liquid Oxycodone on 6/2/22. The Director of Integration confirmed that the dose and frequency for the liquid Lorazepam and Oxycodone were not documented in the patients clinical record. The hospice's Director of Integration reported Staff V, Former Hospice RN, did not write an order for the patient to take take 2 Hydrocodone-Acetaminophen 10mg-325mg every 4 hours for pain on 5/31/22 in either the patient's clinical record or in the hospice electronic prescription system. 
 
13) Review of the hospice electronic prescription record revealed 2 physician orders signed by the hospice Medical Director, dated 6/2/22. The orders were as follows: Oxycodone 20 mg/ml concentrate, take one ml (20 mg) by mouth every 4 hours for pain and Lorazepam 2 mg/ml oral concentrate, take 0.5 ml by mouth every 2 hours as needed for anxiety. 
 
14) A social worker visit note, dated 6/3/22 at 11:50 AM to 12:44 PM, included documentation the social worker assessed the patient was alert and oriented to person, place and time, but was also forgetful and lethargic. The social worker documented the patient stated having feelings of depression and loss of quality of life due to the patient's illness. The patient did not indicate that the patient was at risk for harm to themselves, but did express an overall frustration with having to live in the patient's current state. The patient expressed confusion with taking medications and requested only comfort medications (medications used to treat pain and alleviate other symptoms that would cause the patient discomfort, such as anxiety or nausea). The social worker reported informing the RN case manager (Staff V, Former Hospice RN) at the visit of the patient's request for comfort medications only. 
 
15) A skilled nursing visit note, dated 6/3/22 at 2:27 PM to 3:31 PM, included documentation by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, assessed the patient's pain was at a "7" intensity level out of 10, with 8 being the worst in the last 24 hours, taking breakthrough pain medication as needed 2 to 3 times per day, abnormal breath sounds with diminished lung sounds (indicated some difficulty in breathing), fatigue at a 2 of 10, alert and orientated to person, place and time, but also confused, and no signs or symptoms of depression, anxiety or abnormal psychiatric findings. The clinical record lacked documentation of any medication changes to accommodate the patient's request for comfort medications only. The patient continued to have physician orders to take the following medications not used for comfort: Aspirin, Plavix, Calcium Citrate, Levothyroxine and Trazadone.
 
16) A skilled nursing visit note, dated 6/4/22, included documentation by Staff P, RN, that she assessed the patient's pain was at a "6" intensity level out of 10, with 7 being the worst in the last 24 hours, respirations within normal limits and a fatigue score of 7 of out 10 (with 10 being the worst) and drowsiness a "5" out of 10 (with 10 being the worst). Staff P, RN documented the patient reported uncontrolled pain, frustrated with not feeling well and confusion. The patient did not know what to take for comfort and could not find the Dexamethasone. Staff P, RN, documented she contacted the Medical Director for clarification of the plan. The nurse documented she obtained new orders for a refill of Dexamethasone and sent the medication order to the pharmacy. The patient is to use Oxycodone for routine needs and Morphine for breakthrough pain. 
 
17) A skilled nursing visit, dated 6/5/22, included documentation by Staff U, RN, that the patient's respirations were 18 breaths per minute and within normal limits, had a pain intensity rating of zero. The nurse documented that the patient's family reported they were running out of resources to care for the patient in the home. The patient's primary caregiver was not going to be available for the next 90 days. The patient was ready for placement outside of the home. Staff U, RN, documented she contacted the IDG members. The nurse documented the patient's pain was well controlled. 
 
18) A skilled nursing visit note, dated 6/6/22 at 9:36 AM to 10:24 AM, included documentation by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, assessed the patient's pain was at a "7" intensity level out of 10, with 8 being the worst in the last 24 hours, respirations within normal limits with lung sounds diminished. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented the patient reported feeling a lot better and post nasal drainage was gone and pain was better with pain only when mobile. The patient reported being interested in placement over the weekend, but now does not want to leave the patient's home. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented she discussed respite services (a temporary stay in a nursing facility for up to 5 days) and the patient was interested. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented she informed the hospice's social worker of the patient's discussion about respite services. 
 
19) The clinical record included documentation of 2 separate nurses visit notes, dated 6/7/22; one note was titled, "RN Continuous Care Evaluation" and a second note was titled, "Death Visit", and Staff V, Former Hospice RN, signed both visit notes.
 
a) The visit note, titled, "RN Continuous Care Evaluation", dated 6/7/22, included the following documentation: Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented she arrived at the patient's home at 9:19 AM and the visit lasted until 3:07 PM. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented the patient was restless and agitated due to pain and had a pain intensity rating of 10. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented that Staff V administered Oxycodone and Lorazepam every 15 minutes and that Staff V sat with the patient and family administering medications and providing comfort. The clinical record lacked documentation of a physician order for the patient to have Oxycodone or Lorazepam at the frequency of every 15 minutes as documented by Staff V, Former Hospice RN. The clinical record and electronic prescription record lacked documentation of any new physician orders after 6/2/22. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented that Staff V assessed the patient's vital signs as follows: Temperature at 9:42 AM was 98.3 degrees Fahrenheit (within normal range of temperature), a radial (wrist) pulse of 86 and irregular at 9:46 AM, a blood oxygen saturation level of 69 percent at 9:46 AM at room air (values under 90 percent are considered low) and respirations at 18 breaths per minute and "within normal limits" at 10:39 AM (which would indicate the patient was not in any kind of respiratory distress). Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented, "approximately noon; patient displaying periods of apnea (absence of breath). Breaths per minute reduced to 9." Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented, "2:00 PM significant changes-shallow breathing. Breaths per minute 4."
 
b) The visit note, titled "Death Visit", dated 6/7/22, included the following documentation: Staff V, Former Hospice RN. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented the patient died at 3:02 PM with Staff V and family present at the bedside. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented Staff V provided post mortem cares and a family member would destroy the patient's medications including Oxycodone 20 ml (liquid) and Lorazepam 25 ml (liquid). 
 
The skilled nursing visit notes, dated 6/7/22, lacked documentation of an ongoing clinical assessment by the nurse every 15 minutes or every hour which warranted the administering of medications every 15 minutes (as documented by Staff V, Former Hospice RN) or every hour (as reported by Staff V), lacked documentation of contact with a physician or licensed healthcare practitioner (such as the Medical Director or the hospice ARNP) and lacked an order by physician or other licensed health care practitioner for the administration of any medications every 15 minutes or every hour, either at a scheduled frequency or as needed. 
 
 
i. On 7/12/23 at 9:16 AM, during an interview, the hospice Medical Director reported working for the hospice since October 2021. The Medical Director remembered Patient #4, but could not recall if Staff V, Former Hospice RN, contacted him/her for orders on either 6/2/22 or 6/7/22. The Medical Director explained a typical dose for liquid Oxycodone would be 20 mg/ml, give 5 mg every 4 hours as needed, not scheduled, and then advance to every 2 hours as needed. A typical dose for Lorazepam Intensol (liquid) would be 2 mg/ml, give 0.5 mg every 4 hours as needed. The Medical Director was unsure why the hospice would have switched over to liquid since the medications could be crushed and put through Patient #4s Peg tube. If a patient was not responding to the current dose and frequency of a pain medication, the Medical Director reported he would look first at increasing the dose before increasing the frequency. The Medical Director reported he would also use longer-acting pain medications (slower acting medication with a longer duration of pain relief), such as Fentanyl through a patch or Oxycontin (same as Oxycodone) to decrease the amount of as needed pain medication. The Medical Director reported he did not do euthanasia, and he would never give a patient pain medication if their respirations were down to 9 breaths per minute. If a patients breath is down to 9 breaths per minute, this indicates that the patient is comfortable. The Medical Director reported he would not prescribe the pain (Oxycodone) and antianxiety (Lorazepam) medication every 15 to 30 minutes except for extreme circumstances such as episodes of air hunger where the patient is gasping and choking for every breath, and the Medical Director reported he could remember ordering medication at this frequency less than 10 times in their entire career. The Medical Director explained that he will almost never schedule pain medications shorter than 6 hours, because ";it is too much drug and not enough assessment" to schedule pain medications any shorter than 6 hours apart. The Medical Director explained that with as needed pain medications, the nurse should always be assessing the patient prior to giving the medication. The Medical Director reported he could not make a determination on whether or not the medications Staff V, Former Hospice RN, caused the premature death of the patient, but remembered the patient had been on their ";Voyage Program" (the hospices procedures for when the patient is near death that includes daily visits by hospice staff) and the patient's death was not unexpected. The Medical Director explained that if Staff V, Former Hospice RN, continued to give the patient the medications for pain and anxiety once the patients respirations were down to 9 and then 4, this could have resulted in the patient passing sooner. 
 
j. On 7/12/23 at 10:12 AM, during an interview, the hospice's Advanced Registered Nurse Practitioner (ARNP) reported she has worked for the hospice since 2014. The ARNP explained her role as mainly doing visits to recertify patients for hospice services, provides support to the nurses and Clinical Manager and works under the direction of the hospice Medical Director. The ARNP reported she frequently ordered medication changes and refills for hospice patients if the patient did not have an attending physician. The ARNP reported she did not remember Patient #4, and explained she never saw the patient in person. The ARNP reported she may have ordered comfort medications for the patient, but she could not recall. The ARNP explained she worked closely with the Medical Director, talks with the Medical Director "a lot" and would prescribe medications the same as the Medical Director. The ARNP reported she would not order the use of Oxycodone and Morphine at once and she would never order any medication every 15 minutes. The ARNP further explained the medications should be ordered as needed, not any shorter than every 2 hours and not scheduled. The ARNP reported she might do a one time order if a patient was in pain, and then go back to as needed. The ARNP reported the ARNP has never ordered a medication for every 15 minutes. 
 
k. On 7/11/23 at 3:35 PM, during an interview, Staff V, Former Hospice RN,(dates of employment 2/15/22 to 5/9/23) confirmed she was present in the patient # 4's home and with the patient when the patient died. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, described the patient as incoherent and terminally restless when Staff V arrived to the home on 6/7/22.. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported she and a family member of the patient's helped the patient into bed and the family member laid down with the patient in the bed. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported the patient asked for Staff V to call another family member to come to the home. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported she ended up staying close to 8 hours that day (6/7/22). Staff V, Former Hospice RN, explained she administered hourly medications while present in the home and she contacted the hospice's ARNP for medication orders. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, explained she administered all of the patient's medications through the patient's Peg tube. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, further explained that she would flush the Peg tube with water, put medications through the Peg Tube and then flush the tube again with water after administering the medications. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported she gave the patient Morphine and Lorazepam together every hour, and, at one point, had to send a family member to pick up more medication from the pharmacy. When the surveyor read the visit note documentation to Staff V, Former Hospice RN, and questioned the documentation of administering Oxycodone and Lorazepam every 15 minutes, Staff V responded, "Every 15 minutes was probably how it was ordered by the Medical Director (stated the Medical Director by name) or ARNP (stated the ARNP by name)." Staff V, Former Hospice RN, explained she did not recall if she gave the patient Oxycodone or Morphine. Staff V just knew that she was giving the patient medications frequently and giving the medications as ordered. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, denied the patient ever asked her to hasten the patient's death. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, explained the patient told her weeks before the patient's death that the patient had spent the last 10 years not eating, and if the patient could go, the patient would. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported she educated the patient on not being the purpose of hospice to help end the patient's life. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, reported she received physician orders from both the Medical Director and ARNP for medications the day the patient died. 
 
l. On 7/11/23 at 1:51 PM, during an interview, Patient # 4's family member and identified patient representative, reported being present for the day the patient died on 6/7/22. On 7/11/23 at 11:50 AM, during an interview with the Administrator, Clinical Manager and Director of Integration, the Clinical Manager reported she provided 1:1 education to each nurse regarding the hospices policy for attending the patients death at home on 7/6/23. The Director of Integration reported the hospices Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program reviews 100 percent of admission visits and death visits. The hospice QAPI did not have a process in place to review 100 percent of all regular visit notes. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, also did not write an order to provide the controlled medications every 15 minutes.
 
The hospice failed to ensure hospice nursing staff administered medication only as ordered by a physician (or other licensed healthcare practitioner) and followed the patient's Plan of Care.
 
2. Patient #3 had a hospice admission date of 4/29/22, received routine home care hospice services while residing in a private home and died at home on 5/13/23.
 
Review of the clinical record revealed the following:
 
a. The POCs, dated 2/23/23 to 4/23/23 and 4/24/23 to 5/13/23, included IDG orders for skilled nursing services and a physician order for the hospice nurse to insert/maintain a urinary catheter size 16 French with a 10 cubic centimeter (cc) balloon (device inserted into the bladder and filled with fluid to hold the catheter in place), may irrigate with normal saline and change catheter every 30 days or as needed. 
 
b. A skilled nursing visit completed by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, dated 3/27/23, included documentation Staff V changed the patient's urinary catheter on 3/27/23. Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented she planned to change the patient's catheter next on 4/27/23.
 
c. The skilled nursing visits completed by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, dated 4/20/23 and 4/27/23, included documentation the patient had not had a change in genitourinary (bladder and structures of the body related to the urinary system) status and lacked documentation Staff V changed the patient's urinary catheter. On 4/27/23, Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented the patient's urinary catheter was in place, draining dark colored urine, pus-like with large amounts of sediment. 
 
d. The skilled nursing visits completed by Staff V, Former Hospice RN, dated 4/24/23 and 5/1/23, included documentation that the patient's urinary catheter was last changed on 4/20/23 and was next due to be changed on 5/20/23. On 5/1/23, Staff V, Former Hospice RN, documented the patient's catheter was in place draining pus-like amber colored urine.

Review of the Arizona Adult Protective Services website, located at https://des.az.gov/services/basic-needs/adult-protective-services/report-adult-abuse, revealed, ". . . Arizona Adult Protective Services (APS) investigates reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults. APS may also become involved when there is a claim of self-neglect, which is when an adult with physical or mental impairments is not able to meet their basic needs (such as food, shelter, health care, managing money, etc.), which then impacts the adults physical health, mental health or general safety. The goal of APS is to prioritize an adults right to make their own decisions while keeping them safe.
APS tries to support the vulnerable adults in their current home, and to augment the skills they need to take care of themselves by providing services that can help with challenges the adult may be having. However, APS must always balance the need to protect the safety of the vulnerable adult with the adults right to make their own decisions.
APS does not conduct safety checks, but local law enforcement does. Law enforcement and APS work together, and if law enforcement believes an individual is a vulnerable adult, they will contact APS . . ."

Patient 4 was also at risk for ineffective drug therapy and adverse drug reactions (a harmful, unintended, or unexpected reaction to a drug or medication when taken at normal doses) related to noncompliance with drug therapy that could lead to seizures (a sudden, uncontrolled electrical disturbance in the brain that can cause changes in behavior, movements, or levels of consciousness), coma (deep state of unconsciousness where a person is unresponsive), hospitalization, and death. On 7/22/2025 at 3:52 p.m., the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) called an Immediate Jeopardy (IJ, a situation in which the provider's non-compliance with one or more requirements of participation has caused, or likely to cause, serious injury, harm impairment, or death to a patient) in the presence of the Chief Nursing Officer, Vice – President for Operations, Patient Care Coordinator, General Manager, Medical Director, Performance Improvement Specialist, and National Patient Care Supervisor, related to the hospice agency’s (HA, agency who provides specialized care and support for people with a serious illness who are nearing the end of life) failure to: The Hospice Agency (HA, agency that provides specialized care and support for people with a serious illness and nearing the end of life) failed to conduct a complete medication profile review for one of 23 sampled patients (Patient 4) by failing to:1. Ensure the visiting nurses (VNs) identified a discrepancy during the medication profile review when Patient 4’s caregiver (PCG 4) administered Humulin R (Insulin Regular, Human, short-acting synthetic insulin that lowers the blood sugar) 20 units subcutaneously at bedtime to Patient 4 when the physician’s order, dated 8/8/2024, indicated to administer Humulin R insulin 17 units subcutaneously at bedtime to Patient 4. 2. Ensure all the assigned licensed staff to Patient 4 monitored and evaluated Patient 4’s insulin effectiveness and side effects in accordance with the federal regulations and professional standards of practice by assessing Patient 4’s compliance with the insulin order and PCG 4’s understanding of the insulin order during the medication profile review. On 7/22/2025 at 4:15 p.m., the survey team completed the survey tasks and conducted an exit conference while onsite in the presence of the Chief Nursing Officer, Vice – President for Operations, Patient Care Coordinator, General Manager, Medical Director, Performance Improvement Specialist, and National Patient Care Supervisor. On 7/22/2025 at 4:40 p.m., the HA was unable to submit an IJ removal Plan (includes all actions the agency has taken or will take to immediately address the noncompliance that resulted in or made serious injury, serious harm, serious impairment, or death likely). The survey team exited the HA with IJ not removed. Findings: During a review of Patient 4’s Case Sheet, the Case Sheet indicated Patient 4’s start of care (SOC) date of 8/8/2024. The Case Sheet indicated Patient 4 had a terminal diagnosis of chronic congestive heart failure (CHF, gradual weakening of the heart leading to the inability to pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs) and a secondary diagnosis of hypertension (high blood pressure). During a review of Patient 4’s Interdisciplinary Care Plan, dated 8/8/2024, indicated the following interventions:1. Visiting Nurse (Registered Nurses [RNs] and Licensed Vocational Nurses [LVNs]) to assess and monitor symptoms at each visit for diabetes mellitus (condition characterized by high blood sugar due to the body’s inability to produce enough insulin or its inability to effectively use the insulin).2. Instruct [PCG4] to notify the HA of any change in condition. During a review of Patient 4’s Pre-Admit Evaluation, dated 8/8/2024, the Pre-Admit Evaluation, obtained from the “Physician Office,” indicated previous medication order for Humulin L (Insulin Zinc, Human, intermediate-acting synthetic insulin) 100 units per ml vial injection 17 units subcutaneously daily at bedtime. During a review of Patient 4’s Plan of Care (POC) as of 7/17/2025, the POC indicated Patient 4’s other diagnoses that included type 2 diabetes mellitus (type of diabetes wherein the body could not produce enough insulin to maintain normal blood sugar levels), stage 4 chronic kidney disease (Stage 4 CKD, severe stage prior to kidney failure wherein the kidneys are significantly damaged and filtering blood at a severely reduced rate), and vascular dementia (decline in thinking skills caused by conditions that block or reduce blood flow to the brain). During a review of Patient 4’s Chart Medication List/Signed Physician Orders, dated 7/17/2025, it indicated physician order for Humulin R (Insulin Regular, Human) 100/ml (milliliter, unit of measurement) vial, inject 17 units (=0.17 ml) subcutaneously at bedtime for diabetes mellitus. During an interview on 7/21/2025 at 12:48 p.m., PCG 4 stated she would administer 20 units of Humulin R to Patient 4 at bedtime. PCG 4 stated she did not check Patient 4’s blood sugar before dinner and at bedtime. However, PCG 4 stated Patient 4’s blood sugar in the morning would range from 70 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL, unit of measurement) – 90 mg/dL (blood sugar below 70 mg/dL is considered low and may require immediate medical attention if severely low). PCG 4 stated she did not inform the visiting nurses about the insulin dosage administered to Patient 4 and Patient 4’s blood sugar because “they (visiting nurses) did not ask.” PCG 4 stated she has been administering 20 units of Humulin R since the start of care with the HA (8/8/2024). During an interview on 7/21/2025 at 1:11 p.m., Licensed Vocational Nurse (LVN) 1 stated she conducted medication reconciliation at every home visit by going through the medication list, noting medications that require refills, and providing patient education about the medications as needed. LVN 1 stated Patient 4’s physician’s order indicated to administer Humulin R 100 mg/ml 17 units subcutaneously at bedtime. LVN 1 stated she did not ask how much insulin PCG4 administered to Patient 4. LVN 1 stated she did not ask Patient 4’s blood sugar level. LVN 1 stated Patient 4 did not have a glucometer (device to measure the concentration of blood sugar) at home. LVN 1 stated she did not know Patient 4’s baseline blood sugar levels/range. LVN 1 stated Patient 4 did not have any regular laboratory tests drawn to determine blood sugar levels. LVN 1 stated it was important to know Patient 4’s blood sugar range and if Patient 4’s blood sugar was below 90 mg/dL, she would notify the physician and follow the physician’s orders. During an interview and concurrent review of Patient 4’s medical records with the Director of Patient Care Services (DPCS) and the Administrator on 7/21/2025 at 1:58 p.m., Patient 4’s assessments, physician orders, and plan of care were reviewed. The DPCS stated the visiting nurse must conduct the medication reconciliation during each home visit by verifying the medication container with the physician’s order, including the dosage, frequency, compliance with the medication order, and providing patient teaching regarding the medication. The DPCS stated if the visiting nurse identified that the PCG was administering Humulin R 20 units to Patient 4, it must be considered a medication error. The DPCS stated the HA must follow the medication error procedures and Patient 4 must be assessed for any adverse reactions. The DPCS stated there was no documented evidence of the assessment of Patient 4’s baseline blood sugar levels prior to the start of hospice services and while under hospice care. The DPCS stated baseline blood sugar levels must be documented to determine if the blood sugar levels were labile (fluctuating significantly) or not. The DPCS stated if the blood sugar levels were labile, parameters (set limits) for the insulin order must be ordered and documented. During an interview on 7/22/2025 at 12:35 p.m., Patient 4’s primary care physician (PCP) 1 stated PCP 1 was able to prescribe insulin orders for Patient 4 based on the Patient 4’s previous insulin orders prior to the admission to the HA. PCP 1 stated for hospice patients (in general), the visiting nurse must ask the PCG or family for the patient’s blood sugar at every visit to determine insulin effectiveness and insulin side effects. PCP 1 stated for hospice patients (in general), it would be more concerning if the blood sugar was “too low—less than 70 or 80 mg/dL” because patient could get unresponsive and have seizures, and insulin administration might need to be discontinued. PCP 1 stated the physician’s order for insulin would require blood sugar parameters for regular insulin. During a review of the HA’s policy and procedure (P&P), titled “VS Obtaining Orders,” dated 10/26/2022, P&P 1 indicated the following:1. A physician order must be obtained for all drugs and biologicals.2. Nurses must communicate with the physician to discuss the patient’s assessment findings and rationale for requesting a new or changed order.3. If a physician order could not be followed or the patient declines to follow the order as given, the reason and the communication with/notification of the physician must be documented. During a review of the HA’s policy and procedure (P&P), titled “VS Pharmacy Process,” dated 6/13/2025, the P&P 2 indicated the HA’s nurse was responsible for medication reconciliation (process of obtaining the most accurate list of all medications of the patient that included the name, dosage, frequency, and route, by comparing the physician orders with the medications on hand) by monitoring medication amounts, medication labels, and patient/PCG education needs. The P&P indicated the CML (Chart Medication List) must be reviewed during each patient visit and during Interdisciplinary Group (IDG, team responsible for the holistic care of the hospice patient) meetings. During a review of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidance, titled “Types of Insulin,” dated 5/15/2024, the guidance indicated the following:1. Regular/short-acting insulin are usually taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal.2. Regular/short-acting insulin onset time (how quickly insulin lowers the blood sugar) is 30 minutes.3. Regular/short-acting insulin peak time (period when insulin is at maximum strength that allows adjustment of food intake or activity level to prevent severely low blood sugar) is 2-3 hours.4. Regular/short-acting insulin duration (how long insulin works to lower your blood sugar) is 3-6 hours.5. Intermediate-acting insulin “covers insulin needs for half a day or overnight” with onset of 2-4 hours, peak time of 4-12 hours, and duration of 12-18 hours.[Source: https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/about/how-to-use-insulin.html] During a review of a published journal from the American Diabetes Association (ADA), titled “Diabetes Care: 13. Older Adults: Standards of Care in Diabetes---2025,” dated 12/9/2024, the publication indicated the following:1. It is recommended that episodes of hypoglycemia at routine visits must be ascertained and addressed because older adults with diabetes have a greater risk of hypoglycemia, especially when treated with hypoglycemia agents, such as insulin.2. Older adults might be at a higher risk of hypoglycemia for many reasons, including irregular meal intake, insulin deficiency requiring insulin therapy, and worsening kidney function.3. Older adults have higher rates of unidentified cognitive impairment and dementia, leading to difficulties in performing complex self-care activities, such as blood sugar monitoring and insulin dose adjustment.4. Cognitive decline has been associated with increased risk of hypoglycemia, and severe hypoglycemia has been linked to increased risk of dementia.5. Glycemic goals (target blood sugar levels) and pharmacologic treatments might need to be adjusted to minimize the occurrence of hypoglycemic events.6. For people with diabetes receiving palliative care and end-of-life care, the focus must be to avoid hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia while reducing the burdens of glycemic management (process of regulating blood sugar levels). Thus, as organ failure develops, the treatment plan would have to be deintensified and one or more agents would need to be discontinued. At the end of life, most agents for type 2 diabetes might be removed. [Source: https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/48/Supplement_1/S266/157556/13-Older-Adults-Standards-of-Care-in-Diabetes-2025][Source: https://doi.org/10.2337/dc25-S013]

The Complainant was contacted and interviewed on August 19, 2024 at 8:39 a.m. The Complainant stated that, ";Things happen, Ill give that to them," but that the medication error of prescribing 200mg of Metoprolol to the patient reported in the complaint was not the first issue they experienced with the care provided by Hospice of the West. 
The Complainant stated that they, as the primary caregiver and surrogate decision-maker for the patient, met with a nurse, who reviewed the patients medications with the Complainant. The Complainant noted at the time that the patients medications had been ";pared down to the essentials" but otherwise no changes had been made. The Complainant stated that on July 4, 2024, Latanoprost was ordered for the patient but was not delivered for the patient until a stat order was placed and the medication received on July 12, 2024. The Complainant stated they reported this issue to Hospice of the West and stated the responsiveness on this issue was ";very appropriate."
On July 4, 2024, the patient began taking all other medications ordered, including Metoprolol. The Complainant reported that the Complainant was made aware by staff at the facility where the patient resided that the patient had been prescribed ";ten times the amount" of Metoprolol than the patient was intended to be prescribed. The Complainant reported this to the hospice nurse who came to see the patient and stated the hospice nurse told the Complainant this was ";not possible" and that what the Complainant read on the MAR (medication administration sheet) ";must be a typo."
The patient continued to receive 200mg of Metoprolol from July 4 to July 25, 2024 according to the Complainant. The Complainant reported to the nurse that the patient had a heart rate in the 40s, was shaking and had not been responsive for weeks. The Complainant stated the hospice nurse told the Complainant this was a normal part of the dying process.
The Complainant stated that the nursing home sent the Complainant a photograph of the prescription bottle to provide the hospice and the hospice finally agreed there was a medication error. But the Complainant stated that the hospice was not apologetic and instead ";tried to deflect blame" onto the nursing home. The Complainant stated the Complainant contacted Hospice of the West. The Complainant stated, ";I wanted to know, what are you going to do?" The Complainant stated they were ignored by the first person they spoke to. The Complainant stated they continued to pursue the issue and were put in contact with a second staff person identified as Employee #1 who apologized to the Complainant for what had happened.
The Complainant stated that Employee #1 called the Complainant daily to give updates regarding an investigation Employee #1 stated was being conducted by Hospice of the West; however, the Complainant stated that once the Complainant filed a complaint with Arizona Department of Health Services, Employee #1 ceased contact with the Complainant.

Interviews were conducted with Employees #1 and #3 on August 21 and August 22. Employee #3 stated that patients who are unhappy with the medication service provided by the hospice can instead pick up their medications at the pharmacy of their choice at no additional cost. But when asked how this right is communicated to patients, Employee #3 could not direct Compliance Officers to specific information provided to patients. This right did not appear to be clearly communicated in the admission materials provided by Hospice of the West to patients. 
Both Employees #1 and #3 acknowledged and agreed that adverse trends affecting patient care should be identified, a root cause analysis performed and actions to improve agency performance should be taken in accordance with policies and procedures; however, Employee #1 was asked to provide all performance improvement plans initiated by HOW in 2023 and 2024 related to the provision of patient care and related to pharmaceutical services. The two PIPs initiated, one initiated in March 27, 2023 regarding live discharge rates, and the other initiated March 1, 2024 regarding the transition to OnePoint Pharmacy as a subcontracted provider, did not appear to address the complaints and grievances reported by patients.

Based on interview, review of facility policies and procedures and review of facility documents, the Department has determined that Hospice has failed to ensure that the Governing Body failed to ensure the QAPI (Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement) program was reviewed and evaluated for effectiveness at least every 12 (twelve) months with documentation maintained of governing body oversight and that a quality improvement plan was implemented that included, at minimum, a method to make changes or take action as a result of identifying concerns about the delivery of a service relating to patient care. Failure to implement methods to make changes or take action stemming from the identification of concerns regarding the delivery of service relating to patient care can result in negative trends in patient care continuing unabated, resulting in entrenched substandard patient care.
Findings include:

Facility policy titled, ";...Governing Body...." updated April 23, 2023 revealed: ";...Duties of the Governing Body will include the following...Ensuring that hospice-wide performance improvement plan (QAPI)...Is defined, implemented, maintained and evaluated annually...Addresses priorities for improved quality care and patient safety...Takes actions to demonstrate improvement in hospice performance...Improvement actions are evaluated for effectiveness...Approving frequency and specific plan for performance improvement data collection...."
Facility policy titled, ";...Regulatory Compliance—Auditing and Monitoring...." revealed: ";...Care Hospice conducts regular audits...in accordance with an audit protocol established by the QAPI Committee...that...may include, but are not limited to...Program statistics...Patient outcomes...Contracts...Patient/Caregiver satisfaction surveys...Code of Conduct...Reporting mechanisms...Disciplinary actions...Response and corrective actions, and Auditing and monitoring functions...Components of the compliance program that are regularly audited and monitored include...Standards of conduct...Compliance policies and procedures...Disciplinary actions...Response and corrective actions, and...Auditing and monitoring functions...Findings from the audits of hospice programs and the compliance program are used to identify and resolve problems...The Administrator (Program Director) compiles a summary of audit findings for the regular reports to the Governing Body and for inclusion in the Annual Evaluation Report...The Compliance Officer provides the Governing Body with a summary of audit findings...."

Based on record review, observation, and interview, the hospice agency failed to ensure nursing care that optimized dignity and personal privacy at one of three skilled nurse home visits with hospice patients (Patient #16) was completed at an assisted living facility (ALF). This failed practice placed Patient #16 at risk for psychological harm from feelings of poor self-esteem and/or self-worth and a potential for a poor quality of life. 
 
 
 

 
Findings: 
Record review from 3/6-13/25 of Record #16 revealed a start of care (SOC) date of 2/26/25 with a benefit period of 2/26/25-5/26/25. The patient's terminal diagnosis was Parkinson's Disease. 
During an observation on 3/7/25 at 8:30 AM, Licensed Nurse (LN) #1 was observed to locate Patient #16 at his/her residence: an Assisted Living Facility (ALF). LN #1 went to Patient #16's room and found the patient was not present in his/her room. LN #1 proceeded to the ALF dining room and located the patient, who was seated alone at a small table. Patient #16 was finishing breakfast. The patient agreed, when LN #1 asked, to be assessed. LN #1 did not offer a choice of returning to the patient's room for privacy. LN #1 stated, "I heard you were short of breath yesterday." LN #1 proceeded to take the patient's vital signs with a rolling vital sign tower. LN #1 obtained the patient's oxygen saturation rate and found the oxygen saturation rate to be 93%. LN #1 asked Patient #16 if he/she wanted oxygen. Patient #16 agreed to the oxygen, and LN #1 stated he/she would get the oxygen concentrator. There were four ALF dining room attendants from the ALF in the dining room as well as seven patients sitting at nearby tables with one patient about ten feet from Patient #16. LN #1 took the patient's blood pressure. "Your blood pressure is good,' LN #1 stated. LN #1 palpated Patient #16's abdomen and asked the patient, "Are you constipated? How is your appetite?" LN #1 stated, "The abdomen feels soft and does not appear full." Patient #16 denied being constipated and stated his/her appetite was good. LN #1 looked at both feet by removing his/her socks and sandals. LN #1 asked, "Do you feel anxious at all?" Patient #16 denied any anxiety. LN #16 proceeded to listen to Patient #16's abdomen with the stethoscope and stated the abdomen sounded fine. "Do you want to work on breakfast?" LN #1 asked. The patient stated, "Yes." LN #1 applied gloves and disinfected the vital sign tower and rolled it to the supply room. After obtaining the oxygen concentrator and rolling that to the dining room, LN #1 placed the oxygen tubing onto the patient. 
During an interview on 3/12/25 at 2:38 PM, the Administrator stated, when asked if a home visit should be conducted in a public place like an ALF dining room, "If patient is able to give consent we would allow this, but otherwise it should be private."

Privacy and Security - You have the right to personal privacy and security during home care visits."

The Complainant stated that they, as the primary caregiver and surrogate decision-maker for the patient, met with a nurse, who reviewed the patients medications with the Complainant. The Complainant stated they reported this issue to Hospice of the West and stated the responsiveness on this issue was ";very appropriate."

The Complainant reported that the Complainant was made aware by staff at the facility where the patient resided that the patient had been prescribed ";ten times the amount" of Metoprolol than the patient was intended to be prescribed. The patient continued to receive 200mg of Metoprolol from July 4 to July 25, 2024 according to the Complainant. Based on record review and interview, the agency failed to immediately investigate Patient's (Patient #13) allegation of sexual abuse, to include having conducted an assessment; failed to report a basis to believe sexual harm to an endangered adult as required by their policy and Indiana Code 12-10-3-9; and failed to take actions in accordance with agency policy to prevent further violations while the alleged sexual abuse was investigated to determine if it was verified for 1 of 1 patients whose clinical record evidenced an allegation of sexual abuse (Patient #13) of a total sample of 16 active patients, with the potential to affect all 192 hospice patients.

Findings include:

1. An agency policy received from the administrator on 2-11-22 at 1:25 PM titled, "Abuse and Neglect," last revised 6-14-19, ID 654806, stated " ... I. Purpose ... A. To communicate the guidelines to identify and report suspected abuse and neglect ... Scope ... A. Applies to all Hospice team members ... G. Examples that may warrant referral ... 5. Indiana University Health Hospice reports all suspected cases of abuse ... in compliance with appropriate state statutes to appropriate protection organizations including law enforcement. VI. Procedures ... Hospice Administrator will be made aware of all cases of suspected and confirmed abuse ... B. If any of above abuse activities are suspected, ... the Hospice Administrator will be notified, and a report will be called to the Adult Protective Services Hotline ... G. Hospice personnel will observe all Patients for unexplained...evidence of sexual abuse..."

2. A review of an Indiana statute, IC 12-10-3-9, revealed a "Duty to report endangered adult Sec. 9. (a) An individual who believes or has reason to believe that another individual is an endangered adult shall make a report under this chapter. (b) If an individual is required to make a report under this chapter in the individual's capacity as a member of the staff of a medical or other public or private institution, school, hospital, facility, or agency, the individual shall immediately notify the individual in charge of the institution, school, hospital, facility, or agency, or the individual's designated agent, who also becomes responsible to report or cause a report to be made."
