Based on interview and document review, the agency failed to report alleged incidents of possible mistreatment to the designated state agency within 5 working days for 3 of 13 patients (P1, P2, and P3) who had an allegation of drug diversion by a hospice employee. This had the potential to affect all 66 current patients receiving hospice services from this branch. 

When interviewed on 12/14/22, at 9:45 a.m. CP-A stated he called the hospice agency on 10/24/22, and notified clinical manager (CM)-A that P1, P2 and P3 had oxycodone 20 milligrams (mg) filled on 10/22/22, and the medications had been picked up by RN-A. CM-A was notified of the quantities of the medication that had been picked up and asked if the agency could verify these patients required the high doses and quantities of oxycodone ordered. CM-A stated she would look in to it. After the phone call, CP-B continued to see RN-A pick up medications for hospice patients of the agency. On 11/25/22, the pharmacy received prescriptions for a new hospice patient, P1, that included very high doses of oxycodone as well as fentanyl tablets. P1's past history of prescriptions was reviewed and there was no indication of medication use to warrant the amount of pain medication ordered. RN-A verified the prescriptions were correct. P1's past history of prescriptions was also reviewed. P1 received medications from CP-B's pharmacy as well as from the hospice's mail order pharmacy that the agency typically used. Receiving medications from both of the pharmacies was unusual and the prescribing physician (MD)-A was notified. 
During interview with MD-C on 12/13/22, at 1:30 p.m. MD-C indicated she was first made aware of concerns with the hospice patients' medications on 11/25/22, when CP-B called. She notified the regional director of clinical operations (RDCO) the evening of 11/25/22, to request they investigate the matter. 
When interviewed on 12/14/22, at 11:40 a.m. the vice president of clinical services (VP)-G stated filing a vulnerable adult (VA) report would have been the chief compliance officer's (CCO) task. CCO-E stated the agency had not filed VA reports to the state agency because there had been no harm to the patients. The allegation of drug diversion was investigated by the agency and the hospice employee was terminated. The agency notified the hospice medical director and the board of nursing and felt no more needed to be done. There was no evidence the medications were ever in patient homes and the misappropriation of medication was against the agency and the pharmacy and not the patients. The agency determined the police needed to be called and the matter did not require a VA report to the state agency. 
During a group interview with attorney (ATT)-D, chief compliance officer (CCO)-E, director of human resources (HR)-F, and vice president of clinical services (VP)-G on 12/14/22, at 10:45 a.m. ATT-D stated they had been working around the clock to identify potential patients that may have been affected by RN-A's potential drug diversion. Twenty-three patients had been identified with pain medications ordered but not listed on their medication administration records (MAR). 
During a group interview on 12/15/22, at 9:30 a.m. with CM-A, CCO-E, HR-F and VP-G, CM-A indicated she received an email from the regional director of clinical operations (RDCO)-H on 11/28/22, to investigate a complaint related to potential drug diversion by RN-A. CM-A received a list of patients with suspected drug diversion and reviewed the patient charts. RN-A was interviewed on 11/28/22 and placed on administrative leave. CM-A had not filed a VA report with the state agency and thought RDCO had filed one. 
The agency's undated policy Assessment of Possible Abuse/Neglect indicated the agency would report all suspected cases of abuse, neglect, or exploitation in compliance with appropriate state statutes to appropriate protection organizations. The clinician would submit a verbal report of the suspected abuse/neglect to the proper authorities in accordance with state law and complete a suspected abuse and/or neglect investigation report within 24 hours of the incident.

Based on policy review, record review, and interview, the provider failed to ensure the patient's right to be free from abuse by failing to immediately conduct an investigation into allegations of potential abuse and by discontinuing hospice aide services without determining validity of the allegation in, one of three records reviewed (Record/Patient #1). This deficient practice has the potential to affect all patients receiving care from the provider.

Findings included: Review of the provider's undated policy titled, "Abuse Neglect and Exploitation," showed all allegations are to be immediately and thoroughly investigated until concluded. RECORD/PATIENT #1:Review of the clinical record showed the hospice received notification from the long-term care facility (LTCF) on 03/10/2026 at 5:35 PM that the patient alleged the hospice's certified nursing assistant (CNA) caused harm during a shower and left a bruise.Record review showed the provider failed to initiate and complete an internal investigation into the alleged abuse. The provider failed to provide any documentation that showed a determination regarding the validity of the allegation. Review of the interdisciplinary group (IDG) comprehensive assessment details dated 04/06/2026, showed hospice aide services were discontinued in response to the allegation, without evidence the hospice conducted an investigation or determined the validity of the allegation prior to discontinuing services.During an interview on 04/14/2026 at 11:04 AM, certified nursing assistant (CNA) A stated that:- The patient had bruises on the top of his/her left arm and behind the left elbow;- The patient did not want a shower, but the CNA was persistent, and the patient agreed to take a shower;- During the shower, the patient was vocalizing and moaning;- The LTCF staff reported the patient told them the CNA had abused him/her; and- The CNA subsequently provided showers to the patient with another staff member present; however, on 04/02/2026, the patient made another allegation that the CNA caused harm during care, and the aide visits were discontinued. During an interview on 04/14/2026 at 11:48 AM, the registered nurse case manager (RNCM) stated that:- The patient reported to LTCF staff that the CNA caused bruising during care; and- Confirmed the hospice did not conduct an internal investigation. During an interview on 04/14/2026, the RN coordinator stated that:- The LTCF conducted its own investigation; and- Confirmed the hospice did not conduct an internal investigation. During an interview on 04/14/2026 at 12:36 PM, the administrator stated that:- The aide was removed from patient care until the allegation was cleared; and- Confirmed the hospice relied on the LTCF and the State (Department of Health and Senior Services) to determine the outcome rather than conducting its own investigation.

Based on observation, hospice medical record review, review of police reports, review of emergency medical services (EMS) reports, review of hospital documentation, review of local forecast information, review of the facility investigation, and staff interview, the facility failed to ensure all real or potential threats to the safety of the patients were addressed to prevent patient elopement. This affected one (Patient #1) of nine medical records reviewed and had the potential to affect all patients in the facility. The facility's census was 1106. Findings include:

Review of the medical record for Patient #1 revealed an admission to the Troy inpatient unit (IPU) and hospice on 11/22/25 at 12:50 PM. The pre-admission note completed by hospice staff dated 11/20/25 documented Patient #1 was 72 years old and unable to sign his own consents due to sundowning at this time. Patient #1's diagnoses included chronic systolic congestive heart disease, non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), coronary artery disease multiple vessels with severe left anterior descending artery, Lewy body dementia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and diabetes. The pre-admission note stated Patient #1 was admitted to the hospital on 11/15/25 (prior to the hospice admission) for a mental status change and dizziness. Patient #1 required a sitter and medication management for increased confusion. Patient #1 was able to ambulate with one person assistance to the nurse's station from his room with frequent breaks. Per the physical and occupation therapy notes, Patient #1's standing tolerance was six minutes. Patient #1 had been having a fall average of once a week and that Patient #1 would get combative with sundowning at night. The note requested that the inpatient unit manage the patient for pain and agitation and that the patient would need family assistance with placement. Review of the IPU hand off report dated 11/22/25 revealed the day shift nurse noted that the patient wandered and no sitter was arranged. It stated Patient #1 was on fall precautions and Patient #1's door was to be open for observation of him. Review of the nurses note dated 11/22/25 at 7:20 P.M. revealed due to a report received about the potential for Patient #1 to wander, the fire doors in the hallway were closed and the back entryway doors that lead to the outside were manually locked. Frequent rounding was to be completed by this nurse as well as Patient Care Services/Aides (PCS). Review of the nurses note dated 11/22/25 at 9:50 P.M. revealed the nurse documented that they did not disturb Patient #1 at this time for an accucheck (a device used to measure blood sugar readings) and assessment. Patient #1 continued to rest in bed with eyes closed and they would attempt at a later time. Review of the nurses note dated 11/22/25 revealed staff noticed Patient #1 was not in his room on 11/22/25 at 9:59 P.M. and began to search for him. The Information Technology (IT) department (located off-site) checked the security cameras and observed Patient #1 walking out the front automatic doors on 11/22/25 at 9:46 P.M. The hospital security team for the neighboring hospital was notified at 10:09 P.M. and 911 was called at 10:23 P.M. An attempt was made to reach the patients daughter at 10:28 P.M., no answer was received, and staff were unable to leave a message, so the resident's son was called at 11:31 P.M. and notified of the elopement.Review of the website titled Accuweather.com revealed the weather in Troy on 11/22/25 was a high of 50 degrees F and a low of 36 degrees F. Review of the Miami County Sheriff's Office report dated 11/22/25 noted they responded to the hospice facility. Staff stated they immediately began searching the facility for the patient and notified campus security. The Sheriff's department requested a last known clothing description and was advised they did not believe Patient #1 was wearing any clothing due to the clothing he had arrived in, was on the floor of his room and his shoes were also in his room. Due to this information, the officer requested EMS response due to the temperatures in the 30's. The Officer went to one of the ponds and began searching on foot. Another deputy began searching the second pond on the property. A drone was requested to assist with the search and a BOLO (be on the lookout for) was sent out. Several units began searching the property. Campus security was able to pull up surveillance footage from another facility that showed a male walking towards the interstate. Patient #1 was then located in a cornfield just north of the hospital. Officer went to that location and observed the patient in a pair of boxers with no shoes. The Officer advised personnel to have the patient wait and have the squad respond to this location as the patient was bleeding from hands and feet. Patient #1 was visibly cold from being out in the elements. A Troy Fireman advised they would carry the patient out to the deputy's truck due to the terrain. Patient #1 was loaded into the back of the deputy's truck without incident and then transported by squad. Review of the EMS note dated 11/22/25 noted they received call at 11:11 P.M. and arrived on scene at 11:20 P.M. They were notified of a missing person, possibly found in the tree line near the hospice. The medic crew arrived and found Patient #1 sitting in the back of a Miami County Sheriff pickup truck. Patient #1 was covered with blankets. Patient #1 had been located in the field after getting out of the facility. The Sheriff did not think Patient #1 was injured, but needed to be taken in for evaluation. Per the family, he was missing for an hour. Patient #1 was wearing a white t-shirt and underwear when he was found outside. Patient #1 reported he was cold and his feet hurt. Patient #1 had walked through a corn field and had multiple small scrapes to his feet and left hand and his feet were noted to be muddy. All bleeding was controlled. Patient #1 was able to get out of the cruiser, was walked to the cot, secured to the cot, and secured in the ambulance. Box heat was turned up. Per the patient he was very cold. Patient #1's temperature was 96.4 degrees Fahrenheit (F) (normal ranging from 97 degrees F to 99 degrees F), blood pressure 125/57 millimeters of mercury (mmHg) (normal range being around 120/80 mmHg), pulse 115 beats per minute (BPM) (normal rages from around 60 to 100 BPM), respirations 20 breaths per minute (normal ranges from around 12 to 20 breaths per minute), and oxygen saturation of 96 percent (%) (normal ranges from around 92% to 100%). Patient #1 was confused as to where he was but recalled being in a field. Patient #1 appeared to have the mental capacity of a dementia diagnosed patient. Transport to the emergency department (ED) began and report was called to the ED. Patient #1 remained alert and talking throughout transport. Patient #1 arrived in the ED at 11:35 P.M. Hypothermia from cold exposure and dementia were listed as complaints. Review of the hospice nurses note dated 11/22/25 at 11:25 P.M., the facility was notified that Patient #1 was in the ED of the neighboring hospital and was being treated for hypothermia. Review of the hospital ED notes dated 11/22/25 at 11:34 P.M. revealed the physician's note stated Patient #1 had been wearing only a t-shirt and underwear and had a temperature of 95.5 degrees F rectally on arrival. Patient #1 had various scrapes and abrasions to his lower legs and feet and ear. The patient was found in a corn field and was outside for approximately one hour by report from the police officer on the scene. Patient #1 denied complaints other than feeling cold. The patient was placed on a Bair hugger system (forced air-warming system). Review of the hospice nurses note dated 11/23/25 at 2:32 A.M. revealed the patient was discharged back to the inpatient unit with a family member one on one with Patient #1 at bedside until transfer could be arranged to the Dayton inpatient unit.Review of the facility investigation revealed a root cause analysis meeting was held on 12/03/25. The root cause identified the exit doors did not alarm and were not locked, there were only three staff for two nursing units, and the IPU did not have access to camera footage. Staff also did not contact the Team Leader when they realized Patient #1 was exit seeking and he did not have a bed alarm. The analysis noted there was no security staff at the Troy IPU and the hospital security was out of the hospice's control. The analysis stated Emergency Services could have been contacted sooner to expand the search for Patient #1. They identified a need for education, access to facility cameras, motion sensor alarms, and flashlights. The investigation revealed no documentation of implementation dates or a goal date of completion, no staff educations and no documented staff witness statements.Observation on 12/04/25 at 11:18 A.M. revealed the inpatient unit was observed as a stand-alone building located on a hospital campus. Additionally, the inpatient unit and hospital campus was surrounded by fields, wooded areas, two ponds, and was just off of a four-lane highway that was heavily traveled with a speed limit of 70 miles per hour.Interview on 12/04/25 at 12:47 P.M. with the Team Leader for the Inpatient Unit, the Director of Care for the Inpatient Units, and the Director of Accreditation Readiness stated on 11/22/25 a patient eloped and a root cause investigation was completed. They stated Patient #1 had no harm, was evaluated at the hospital, transferred back to this inpatient unit in Troy, and was later transferred to the inpatient unit in Dayton since they had security on-site and a WanderGuard system. The Team Leader stated that the referral from the hospital initially stated that Patient #1 was unsteady on his feet, used a walker, and was not very mobile per the occupational therapy notes. Because of this, they did not think Patient #1 was capable of wandering. They had reviewed his hospital record and the family was insistent that he went to the Troy IPU. They stated normally any potential wander risk patients would go to the Dayton IPU and they had informed the family, prior to his admission, that if he started to wander, he would have to be sent to the Dayton IPU. The Team Leader stated that it was her understanding that the family wanted Patient #1 at the Troy IPU and that was a risk they were willing to take. Interview on 12/04/25 at 1:40 P.M. with the Team Leader for the Inpatient Unit, the Director of Care for the Inpatient Units, and the Director of Accreditation Readiness revealed a review of the facility investigation and root cause analysis. The Team Leader stated they had internal discussions prior to the meeting on 12/03/25, but had assembled the entire group on 12/03/25 for the root cause meeting. They stated when Patient #1 had returned to the Troy IPU, the staff were instructed that someone had to be with him at all times until he was transferred to the IPU in Dayton. The family came with Patient #1 from the hospital and stayed at his bedside until he was transferred to the Dayton IPU and placed on the WanderGuard hallway, as the Troy IPU did not have a sitter available. The Director of Care stated that they had not done any formal education yet, but did tell the staff that they could make the decision to transfer patients to the Dayton IPU due to behaviors observed. The Team Leader stated she was planning to email the education out on this day [12/04/25] to staff and there were scheduled staff meetings next week where this education was to be discussed. The Team Leader stated they normally did not accept patients with a history of wandering at the Troy IPU. If a patient had a history of wandering that they learned about after admission, they transferred the patient to Dayton IPU if they were mobile. Interview on 12/04/25 at 3:55 P.M. with Night Shift Registered Nurse (RN) (Staff F) revealed that she received report from Day Shift RN (Staff G) that Patient #1 was pretty active and walking around the unit and had noted Patient #1 could wander. Patient #1 did laps of the nursing station during the day shift and then put himself to bed. Staff F stated when she arrived [indicating on 11/22/25], Patient #1 was in bed asleep. They manually locked the ambulance doors and closed the fire doors between the two units. They had considered manually locking the front doors, but then they would have had to unlock and re-lock them for any staff or visitors to come and go, and it would have also been a fire hazard. She stated Patient #1 was sleeping the entire shift until they found his bed empty. They were letting him rest as long as possible since he did not have any medications due and she had not completed her assessment of him at this point. Staff F stated she thought she was in the medication room when he eloped. The aide was keeping an eye on him from the nurses station until she did her 9:00 P.M. rounds and Staff F was also keeping an eye on his room too. She stated the aide answered the call light in the room next door to Patient #1's, where they had an actively dying patient. Staff F went to see why the call light was on and looked into Patient #1's room on her way to the actively dying patient's room and did not see Patient #1. Staff F stated she went into Patient #1's room and checked the room and the bathroom. They immediately began searching for Patient #1 inside and outside and making calls. The aide walked over to the hospital searching for Patient #1 and notified the hospital campus police as Staff F was calling them. Staff F stated it was cold outside, maybe in the 30's [degrees F] with no precipitation. Interview on 12/08/25 at 11:15 A.M. with Staff G revealed that she admitted Patient #1 and he was alert and oriented at that time. She reviewed his medical records and noticed he had sundowners and kept an eye on him. She stated Patient #1 just wanted to walk around, stating he could walk out of his room, around the building and to the bathroom unassisted, he had intact skin and was answering questions appropriately. She stated Patient #1 walked out of his room several times and as the day ended he started to get confused. She stated they rounded on him every hour and sat closer to his room to keep an eye on him. They did not think he needed a sitter so no arrangements were made. She stated she told the night shift nurse to keep an eye on him as he liked to walk and wander. She stated Patient #1 did not try to leave the building on day shift. Staff G stated they did not receive any paperwork from the hospital that said he wandered, but in the hand off report from the hospital and in his hospice record it mentioned sundowning. Interview on 12/09/25 at 1:20 P.M. with the Director of Care Inpatient Units (Staff B) stated that they did not have an elopement precautions policy. They had portable bed alarms, but no bed alarm was used for Patient #1 before he eloped.

Based on observation, interview, and record review, the hospice agency (HA, agency providing care to terminally ill patients who have six months or less to live) failed to implement its Patient Care-Abuse and Grievances (complaint) policies for two of eleven sampled patients (Patient 2 and Patient 8) by failing to:
1.Ensure Patient 2 was free and protected from physical abuse (refers to abuse perpetrated through any action intended to cause physical harm or pain, trauma, or bodily harm [e.g., hitting, slapping, punching, kicking, pinching, etc.]) from Certified Home Health Aid (CHHA).
2.Ensure the HA conducted an investigation regarding the alleged physical abuse of Patient 2.
3. Ensure the HA reported the alleged physical abuse incident to the Department of Public Health and the Local law enforcement.
4. Ensure the HA conducted a thorough investigation on a complaint of CHHA being rude to Patient 8.
As a result, Patient 2 sustained red markings to her right arm when CHHA provided nursing care on 3/6/2024 at Patient 2s Skilled Nursing Facility (SNF), and Patient 8s complaint of CHHA being rude to her on 2/28/2024 and not investigated.
On 3/21/2024, at 3:30 p.m., the Department of Public Health called an Immediate Jeopardy (IJ, a situation in which the provider's non-compliance with one or more requirements of participation has caused, or likely to cause, serious injury, harm impairment, or death to a patient) in the presence of the agencys Administrator (ADM) and the Branch Director related to the hospice agencys failure to ensure Patient 2 was free and protected from physical abuse, conduct an abuse investigation and report the alleged physical abuse to the Department of Public Health and the local law enforcement, and conduct a thorough investigation on a complaint of the CHHA being rude to Patient 8. 
On 3/22/2024, at 12 p.m., the HA gave the IJ Removal Plan (the facilitys plan of action to correct the deficient practices) to the surveyors in the hospice agency. The survey team reviewed the IJ Removal Plan and notified the ADM and the Branch Director the IJ Removal Plan was not accepted on 3/22/2024, at 12:50 p.m.
On 3/22/2024, at 4 p.m., the survey team completed the survey tasks, and exited the HA with the IJ situation not removed.
On 4/24/2024, the HA submitted an acceptable IJ Removal Plan as follow:
1. On 3/13/2024, Home hospice aide (HHA) was suspended from the field and placed on suspencion.
2. On 3/22/2024, the HHA was reinstated 03/19/2024 after investigation did not substantiate allegations. RN case manager (RNCM) completed full, in person assessments for all patients seen by Traditions HHA after he returned to work 03/19/2024. Visit notes are attached for Patient 2 and Patient 8.
3. On 3/18/2024, The Branch Director issued HHA a final written warning as the investigation's outcome into substantiated allegations of rudeness and unprofessional behavior at the facility 03/06/2024.
4. On 3/22/2024, Patients with aide care plans were reassigned from HHA to an RN with communication to appropriate patient, caregiver, and/or facility.
5. On 3/22/2024, The Branch Director reported potential patient abuse to the California Department of Health. Branch Director reported to the Ombudsman (an official appointed to investigate individuals' complaints against maladministration) and Adult Protective Services (APS) for Patient 2 and Patient 8.
6. From 3/26/2024 to 3/28, RNCM completed full, in-person assessments on all current patients of the branch, with no safety or abuse identified.
7.On 3/27/2024, Patient 8 was transferred to another hospice agency.
The survey verified the IJ removal plan implementation onsite and removed the IJ on 4/24/2024, at 11am in the presence of the Branch Administrator.

Findings:
a. During a review of Patient 2's Patient Information Report (admission Record), the Patient Information Report indicated the HA admitted Patient 2 on 2/14/2024 with diagnoses including hypertensive heart disease with heart failure (heart disease due to unmanaged high blood pressure for a long time that causes added strain on the heart and leads to heart failure), and dementia (loss of memory and other mental abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life).

During an interview on 3/19/2024, at 11:30 a.m., with the HAs Branch Director (BD), the Branch Director stated on 3/6/2024, at around 6 p.m., while at an out of state airport waiting for her flight home, she received a phone call from the HAs office staff (unidentified) who informed her of an incident regarding the CHHA that had just been reported to the HA by a SNF staff. The BD stated she followed up and spoke with the SNF Social Worker (SW) on 3/7/2024, via telephone, who informed her of CHHA physical abuse allegation with Patient 2 and that the SNF was filing a complaint with the Department of Public Health. The BD stated she interviewed the CHHA who indicated it was a dispute between him and the SNFs Certified Nursing Assistant 1 (CNA1). The BD stated per that interview with the CHHA, the HA unsubstantiated (not proven to be true) their side of the complaint. The BD stated she did not interview anyone else regarding the physical abuse allegation and the Registered Nurse (RN) Case manager, the chaplain (a religious leader), and the MSW visited Patient 2, at the SNF after the alleged physical abuse allegation. The BD stated the CHHA took online in-services regarding customer services (unidentified dates). The BD stated the CHHA was the only CHHA for the HA and was providing patient care.
During an interview on 3/19/2024, at, 3p.m., with the CHHA in the HA office, the CHHA denied abusing Patient 2 and stated he worked for the HA providing patient care on 3/7/2024, 3/8/2024, 3/11/2024, 3/12/2024, and 3/13/2024, before the HA inform him while in the HA office on 3/13/2024, and after visiting a patient, that he was being suspended while the HA was to investigate the allegation. The HHA stated he had a zoom interview with the HAs Compliance and Human Recourses staff and that he returned to work on 3/18/2024. The HHA stated he refused to sign the Employee Counseling Form given to him by the HA because he did not abuse patient 2 and by signing the form is an admitting he did it.
During a concurrent home visit observation and interview, on 3/20/2024, at 11:30 a.m., inside Patient 2s room at the SNF, with the HAs RN Case Manager (RNCM). Patient 2 was lying in a hospital bed and awake. Patient 2 spoke very softly and was unable to understand. The RNCM stated he received from CHHA on 3/6/2024, regarding a dispute at the SNF with the SNFs CNA. The RNCM stated he was informed by the BD of the allegations regarding the CHHA on 3/18/2023, and that he did not investigate the alleged incident as he did not get involved in administrative concerns and did not have administrative privileges. 
During an interview on 3/20/2024, at 11:30am, inside Patient 2s room with Patient 2s roommate, Patient 2s roommate stated, on 3/6/24, the CHHA went inside their room to provide care to Patient 2, slammed the room the door in a SNFs staffs (unidentified) face. Patient 2s roommate stated the SNFs CNA went in the room and asked the CHHA if he needed help and the CHHA stated ";no." Patient 2s roommate stated the SNF CNA was inside the room beside her (Patient 2s roommate) while CHHA bathed Patient 2 and they could hear the CHHA slamming drawers, and patient 2 was whimpering (sobbing). Patient 2s roommate stated the SNF CNA asked CHHA if he needed help, and they began arguing. Patient 2s roommate stated CHHA roughly snatched the curtain between the two patients (Patient 2 and Patient 2s roommate) and while moving around, CHHA hit her bedside table, which flew into Patient 2 who was sitting up in her bed striking her right upper arm. The CHHA was informed by the SNF CNA, that he knocked Patient 2s roommates bedside table into Patient 2 and the CHHA stated he did not know the table was there and never apologized to Patient 2 and left the room slamming the door to their room as he walked out. Patient 2s roommate stated the SNF CNA, checked on Patient 2 and noticed multiple red markings on her right arm, and Patient 2 was upset. Patient 2s roommate stated the SNF CNA went out of the room, got the SNF MSW and they checked Patient 2 and noticed red marking on her right arm.
During an interview on 3/20/2024, at 2:30 p.m., with the SNFS Social worker Director and the Administrator in the SNFS Director of Nurse office, the SW stated on 3/6/2024, she was informed by SNF staff of the CHHA behavior to the SNFs CNA and Patient 2 had red spots on her right arm. The SW stated she asked Patient 2 in Spanish what happened, and Patient 2 brushed over her right hand which had the red marking. The SW stated she informed the HA, however, did not receive a call back from the BD until the next day on 3/7/2024. The SNF SW stated she followed up with the HAs via phone call one to two days letter to see what the HA had done regarding CHHA and was informed by the BD the CHHA had appealed the allegation, was still working and the investigation had not started yet. The SNF SW informed the HA.
During a telephone interview with the SNF CNA on 3/21/20 24, at 4 p.m., the SNF CNA stated that on 3/6/2024, she was called in the room by a staff member (unidentified) who informed her that the CHHA had slammed the door in her face hitting her nose. The SNF CNA went to ask the CHHA if he needed help bathing Patient 2 and he stated no, and the SNF CNA went inside Patient 2s room to talk to Patient 2s roommate. The SNF CNA stated while she was talking with Patient 2s roommate, they could overhear Patient 2 whimpering as she was being bathed by the CHHA and the SNF CNA asked the HAs HHA, are you OK?" The SNF CNA stated the CHHA said back to her ";are you ok?" and the SNF CNA and the CHHA began to argue because she stated that she was also the nurse who took care of Patient 2. The SNF CNA stated the CHHA came up to her face while she was at the bedside of Patient 2s roommate and started yelling and arguing with her, and roughly snatched the curtains between the two patients and continued bathing Patient 2, while slamming drawers on Patient 2s side. The SNF CNA stated the CHHA knocked Patient 2s roommates bedside table striking Patient 2 in the right arm as she sat in her bed. The SNF CNA stated she told the CHHA, ";you just hit," Patient 2 with the table and the CHHA said he did not know the table was there. The SNF CNA stated the CHHA did not apologize, gathered his belongings, opened the door to the hallway and slammed it shut after he walked out. The SNF CNA stated she did not see him hit Patient 2 as the curtain was closed but heard Patient 2 whimpers during the bath. The SNF CNA stated she went to check on Patient 2 who was upset and holding her right hand and saw multiple small red marks on her arm that got darker the next day. The SNF CNA stated she went and got the facility social worker, who came and spoke to Patient 2 who just waved her left hand over the red marks on her right hand.
During an interview on 3/21/2024, at 4:30 p.m., with the BD, the BD stated she did not do an investigation/interview the staff at the SNF due to her not knowing she could. The BD stated she did not notify the Department of Public Health of the physical abuse allegation regarding the CHHA to Patient 2. The BD stated she had not informed Patient 2s family regarding the incident because she thought the SNF informed them.
During a review of the agencys policy and procedure titled, ";Patient Care-Abuse, Neglect, & Exploitation-PC15," dated 4/2022, under II.-A-indicated The Hospice Management will: Immediately investigate all alleged violations involving anyone furnishing services on behalf of the Hospice and immediately take action to prevent further potential violations while the alleged violation is being verified. Based on observation, Centers for Disease Control (CDC) Injection Safety: Preventing Unsafe Injection Practices, and staff interviews, it was determined staff failed to date multidose vials (MDV) of medication when opened.This deficient practice had the potential to negatively affect all patients served by this agency.Findings include:CDC Injection Safety: Preventing Unsafe Injection PracticesDate: March 26,2024Key PointsUnsafe injection practices put patients and healthcare providers at risk. This harm is preventable...Why it mattersSafe injection practices are every provider's responsibility...Key Points for MDVOnce a MDV is opened (ergo, needle-punctured) the vial should be dated and discarded within 28 days unless the manufacturer states another date for that opened vial...

Patient#13: On 6/18/26 LPN made a visit to patient and documents that patient was smoking with his oxygen and caught his face on fire. LPN documents no facial hair remains on patient. Also documents he has first degree burns and the top layer of skin peeled off bilateral cheeks and upper lip. She educated to keep area clean and dry and suggested the patient use Vaseline and his tri cream that he already has in home to help with the burns. LPN documents that no wound care is needed. It should be noted that the use of Vaseline and the tri cream are petroleum based and contraindicated in the use with oxygen. Use of these items with oxygen could cause harm to the patient. There is no evidence of documentation in the chart that the LPN consulted with an RN or an MD for assessment and treatment of the patient. This is not consistent with accepted standards of nursing practice.

Based on interview, review of facility policy and procedure and review of facility documents, the Department has determined the Administrator failed to track quality indicators including adverse events as defined in hospice policy. Failure to track adverse events and demonstrate ability to improve performance can result in substandard patient care due to lack of awareness of adverse trends affecting the care of patients.
Findings include:

Facility policy titled, "...Adverse Event Policy...." reviewed June 1, 2024 revealed: "...Hospice will investigate any incident or injury in which home medical equipment,prosthetics, orthotics or supplies (DMEPOS) provided by Hospice may have contributed to the injury or incident, staff administered medication errors, falls with patient injury requiring medical intervention and drug diversion of Hospice-provided medications. Any action or inaction by Hospice that caused harm to a Hospice patient will also be investigated....When adverse event monitoring reveals a problem area, Hospice will implement changes designed to decrease occurrence of the adverse event. Hospice will assure that the new process is implemented hospice-wide...."
Facility policy titled, "...Quarterly Record Review Process...." reviewed June 1, 2024 revealed: "...Hospice will collect data quarterly on quality indicators...."
 
"...Client Adverse Event/Incident/Occurrence Log...." revealed: "...July 2022...No incident or occurrence...July 2023...No incident or occurrence...."
 
"...Incident Report...1/1/2023 to 12/31/2023...." revealed: "...6...Minor injury...8...Minor injury...12...Minor injury...15...Minor injury...17...Minor injury...18...Minor injury...21...Hospitalization required...23...Minor injury...24...Minor injury...."
The Hospitalization Required injury was logged on 4/4/2023.
In an interview conducted with Employee #1 on July 11, 2024, Employee #1 confirmed that adverse events data had not been collected in accordance with facility policies and procedures.

Upon patient record review, 2 of 13 (Patient #5, 7) did not have evidence in the patient record that the hospice has developed an individualized written plan of care for each patient that reflects all problems identified in the initial and comprehensive assessments. 
Patient 5: On the comprehensive initial assessment, dated 09.16.2021, it was noted that the patient had difficulty swallowing; nectar thick liquids were ordered and a commercial thickener appeared on the patient's medication list for use. The SN note dated 10.27.2021 indicated the patient had developed aspiration pneumonia; the patient was treated with Levaquin and prednisone. There is no evidence of a care plan related to aspiration risk or swallowing status. (corrected on site)
Patient 7: On the comprehensive initial assessment, dated 10.08.2021, it was noted that the patient was an elopement risk; the patient was transferred from an acute care hospital to an ALF, where he was then admitted for hospice services, largely due to previous elopements from his private home. SN note dated 10.26.2021 indicates the patient escaped the ALF twice during the previous week. There is no evidence of a care plan related to elopement risk. (corrected on site)

Based on interview and document review, the facility failed to provide appropriate treatment and management based on patient assessment when P1 had seizures related to a hypoglycemic (low blood glucose) episode and received four times greater than the prescribed amount of morphine. This resulted immediate jeopardy to P1, who death was related to hypoglycemia. 
The immediate jeopardy which began on 8/5/2023 when P1 failed to receive appropriate hypoglycemia management and an opioid (narcotic) overdose. Mayo Clinic Hospice director and was notified of the immediate jeopardy on 9/20/23 at 8:46 a.m.. The immediate jeopardy was removed on 9/20/23 at 5:01 p.m. after verification of an acceptable removal plan was implemented. 

P1's certification of terminal illness dated 7/13/23, indicated P1 was admitted on 7/13/23 with a terminal diagnosis of severe protein calorie malnutrition. Other hospice diagnoses included: type two diabetes mellitus with hyperglycemia (high blood sugar), dysphagia oropharyngeal phase (swallowing problems in the mouth or throat), and P1 had a body mass index (BMI) 19.9 or less indicating P1 was underweight. 
P1's hospice plan of care (POC) dated 7/13/23, indicated P1 was alert and oriented to self, date, and place and had visual and auditory hallucinations. P1 was cachectic (loss of muscle loss) and had a poor appetite. P1's care plan indicated P1's wishes was to live out the remainder of her life in her home and did not want to be sent to the hospital any further. Additionally, the POC identified the patient and caregiver would verbalize a basic understanding of diabetes at end of life with interventions to education on signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia. 
P1's provider orders for life sustaining treatment (POLST) indicated P1 did not want resuscitation, however desired comfort focused treatment. The POLST indicated P1 wanted relief from pain and suffering through the use of any medication by any route and although P1 preferred no transfers to the hospital for life sustaining treatments, wanted to be transferred if comfort needs could not be met in her current location. 
P1's skilled nurse hospice admission progress note dated 7/13/23, indicated P1 had a poor appetite, was cachectic, had difficulty swallowing and was at risk for aspiration, and lost 10% of her body weight in the prior 6 months. The note further indicated P1 had dysphagia that led to recurrent aspiration and or inadequate oral intake. P1 weighed approximately 83 pounds. P1 had pneumonitis due to inhalation of food on 6/9/2023. The progress noted indicated the nurse reviewed P1's medications with the nurse practitioner and P1's metformin and sliding scale insulin was discontinued by the nurse practitioner.
P1's telephone note dated 7/16/23, indicated P1's family member contacted hospice regarding P1's diabetes management and recalled a discussion of stopping medications and blood sugar checks for diabetes. The note indicated P1's metformin (a medication to lower blood glucose) was discontinued on admission and P1 continued on Glipizide 10 mg daily (a medication to lower blood glucose) and NPH insulin 5 units daily. 
P1's nursing progress note dated 7/17/23, indicated P1 had a poor appetite and ate approximately 10 to 30 bites per day and was on a dysphagia diet and was at risk for aspiration. The note also indicated P1 completed an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection on 7/15/23. Additionally, blood sugars (BG) were reviewed with the physician and P1's NPH insulin was increased from 5 units to 10 units every a.m. BG readings since previous the nurse visit ranged from 177 to 225 in the a.m., and 255 to 455 prior to supper.
P1's nursing progress note dated 7/20/23 indicated P1's BG levels ranged from 211-275 in the a.m., and 405-502 at bedtime. Per the progress note, P1's NPH insulin was subsequently increased to 15 units every a.m..
P1's nursing progress note dated 7/24/23, indicated P1 had difficulty swallowing and was at risk for aspiration. P1 ate a pancake during nursing visit and a family member reported P1 was eating a little better the past couple of days. The progress note indicated P1 had approximately 10-30 bites per day. P1's BG levels ranged 270-302 in the a.m., and 285-527 in the p.m. Per the progress note, P1's NPH insulin was subsequently increased to 20 units every a.m..
P1's nursing progress note dated 7/27/23, indicated P1's BG levels ranged from 234 to 317 in the a.m., and 404 to 555 at bedtime and new orders were received to increase P1's NPH insulin to 25 units every a.m.. 
P1's nursing progress note dated 7/31/23, indicated P1 ate 100% of breakfast and a family member stated P1 ate well the last three days. P1's BG levels ranged from 97 to 235 in the a.m., and 115-544 at bedtime and new orders were received for a sliding scale insulin due to continued elevated glucose levels. 
P1's nursing progress note dated 8/3/23, indicated P1's BG readings were reviewed with the NP along with urinary symptoms and no new orders were received. P1's BG levels ranged from 351 to 413 in the a.m., and there were no recorded BG readings recorded at bedtime on 7/31/23 and 8/1/23. The note further indicated the reading of the meter on the evening of 8/2/23, indicated "HI". Further, the note indicated the caregiver contacted the facility director of nursing (DON) who, per the note, did not have access to a computer to verify the sliding scale insulin dose and instructed the aide to administer seven units of insulin. 
P1's telephone contact note dated 8/5/23 at 5:40 a.m., indicated the assisted living facility (ALF) called to report P1 had increased shortness of breath and chest tightness after ambulating to the bathroom and hospice instructed staff to administer morphine 7.5 mg table, which was then given at 5:00 a.m. and contact hospice if no improvement. 
P1's telephone contact note dated 8/5/23 at 8:36 a.m., indicated ALF staff called hospice to report P1's continued shortness of breath. P1's insulin was held due to a low blood glucose reading (unspecified number) and requested further instruction. The nurse directed the ALF staff to administer morphine (unspecified dose) and if ineffective, lorazepam (unspecified dose) could be given at 9:30 a.m. The hospice care coordinator was updated regarding the low BG level and planned to follow up. 
P1's nurse visit note dated 8/5/23 at 12:35 p.m., indicated P1 was in bed and had involuntary repetitive eye movements consistent with seizure activity. P1's body was rigid and had clenched fists and teeth and her pupils were non-reactive. The note indicated orders were received to administer 2 milligrams (mg) or lorazepam every 5 minutes times two doses for seizure activity. The first dose was administered at 1:00 p.m., without a change in symptoms. At 1:15 p.m. it was documented the doses were repeated however the ALF staff stated to the registered nurse (RN)-A that she had retrieved morphine from the medication cart instead of lorazepam and had given morphine to the nurse to administer. P1 inadvertently received 4.5 tablets of morphine which equaled 30 mg of morphine. Further, the RN-A notified the nurse practitioner (NP)-B at 1:22 p.m., and lorazepam 2 mg was ordered and given at 1:30 p.m., for continued seizure activity. RN-A's visit ended at 3:34 p.m., and the progress note indicated seizure activity had subsided by the end of the visit. The visit lacked documentation regarding ongoing monitoring related to P1 receiving 4 times the ordered morphine dose, additionally, P1's respirations were documented as 26 at 1:35 p.m., Staff were instructed to hold oral pills as long as P1 was unresponsive, and the DON was instructed on new orders for scheduled morphine. Additionally, the progress note indicated at 1:29 p.m., P1's BG was 27, at 2:02 p.m., BG was 24, at 2:35 p.m., BG was 37, and at 3:09 p.m., BG was 52. Further, the family member (FM)-A reported P1's BG was 29 upon return to the facility approximately 12:00 p.m. and a repeat BG check was 24. The progress note indicated ALF staff tried crushing glucose tabs mixed with orange juice and administering when the hospice nurse arrived. The note indicated 1 milliliter of glucagon was administered at 2:22 p.m., by the facility nurse. The note lacked additional information regarding further treatment of the low blood glucose. 
P1's nurse postmortem hospice visit dated 8/5/23 at 9:25 p.m., indicated P1 expired at 7:35 p.m.
During interview on 9/18/23 at 1:29 p.m., the hospice administrator stated P1's event wasn't fully finished. The hospice administrator stated P1 resided at an assisted living facility (ALF) and P1's family took her out on an outing and P1 had a seizure in the car due to a hypoglycemic episode and family brought P1 back to the ALF. The administrator further stated P1 had a hypoglycemic seizure and should have received Ativan for the seizures, however an unlicensed staff from the ALF had put morphine in a medication cup and gave the medication to RN-A to administer. 
During interview on 9/19/23 at 9:04 a.m., FM-A stated P1 was picked up from the ALF on 8/5/23 in the morning and started to have a seizure in the car and was brought back to the ALF. FM-A stated P1 that morning received morphine inadvertently instead of lorazepam. FM-A stated P1 should not have had to struggle because she was on hospice and further stated it was traumatic for her and P1. FM-A stated when they arrived at the facility, P1 did not eat much that a.m., was alert and awake, and added they would have reconsidered taking her out if they knew P1 received morphine. FM-A stated the hospice agency did not talk about a general inpatient level of care or going to the hospital to treat low blood sugars or seizures. 
During interview on 9/19/23 at 10:29 a.m., RN-B stated if a patient's symptoms were not managed, she provided direction or called the patient back and would send a nurse to see the patient. RN-B stated ALF staff called and reported P1 complained of shortness of breath and morphine was provided. Additionally, P1's insulin was held that morning. RN-B stated she instructed staff at the ALF to administer morphine and instructed the staff to administer lorazepam if the morphine was not effective. RN-B further stated she ended the call and thought she should have asked what P1's blood sugar was and when RN-B tried to call the facility back, RN-B received no answer. Additionally, RN-B stated she did not provide any instruction to the ALF staff regarding P1's insulin that was held. 
During interview on 9/19/23 at 11:01 a.m., RN-A stated if a patient's symptoms were not managed, she would utilize orders a patient currently had and contact the provider to obtain new orders if needed. RN-A further stated P1 was alert and oriented to place and self and on the day P1 expired, P1 had a significant change and RN-A was notified by a triage nurse that family took P1 out of the facility to go to an event, was not responsive and P1's family brought P1 back to the facility. RN-A stated she arrived at 12:35 p.m., P1 was in bed and was not responding, had repetitive rapid eye movements and was very hypoglycemic and added family was overly excited trying to wake P1 up. RN-A stated the ALF staff were trying to intervene with glucose tablets and orange juice because P1's blood glucose was only 29 when P1 returned from the facility. RN-A stated her concern was P1's safety and addressing P1's low blood sugar and stated she suspected the seizure was due to hypoglycemia and further stated P1 did not have a history of having seizures. RN-A stated she observed P1 lying in bed with no response, with repetitive eye movements, and her fists and teeth were clenched tightly and she was moaning. RN-A stated she contacted NP-B at 12:45 p.m., and received an order to administer Ativan 2 mg every five minutes times two doses for seizures. RN-A stated she administered the first dose of Ativan at 1:00 p.m., and there was no change in P1's response. RN-A directed ALF staff to obtain a second dose of Ativan 2 mg. The ALF staff brought a cup of crushed medication to RN-A who administered the medication at 1:15 p.m., without verifying the medication type or medication dose. RN-A further stated the ALF staff informed RN-A at approximately 1:22 p.m., they crushed four tablets of morphine 7.5 mg (30mg) instead of intended intended four tablets of ativan 0.5 mg to total ativan 2 mg. This constituted four times the amount morphine that was prescribed for P1. RN-A stated she notified NP-B immediately of the medication error and was instructed to administer the second dose of Ativan 2mg. RN-A administered the second dose of Ativan at 1:30 p.m., and stated P1 continued to have the repetitive eye movement but P1's fists and teeth were not as tight as they had been. RN-A further stated P1's blood glucose levels were not resolved and provided the following readings: 1:29 p.m., BG was 27, at 202 p.m. BG was 24, at 2:35 p.m. BG was 37, and at 3:09 BG was 52. RN-A stated orange juice and crushed glucagon tablets were administered in the side of P1's mouth. RN-A further stated the ALF director of nursing inquired why they couldn't administer a glucagon intramuscular (IM) injection and RN-A stated hospice did not have an active order for IM glucagon. RN-A stated she obtained an order for the IM or subcutaneous glucagon injection and the DON administered the medication at 2:22 p.m. RN-A stated P1 was very thin and was 63 inches tall and weighed 83 pounds and stated the first time P1 consumed morphine was on 8/5/23 at 5:40 a.m., and had not consumed the medication previously. RN-A stated P1 never regained consciousness following the episode and stated after this happened, a reporting system was initiated and further stated she expressed concern there was a gray area in managing hypoglycemic episodes and stated since this happened, she had been educated further that 911 could be utilized to administer emergency medications.
During interview on 9/19/23 at 12:51 p.m., NP-B stated a blood sugar in the 20's would cause a seizure. NP-B stated if there is no glucose gel, to crush tablets, mix with juice and administer slowly and it should be started right away and administered every 30 minutes. Once a blood sugar was above 90, the glucose would be stopped and she would re-check a blood sugar an hour later. NP-B stated if P1 was opioid naive (having never received and opioid such as morphine) and received 30 mg of morphine, it would probably make her sleepy and stated she was not aware P1 was given 30 mg of morphine in error.
During interview on 9/19/23 at 1:07 p.m., the hospice medical director (MD) stated he was familiar with P1 and they were investigating the situation as a sentinel event and were looking for opportunities for improvement. MD stated P1's seizures were due to having blood glucose in the 20's and further stated glucagon should be started as immediately as possible and added if a patient is not responsive but is able to swallow glucose gel and apple juice could be given, and if a patient was not able to swallow the role would be to call emergency medical services (EMS) for help. If P1 was seizing, the seizure would make it impossible to give anything orally and is an indication the glucose is needed parenterally (through an intravenous line). MD stated they were looking into informal education regarding that calls to EMS are appropriate in emergent situations, medication management, diabetes management, management of hypoglycemia, but was all these interventions were preliminary and had not been fully implemented. MD further stated P1 had severe hypoglycemia on the day of death and which should be added on the death certificate. MD further stated if P1 had respiratory depression, he would give Narcan to reverse symptoms. The nursing progress note lacked information monitoring was completed. 
During interview on 9/19/23 at 1:55 p.m., the hospice administrator stated they were awaiting further incident review before completing diabetic education to hospice nursing staff and the clinical nurse specialist was completing research on diabetic assessment and reassessment. The hospice administrator further stated there were opportunities with the episode where it should not have taken that long to recover P1's blood sugar levels and wondered if they could have reversed the hypoglycemia when P1's blood sugar was 24. The administrator further stated she spoke with RN-A regarding not administering medications in a facility without first verifying the correct patient, medication route, medication dose, medication amount and administration time which are the fundamentals for safe medication administration. 
During interview on 9/19/23 at 2:29 p.m., the hospice administrator stated they had not provided any education to staff on what to do with a suspected over-dose, but was something they should add. 
The immediate jeopardy which began on 8/5/2023 when P1 failed to receive appropriate hypoglycemia management and an opioid (narcotic) overdose. Mayo Clinic Hospice director was notified of the immediate jeopardy on 9/20/23 at 8:46 a.m.. The immediate jeopardy was removed on 9/20/23 at 5:01 p.m. after verification of an acceptable removal plan was implemented. 
The IJ was removed on 8/5/23, at 5:01 p.m. when the hospice submitted and implemented an acceptable removal plan. This included reviewing medication protocol policies and procedures, developing procedures for emergency diabetic management of hospice patients, training of nurses to ensure proper medication administration and review of patient management for an opioid overdose. Review of policy and procedure revisions was completed and hospice management was then interviewed on implemention of the aforementioned changes in policy and education. This was then verified through on-site document review, observation, and interview.

Based on policy review, Client Occurrence Report, clinical record review, and staff interview, the agency failed to address safety risks for 1 of 1 patient that exited the building without staff knowledge and had a fall with injuries (#1). Immediate Jeopardy was identified beginning 4/6/23 and abated 5/3/23. Findings included:

A policy, ";Safety & Risk Management Policy" (no date), was provided by the clinical director on 5/2/23 at 12:07 p.m. The policy stated, ";[Hospice agency] develops and implements a plan that addresses the safety of patients and caregivers that includes...Implementation and documentation of interventions directed towards eliminating or minimizing safety concerns identified in the patients environment."
A policy/procedure, ";IPU [inpatient unit] Elopement [act or instance of leaving a safe area or safe premises] and Wandering" (reviewed/approved 5/22), was provided by the clinical director on 5/3/23 at 9:00 a.m. The policy stated, ";On admission , a patient is assessed and may be considered at risk for elopement and wandering if he/she remains ambulatory or self-mobile in a wheelchair and...has a history of elopement or wandering at home or in a community...Exhibits in inappropriate behavior or episodes of confusion/agitation...Expresses concern about being in the Inpatient unit (IPU) of a desire to leave...Interventions to prevent elopement or wandering are initiated if the patient is assessed to be at risk...Initiate high risk falls interventions. Allegation of Compliance 
 
1. The plan of correcting the specific deficiency. The plan should address the processes that lead to the deficiency cited: 
 
Immediate Jeopardy was identified due to a patient fall outdoors, in a fenced garden connected to the hospice Inpatient Unit (IPU), resulting in injury. At approximately 11:45 pm on 4/8/2023 the RN rounded to Patient #1's room after previous visit from the other RN in room at 11:00 pm. RN found the bed empty and patient #1 was not in the room. Hospice IPU staff searched the facility and found the patient outside the building, in a fenced-in area, on his knees leaning over a metal bench asking for help. Blood from forehead covered face and glasses. Patient was brought back into the facility. A small laceration was noted to the top of the head. A large hematoma was noted to the top right side of the head. Moderate size skin tears were noted to right and left elbows and abrasions noted to both knees. The Physician on call was notified. She advised that if the daughter was agreeable that the patient be sent to the emergency department. The daughter was called and notified of the event and the status of the patient. The daughter stated that the patient gets outside and falls at home, and that she did not want the patient sent to the emergency department. The administrator on call was notified of the event. Assessments on the patient were provided throughout the night and the daughter was provided an update in the morning on 4/9/2023. Daughter was also advised on the night of 4/8/2023 to call anytime throughout the night if she wanted an update. When patient #1 first arrived at the hospice IPU, he was assessed to be a safety risk due to wandering. Patient was placed in a room directly in front of the nurses station and fall precautions, bed alarm, and flight risk precautions were initiated. 
 
2. The procedure for implementing the acceptable plan of correction for the specific deficiency cited: 
 
· After the nurse assessed Patient #1 on 4/6/2023 on arrival to the IPU, the patient was placed in a room across from the nurses station. 
· Staff were informed of the patient event on 4/9/2023. 
· The wandering patient safety process was initiated immediately after the event.
· The physician updated the patient's medication due to extreme agitation on 4/9/2023.
· Following this event, the patient was observed at least hourly, and was placed in his bed with the alarm on or put in a wheelchair at the nurse station with 1-1 observation.
Effective 5/2/2023, the following will be implemented:
· All patients in the building are now assessed upon admission and daily for flight/safety risks.
· Installation of a door alarm to sound any time the patio door is opened with education that a staff member will immediately investigate who and why the door was opened. 
· Signage to STOP and instruct any patient to request staff assistance, prior to opening the patio door, was installed on the patio door. 
· Use of video monitoring equipment to be utilized on any patient assessed to be a wander/flight risk to allow improved visibility of staff to ensure patient safety. 
· Bed alarms to be used with any patient deemed to be a wander/flight risk. This alarm is to be in the ON position whenever staff is not at the bedside. 
· Following a wandering episode, the nurse will complete visual checks every 15-minutes for the first 4 hrs. followed by every 1-hour visual checks. 
· A check list has been created for the nurses to ensure that when someone is on flight precautions that all of the process is followed. This check list is kept in their report tool and will be reviewed with oncoming staff.
· The Safety problem will be detailed in the plan of care for any patient assessed to be a wander/flight risk. 
· Education will be provided to all IPU staff regarding this plan of correction and the new checklist for flight risk patients. The education will be provided on 5/3/2023 via Teams Meeting. Any staff not in attendance will view the recorded meeting at the start of their next scheduled shift. 
 
3. The monitoring procedure to ensure that the plan of correction is effective and that specific deficiency cited Inpatient Unit Clinical Directors will review all patients assessed as wander/flight risks during morning stand-up to ensure all staff are aware and compliant with new protocols and provide ongoing education.
· Inpatient Unit Clinical Directors will complete chart reviews of patients assessed as wander/flight risk to ensure patient record and plan of care addresses safety documentation. 
 
4. The title of the person responsible for implementing the acceptable plan of correction.
· Hospice IPU Clinical Director

Based on clinical record review, Discharge for Cause report to the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR), facility room observation, and staff interview, the agency failed to implement safety measures following a patient elopement attempt. Immediate jeopardy was identified beginning 07/09/24 at 2:30 PM and was abated on 07/09/24 at 4:52 PM with an acceptable allegation of compliance.
Findings included:

Patient #1 was admitted to the agency on 05/28/24 with a principal diagnosis of brain cancer. Patient #1 was initially admitted as a home hospice patient while he was living with his sister in her apartment.
On 06/14/24, an emergency respite stay was coordinated for Patient #1 at the agencys inpatient unit due to his sister not having paid rent or the electricity bill at that residence. The apartment landlord would not allow the patient to continue to stay at the home without electricity and the patients sister was not able to be located or contacted.
On 06/25/24 the inpatient unit director documented, ";Patient has exited his room by climbing over his outside patio rail and ambulated to Wayne Memorial Drive and this author had to redirect patient to return to his room. When asked what he was doing he stated that he was wanting a cigarette."
In an interview on 07/09/24 at 10:00 AM, the inpatient unit director stated that the aforementioned incident occurred on 06/18/24 at approximately 6:45 PM. She was informed by one of her aides who was driving to the facility that Patient #1 was ";at the road". The inpatient unit director went outside and located the patient by the stop sign, ";kind of wandering down the sidewalk". The inpatient unit director talked to the patient, and he was able to be redirected to return to the facility with her. The patient stated that he had crawled over the bench (which was on the patio of his room) to get to the highway. The inpatient unit director stated that the agencys typical safety measures were not successful for Patient #1 because he had unplugged his bed (which would have alarmed if it were plugged in) due to the mattress inflation being uncomfortable and he refused to have a camera placed in his room for monitoring.
In an interview on 07/09/24 at 10:30 AM, the inpatient unit director stated, ";...normally I dont have wanderers [at the inpatient unit]. If it is a demented patient on the home hospice side who is still ambulatory, I cant accept those patients here because I cant keep those patients safe in the building." She also stated if a patient who was in the facility became confused during their stay and began with wandering behaviors, she would talk to the family and the patient would typically receive medication adjustments to try to control the behaviors chemically.
The inpatient unit director stated that Patient #1's room location was third room from the nurses station and ";within eyes view" which was why he went out through the patio instead of using the room door and walking through the facility's hallways. She added that it was her opinion that Patient #1 would not have accepted a 1:1 volunteer or other staff member to monitor him for safety in his room due to his paranoia, however, this strategy was not attempted. The inpatient unit director stated that there were no safety measures put in place related to blocking or restricting access to the patio door for Patient #1 due to concerns that his agitated and/or paranoid behavior would have escalated if he was unable to independently access the patio outside of his room. This strategy was not attempted.
CREDIBLE ALLEGATION OF COMPLIANCE
THE PROCESS THAT LED TO THE DEFICIENCY:
The process that led to the deficiency was that there was no patient elopement policy or procedure in place to identify patients at risk for elopement and appropriate interventions to prevent patient elopement.
THE PLAN OF CORRECTING THE SPECIFIC DEFICIENCY AND PROCEDURE FOR IMPLEMENTING THE ACCEPTABLE PLAN OF CORRECTION FOR THE SPECIFIC DEFICIENCY CITED:
An Inpatient Hospice procedure 28.32 will be developed and implemented immediately called ";Patient Elopement" effective 7/9/24.
All facility staff on duty at the inpatient facility will be educated in person on 7/9/24 on the new procedure by the Director of Inpatient Services. This education will be logged in the online learning management system. On duty staff will be required to review and sign the Patient Elopement policy (28.32).
The education and procedure review will be recorded and assigned via the online learning management system to staff who were not present at the live training on 7/9/24. They will be required to complete the education and procedure review before starting their next assigned shift. This will be logged in the online learning management platform. 
THE MONITORING PROCEDURE TO ENSURE THAT THE PLAN OF CORRECTION IS EFFECTIVE, AND THAT SPECIFIC DEFICIENCY CITED REMAINS CORRECTED AND/OR IN COMPLIANCE WITH THE REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS:
The Education Manager and Sr Director of Quality, Regulation, and Compliance will validate all inpatient hospice staff have completed mandatory education and Elopement Policy review (28.32) and it is documented in the education record by 7/23/24.
The QAPI and Clinical Department will audit a representative sampling of hospice patient charts on a weekly basis to determine if patient was identified as an elopement risk and if so were measures put in place per the 3HC Elopement Procedure. Once 100% compliance is achieved for 3 consecutive weeks there will be ongoing monitoring via the quarterly clinical record review to ensure continued compliance. Audit results will be reported to the Professional Management Team, and the Inpatient Hospice QAPI Team.

Based on record review and interview, the Hospice failed to ensure 2 of 6 sampled patients (Patient #1 and #22) were free from neglect

This affected Patient #1 who expressed suicidal ideation, and the Hospice failed to develop a Care Plan with appropriate interventions, or communicate the concerns for suicidal ideation between disciplines and care settings, which ended with a family member finding Patient #1 dead by fatal gunshot wound with a gun in his hand. This affected Patient #22 for whom the Hospice was notified by nursing home staff on 06/17/24 that she was found disoriented with pills nearby, but the Hospice did not implement any interventions to address the risk of patient overdose, and Patient #22 died on 06/20/24 after a suspected second overdose on 06/19/24. (L0517). The cumulative effect of these systemic problems resulted in Immediate jeopardy, a situation in which the noncompliance with Conditions of Participation has caused, or is likely to cause, serious injury, harm, impairment, or death to a patient.

Based on review of the Hospice’s Standard (in lieu of Policy and Procedure), patient record review and staff interview, the Hospice provider failed to ensure 2 of 6 sampled patients (Patient #1 and #22) were free from neglect. This affected Patient #1 who expressed suicidal ideation and the Hospice failed to develop care plan with appropriate interventions and/or referrals, and failed to communicate concerns for suicidal ideation between disciplines and care settings, which ended with a family member finding Patient #1 dead by gunshot wound to the head with gunpowder residue on his hands. This affected Patient #22 for whom Hospice staff was notified by nursing home staff on 06/17/24 that she was found disoriented with pills nearby after a return from a leave of absence, but the Hospice did not implement any interventions to address the risk of patient overdose, and Patient #22 died on 06/20/24 after a suspected second overdose on 06/19/24. The findings include:

2. Review of the medical record revealed patient #22, a 78-year-old female, was admitted to the hospice agency on 7/29/23 with terminal diagnosis of atherosclerotic heart disease and secondary diagnosis of heart failure. 
Review of the medical record dated 7/31/23 revealed a Registered Nurse (RN) completed the Initial Comprehensive Assessment that noted the patient was alert and oriented to person, place, situation and time. The patient reported a pain level of ";6" with care plan goal of ";3" or less. The assessment indicated the patient was on opioid type medications for sharp/shooting pain down her left leg and across her back. The patient stated, ";I just want to feel better, I have no quality of life". The RN documented under psychosocial assessment no history of psychiatric illness/substance abuse or suicidal ideation. The RN documented the patient had history of depression since her son passed away in January from Corona Virus Disease.
The Bachelor of Social Work (BSW) completed a Psychosocial Comprehensive Assessment on 8/1/23 and documented the patient denied concerns regarding suicidal ideation or substance abuse history and currently was in acceptance of her terminal illness, had depression and was coping appropriately. The plan moving forward was for SW (Social Worker) to meet with patient twice per month to provide support and education. The plan of care included symptom management regarding ";sense of control and ability to cope" and interventions to provide reassurance, educate regarding hospice services and provide support through being present. The SW assisted patient #22 with nursing home placement per note dated 2/26/24. 
The hospice RN note dated 6/15/24 revealed the nurse visited the patient at the nursing home. During the visit the patient opened her eyes when her name was called but fell asleep while talking. She then opened her eyes and said she felt ";wiped out." The hospice RN did not collaborate with other hospice staff or with nursing home staff to determine the reason for the patient's change in condition and why she was so lethargic. 
On 6/16/24 to 6/17/24, patient #22 went on a Leave of Absence (LOA) from the nursing home and obtained unknown drugs while on leave. The hospice agency did not ensure coordination of communication and were not notified of the patient's leave.
The hospice Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) #LL visited the patient at the nursing home on 6/17/24 from 9 AM to 10:20 AM, and documented the patient was alert and calm. He wrote he was informed by nursing home staff the patient returned from LOA and was found in her room very disoriented. About 5-6 bottles of medications including Ativan and other narcotics were found in the patients room which the nursing home staff secured in a locked box. The hospice LPN did not initiate an incident report or collaborate with the nursing home staff to address why the resident brought the medications to the nursing home or which medications she may have taken.
On 6/18/24 at 11:45 PM, the Telecare Call Action Log by hospice RN #ZZ showed the nursing home LPN called to report patient #22 was found 10 minutes ago foaming at the mouth and unresponsive. The patient had a pulse of 51 bpm [beats per minute]. The nursing home LPN stated she found a cup in the patients room with Ativan, Temazepam and Potassium pills. The LPN also reported the patient had history of self-harming behavior. The patient was sent to the hospital for possible overdose. At 12:45 AM, the ";Hospital called in stated that patient overdose, reason for the visit to hospital..."
On 6/19/24 at 6:43 AM, Telecare Call note by hospice staff #BBB read, ";Facility nurse called in and stated patient came back from the hospital at 0400 (4 AM) but the patient's condition is still bad..."
On 6/19/24 hospice RN #MM visited the patient at the nursing home and documented a visit note at 10 AM. The noted indicated the patient was unresponsive, and foaming at the mouth. The patient was suctioned, and family notified of the situation. The family informed this situation has occurred many times..."
On 6/20/24 RN #MM documented a visit at the nursing home from 8:45 AM to 9:55 AM. The note showed the patient had no response to stimuli and was clammy. The patient was not able to swallow, and all medications were discontinued except for comfort. 
On 6/20/24 at 10:35 AM, the hospice chaplain visited the patient at the nursing home and documented death at this time was imminent. She had decreased response to verbal and visual stimuli. The date and time of death according to the hospice Case Sheet was on 6/20/24 at 1:30 PM. 
On 8/27/24 at 12:43 PM, interview and concurrent record review was conducted with General Manager (GM) DD in person and other staff on the phone from program #78 including Senior Patient Care Administrator (PCA) #II, Performance Improvement Specialist (PIS) #JJ, and Associate GM #KK. The staff verified they did not have a General Manager for program #78 at this time. They explained this incident was suspected suicide as the patient was found with bottles of pills nearby. Hospice staff indicated they did not know what day she went on leave and thought that a friend brought her home, and that is how she obtained pills and brought them back to the nursing home. 
The Senior Patient Care Administrator verified she was responsible to ensure a thorough investigation and root cause analysis was done post incidents. She verified that hospice staff did not talk to the nursing home staff to find out exactly what happened. She said they did identify areas of opportunity for communication and education. They needed to educate the nursing home staff that hospice should have been notified immediately after drugs were confiscated from patient #22. She stated, ";the main thing that was lacking was our communication between facility staff and hospice staff. I think mainly being aware the patient went out of the facility so that we would have known when she came back, she was having a hard time adjusting to being at the facility". The Senior Patient Care Administrator noted they needed to improve their communication with the nursing home staff and should have implemented measures to keep the patient safe. She acknowledged they had not revised the care plan after it was identified the patient brought in medications to the nursing home and was found disoriented.
