Based on interviews and record review, the hospice agency (HA) failed to ensure the responsible party (RP 1) of one of 23 sampled patients (Patient 1) understood and agreed with Patient 1's plan of care for continuous care initiated on 11/20/2024, that included individualized goals, interventions, and expected outcomes to manage pain.
 
This failure resulted in the further decline in Patient 1s condition with ineffective pain management due to the disagreement with Morphine (opioid, a controlled medication to treat moderate to severe pain that can cause respiratory distress and death when taken in high doses) administration and medication discrepancies between the HA staff and the familys expected outcomes for Patient 1.

During a review of Patient 1s Case Sheet (admission record), indicated Patient 1s Start of Care (SOC) date on 11/12/2024 with primary diagnosis of nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH, blood clot in the brain) and secondary diagnosis of hemiplegia and hemiparesis (paralysis and weakness in one side of the body), affecting the right side.
 
During a review of Patient 1s Initial Certification, dated 11/15/2024, indicated Patient 1 had dementia (decline in mental ability that interferes with daily life) and was dependent on caregivers for all activities of daily living (ADL).
 
During a review of Patient 1s Interdisciplinary Plan of Care Revision/Physician Orders (MD order 1), dated 11/20/2024, MD order 1 indicated RN 1 obtained an order from MD 3 to discontinue routine level of care (LOC) and start continuous care (CC, around-the-clock hospice care at home to manage a crisis situation) on 11/20/2024 at 4 PM for pain.
 
During a review of Patient 1s Nursing – Updated Comprehensive Assessment (Comprehensive Assessment 1), dated 11/20/2024, Comprehensive Assessment 1 indicated the following:
1. RN 1 was unable to take blood pressure due to increased pain with blood pressure cuff inflation, respirations were 18 breaths per minute with no signs and symptoms of respiratory distress, and pain severity score of 6 out of 10.
2. Patient 1 had small intake of pureed food with sips of a nutritional drink.
3. RN 1 notified Medical Doctor 3 (MD 3) regarding Patient 1s unmanaged pain.
4. HA to start CC on 11/20/2024 at 4 PM.
5. The primary symptom communication source was Caregiver 3, and the visit start time was 3:10 PM. There was no documented evidence of communication attempts to RP 1 after the 11/20/2024 Skilled Nursing visit.
 
During a review of Patient 1s Interdisciplinary Care Plan: Continuous Care Shift Care (CP 1), dated 11/20/2024, CP 1 indicated the following:
 
1. The reason for CC was pain.
2. The interventions included observing for signs and symptoms of pain, documenting how the interventions helped, and calling HA for any changes in condition, concerns, or if interventions are ineffective and symptoms persist.
3. The additional interventions for the skilled nurse included documenting symptom severity rating, administering medications per physician orders, and calling the physician if medications are ineffective.
 
During a review of Patient 1s Focus Visit: Updated Comprehensive Assessment (Comprehensive Assessment 2), dated 11/21/2024, Comprehensive Assessment 2 indicated the following:
1. There was no documented evidence of physician notification regarding the change in condition and the expected outcome/s. Patient 1 had a decline in vital signs with blood pressure of 83/56 and respirations of 10 breaths per minute and Patient 1s status changed to ";imminent (signs or symptoms are consistent with a prognosis of less than 5 days)" with decreased response to verbal and visual stimuli.
2. RN 1 documented, ";Family was upset with patient appearing sedated, asked nurses to hold Roxanol (liquid form of immediate-release Morphine)." There was no documented evidence that RP 1 was informed of the change in expected outcomes/ for Patient 1.
3. RN 1 documented to ";Continue Current Plan of Care." There was no documented evidence of any revisions to Patient 1s plan of care interventions for pain management and expected outcomes.
 
During an interview on 12/5/2024 at 9:24 AM, RP 1 stated she was surprised to see a HA nurse when she got home from work. RP 1 stated LVN 4 stated she was there for pain management but ";did not give much information." RP 1 stated prior to CC initiation, Patient 1 was able to open eyes, nod, say ";Yes," ";No," ";Better" in Patients native language. RP 1 stated, ";They said they were there for pain management. We were hoping one day, pain would be managed, and we could take [Patient 1] to the beach again." RP 1 stated on 11/21/2024 at 6:30 AM, Patient 1 had bluish gray lips and looked like a ";corpse." RP 1 stated he was not responsive but was still breathing. RP 1 stated she was not notified immediately when Patient 1 was placed on oxygen therapy at 2 liters per minute via nasal cannula. RP 1 stated she believed Patient 1 was ";overdosed with Morphine," so she requested the staff to hold the Morphine doses. RP 1 stated on 11/22/2024, Patient 1 ";looked better" after Morphine doses were held but Patient 1 was ";still not responding." RP 1 stated she then administered to Patient 1 glucose liquid (to treat low blood sugar) and 2 doses of Narcan (medicine that reverses an opioid overdose) she bought over the counter, then Patient 1 started to respond, woke up, and yelled, ";No, Mama! No!" RP 1 stated she called 911 and was admitted in the hospital for about 11 days, given antibiotics, and discharged to home with home health services. RP 1 stated Patient 1 gained back his appetite at the hospital and still had pain with movement.
 
During an interview on 12/5/2024 at 1:52 PM, Registered Nurse 1 (RN 1) stated during a routine visit on 11/20/2024, Patient 1 presented with grimacing and moaning when touched. RN 1 stated caregivers and staff were not able to ";touch" him, ";barely able to change him (adult incontinence pad)." RN 1 stated she obtained an order from the physician (MD 3) to initiate the CC to ";get his pain under control." RN 1 stated she reached out to the CC team to start CC for Patient 1 because the CC team was in-charge of staffing and scheduling. RN 1 stated she discussed the CC plan of care with Caregiver 3, because the legal decisionmaker, RP 1, ";was not able to answer" her calls and was ";always at work." RN 1 did not recall if she documented her call attempts to RP 1. RN 1 stated during her follow-up visit on 11/21/2024, RN 1 stated Patient1 declined, and she documented the vital signs obtained. RN 1 stated she was informed that the family requested to hold the Morphine order due to Patient 1 ";appearing sedated." RN 1 stated she did not notify the physician because the CC staff would notify the CC team regarding the changes in Patient 1s condition and refusal of Morphine. RN 1 stated she spoke with Caregiver 3, who was mostly present at the bedside with Patient 1.
 
During an interview and a concurrent review of Patient 1s clinical records on 12/5/2024 at 2:41 PM, Director of Patient Care Services (DPCS) stated she was not aware RP 1 had POA to make healthcare decisions for Patient 1. DPCS stated RN 1 spoke to Caregiver 3 regarding the CC order but failed to document the call attempts to RP 1. DPCS stated Patient 1s baseline vital signs prior to CC initiation were 118/90, 104/65, 114/71, and 118/60 with respirations ranging from 13-18 breaths per minute. DPCS stated if Patient 1s expected outcome was to decline, the physician did not need to be notified by the skilled nurse.
 
During a review of the HAs policy and procedures (P&P 1), titled ";Symptom Management," dated 6/3/2022, P&P 1 indicated the following:
 
1. Patient and family education is an important part of symptom management and should be included on patient care plans.
2. Symptoms should be care planned with goals, interventions, and outcomes based on assessment findings and patient/family input.
 
During a review of the HAs policy and procedures (P&P 2), titled ";Care Planning," dated 5/16/2023, indicated the following:
1. The VITAS RN must initiate the Continuous Care Shift Care Plan of Care for the patient and include problems and interventions provided to patients and families by the Continuous Care Shift Care staff.
2. The ideal score or goal is rated on a scale of 0-10 and documented on the care plan as a numeric goal.
3. The outcome describes the result desired by the patient/family and team.
4. Interventions must be individualized and include steps/tasks for the IDG to meet the goals and outcomes of the patient/caregiver.
 
During a review of the HAs policy and procedures (P&P 3), titled ";Continuous Care," dated 9/4/2024, P&P 3 indicated the following:
1. The care plan must be updated when a patient is placed on continuous care. The RN, or LPN/LVN in collaboration with a RN, must ensure changes to patient goals, outcomes, and interventions (initiation of the Shift Care POC, includes specific interventions for Shift Care staff) is in place on the POC.
2. The RN must update the visit staff POC and Shift Care POC, as needed, based on findings and analysis. The RN must utilize the information from shift notes to complete assessment, care plan, provide interventions and supervise the care provided.

Based on interview and record review, the HA failed to ensure the physician of one of 23 sampled patients (MD 1) was notified of Patient 1s significant change of condition when Morphine (opioid, a controlled medication to treat moderate to severe pain that can cause respiratory distress and death when taken in high doses) medication order was increased in dosage and frequency, and the refusal of the responsible party (RP 1) for the medication to be administered.
 
The deficient practice resulted in Patient 1 had a decline in vital signs with blood pressure (BP) of 83/56 and respiratory rate (RR) of 10 breaths per minute, and Patient 1s status changed to ";imminent" (ready to take place) with decreased response to verbal and visual stimuli.
 
 

During a review of Patient 1s Case Sheet (admission record) indicated Patient 1s Start of Care (SOC) date on 11/12/2024 with primary diagnosis of nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH, blood clot in the brain) and secondary diagnosis of hemiplegia and hemiparesis (paralysis and weakness in one side of the body) affecting the right side.
 
During a review of Patient 1s Initial Certification, dated 11/15/2024, indicated Patient 1 had dementia (decline in mental ability that interferes with daily life) and was dependent on caregivers for all activities of daily living (ADL).
 
During a review of Patient 1s Interdisciplinary Plan of Care Revision/Physician Orders (MD order 1), dated 11/20/2024, MD order 1 indicated RN 1 obtained an order from MD 3 to discontinue routine level of care (LOC) and start continuous care (CC, around-the-clock hospice care at home to manage a crisis situation) on 11/20/2024 at 4 PM for pain.
 
During a review of Patient 1s Nursing – Updated Comprehensive Assessment (Comprehensive Assessment 1) dated 11/20/2024, indicated the following:
1. RN 1 notified Medical Doctor 3 (MD 3) of Patient 1s unmanaged pain the start of continuous care starting on 11/20/2024 at 4 PM.
2. RN 1 was unable to take blood pressure due to increased pain with blood pressure cuff inflation, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute with no signs and symptoms of respiratory distress, and pain severity score of 6 out of 10.
3. Patient was confused but able to make some needs known, Spanish-speaking, and communicated with Caregiver 3.
4. Patient 1 had small intake of pureed food with sips of Ensure.
5. The primary symptom communication source was Caregiver 3, and the visit start time was 3:10 PM. There was no documented evidence of communication attempts to RP 1 regarding the 11/20/2024 Skilled Nursing visit.
6. Patient 1 was not determined a ";high risk for imminent death (signs or symptoms are consistent with a prognosis of less than 5 days).
 
During a review of Patient 1s Interdisciplinary Care Plan: Continuous Care Shift Care (CP 1), dated 11/20/2024, CP 1 indicated the following:
1. The reason for CC was pain.
2. The interventions included observing for signs and symptoms of pain, documenting how the interventions helped, and calling HA for any changes in condition, concerns, or if interventions are ineffective and symptoms persist.
3. The additional interventions for the skilled nurse included documenting symptom severity rating, administering medications per physician orders, and calling the physician if medications are ineffective.
 
During a review of Patient 1s Focus Visit: Updated Comprehensive Assessment (Comprehensive Assessment 2), dated 11/21/2024, Comprehensive Assessment 2 indicated the following:
1. There was no documented evidence of physician notification regarding the change in condition and the expected outcome/s. Patient 1 had a decline in vital signs with blood pressure of 83/56 and respirations of 10 breaths per minute and Patient 1s status changed to ";imminent (signs or symptoms are consistent with a prognosis of less than 5 days)" with decreased response to verbal and visual stimuli.
2. RN 1 documented, ";Family was upset with patient appearing sedated, asked nurses to hold Roxanol (liquid form of immediate-release Morphine)." There was no documented evidence that RP 1 was informed of the change in expected outcomes for Patient 1.
3. RN 1 documented to ";Continue Current Plan of Care." There was no documented evidence of any revisions to Patient 1s plan of care interventions for pain management and expected outcomes.
 
During an interview on 12/5/2024 at 9:24 AM, RP 1 stated she was surprised to see a HA nurse when she got home from work. RP 1 stated LVN 4 stated she was there for pain management but ";did not give much information." RP 1 stated prior to CC initiation, Patient 1 was able to open eyes, nod, say ";Yes," ";No," ";Better" in Patients native language. RP 1 stated, ";They said they were there for pain management. We were hoping one day, pain would be managed, and we could take [Patient 1] to the beach again." RP 1 stated on 11/21/2024 at 6:30 AM, Patient 1 had bluish gray lips and looked like a ";corpse." RP 1 stated he was not responsive but was still breathing. RP 1 stated she was not notified immediately when Patient 1 was placed on oxygen therapy at 2 liters per minute via nasal cannula. RP 1 stated she believed Patient 1 was ";overdosed with Morphine," so she requested the staff to hold the Morphine doses. RP 1 stated on 11/22/2024, Patient 1 ";looked better" after Morphine doses were held but Patient 1 was ";still not responding." RP 1 stated she then administered to Patient 1 Glucose liquid (to treat low blood sugar) and 2 doses of Narcan (medicine that reverses an opioid overdose) she bought over the counter, then Patient 1 started to respond, woke up, and yelled, ";No, Mama! No!" RP 1 stated she called 911 and was admitted in the hospital for about 11 days, given antibiotics, and discharged to home with home health services. RP 1 stated Patient 1 gained back his appetite at the hospital and still had pain with movement.
 
During an interview on 12/5/024 at 1:05 PM, Licensed Vocational Nurse 1 (LVN 1) stated when she started her shift, Patient 1 had respirations from 9-10 breaths per minute. LVN 1 stated at the end of her shift, respirations went down to 7 breaths per minute. LVN 1 stated she was not able to take the blood pressure during the shift due to Patient 1s grimacing, but LVN 1 was able to take radial pulse 90 at the start of shift to 120 at the end of shift. LVN 1 stated she was ";not able to measure" the amount of Morphine left in the bottle but notified the family how many Morphine doses were administered. LVN 1 stated at around 5:45 AM, she placed Patient 1 on Oxygen therapy at 2 liters per minute due to deep breaths with a rate of 8 per minute. LVN 1 stated she did not directly notify the physician or RN about the change in condition but gave the report to the incoming Home Health Aide.
 
During an interview on 12/5/2024 at 1:52 PM, Registered Nurse 1 (RN 1) stated during a routine visit on 11/20/2024, Patient 1 presented with grimacing and moaning when touched. RN 1 stated caregivers and staff were not able to ";touch" him, ";barely able to change him (adult incontinence pad)." RN 1 stated she obtained an order from the physician (MD 3) to initiate the CC to ";get his pain under control." RN 1 stated she reached out to the CC team to start CC for Patient 1 because the CC team was in-charge of staffing and scheduling. RN 1 stated she discussed the CC plan of care with Caregiver 3, because the legal decisionmaker, RP 1, ";was not able to answer" her calls and was ";always at work." RN 1 did not recall if she documented her call attempts to RP 1. RN 1 stated during her follow-up visit on 11/21/2024, RN 1 stated Patient 1 declined, and she documented the vital signs obtained. RN 1 stated she was informed that the family requested to hold the Morphine order due to Patient 1 ";appearing sedated." RN 1 stated she did not notify the physician because the CC staff would notify the CC team regarding the changes in Patient 1s condition and refusal of Morphine. RN 1 stated she spoke with Caregiver 3, who was mostly present at the bedside with Patient 1.
 
During an interview and a concurrent review of Patient 1s clinical records on 12/5/2024 at 2:41 PM, Director of Patient Care Services (DPCS) stated she was not aware RP 1 had POA to make healthcare decisions for Patient 1. DPCS stated RN 1 spoke to Caregiver 3 regarding the CC order but failed to document call attempts to RP 1. DPCS stated Patient 1s baseline documented vital signs prior to CC initiation were 118/90, 104/65, 114/71, and 118/60 with respirations ranging from 13-18 breaths per minute. DPCS stated if Patient 1s expected outcome was to have a decline, the physician did not need to be notified.
In addition, DPCS stated CC team supervisors were not physicians or licensed nurses.
 
During a review of the HAs policy and procedures (P&P 1), titled ";Continuous Care," dated 9/4/2024, P&P 1 indicated the following:
 
1. The RN must collaborate with IDG on Plan of Care (POC) changes and call the physician for changes in condition and new orders.
 
2. The RN must update the POC as the frequent changes in the POC, such as changes in medication, equipment, medical supplies, treatment, and patient/family education, support intensive symptom management and the need for continuous care.
 
3. The RN must review the POC, and the CC shift notes from the last 24 hours prior to beginning patient assessment and include report/input from patient, family/caregivers, CC shift notes and CC shift staff. The RN must document any analysis, clarification, or follow up from the RN assessment as well as report or input received.

Based on interview, and record review, the provider failed to ensure a single individual filled the role as medical director and assumed overall responsibility for the medical component of the hospices patient care program. 

Information provided by the hospice provider from 8/26/24 to 8/28/24 revealed the provider had a total of 20 medical directors employed. There were 16 medical directors, 3 regional medical directors and 1 chief medical director. As of 8/26/24 the patient census was 14,736 under a single Medicare Provider Number (CCN#) 101545. 
The CMS Certification number (CCN) replaces the term Medicare Provider Number, Medicare Identification Number. 
Information provided by the hospice provider on 8/26/24 showed provider had 16 programs throughout Florida with 53 multiple locations. Addresses for 53 locations revealed 3 licensed offices which were in Boynton Beach, Miami Lakes and Melbourne. The Boynton office had 7 multiple locations and 1 inpatient facility, Miami Lakes had 6 multiple locations, and 1 inpatient facility and Melbourne had 2 inpatient facilities and 33 multiple locations. 
Review of 4 of 20 Medical Directors records and Department of Health Licensing information revealed the Chief Medical Director address of record was Maitland, Regional Medical Director #AA's address was Cocoa Beach, Medical Director #XX address was in Panama City and Medical Director #YY address was in Jacksonville. The Regional Medical Director #AAs Medical Doctor license had address of Record in Cocoa Beach, and she also had Controlled Substance Registration Certificate with different hospice provider in Titusville.
On 8/26/24 at 1:40 PM, the Senior Vice President (VP) of Operations #BB explained the medical director was the Chief Medical Officer and he was responsible for nearly 15,000 patients. She noted they also had 3 Regional Medical Directors under supervision of the Chief Medical Officer. The Senior VP of Operations provided documentation that listed 16 medical directors, 3 regional medical directors and 1 chief medical director. 
 
On 8/28/24 at 2:29 PM, Regional Medical Director #AA verified she was not the lead Medical Director and explained there were 3 Regional Medical Directors in Florida., 5 Regional Medical Directors across the country and they currently had 2 vacancies. Regional Medical Director #AA said she covered North Florida and South Alabama and served in a supportive role for patients and staff in those areas. The Sr. VP of Operations #BB was present during the interview and added the Regional Medical Director #AA assisted if one of the other Medical Directors was on leave, assisted with interviews for Medical Director vacancies, and supervised the program Medical Directors.
 
On 8/28/24 at 3:20 PM, a telephone interview was conducted with the Chief Medical Director/Officer. He explained the Regional Medical Directors reported directly to him and he worked with the Chief Nursing Officer to coordinate care with Medical Directors to ensure care was consistent. He said most of the policies and procedures were nursing driven and he provided oversight and input regarding policies. He had Teams call with the Regional Medical Directors every other week to discuss any concerns with medical management, patient care issues and discussed each program. He said he participated virtually in all 16 programs QAPI (Quality Assurance Performance Improvement) meetings and attended QAPI meetings quarterly. When asked about adverse events and his role in the investigation and interventions post investigation, he stated the regional Patient Care Administrators (PCA) would contact him if needed. He stated that they discussed suicides during their last call but it was not part of any recent re-education plan. The Chief Medical Director/Officer was not aware of patient #1 who committed suicide on 7/13/24, patient #20 who committed suicide on 8/17/24, patient #21 who attempted suicide on 6/20/24, patient #22 who had suspected attempted suicide/overdose which resulted in emergency room visit on 6/19/24 and subsequently died on 6/20/24. 
 
Review of the Regional Medical Director's job description dated 8/7/18, read, ";Responsible for participation in leadership to and oversight of physicians in the interdisciplinary delivery of hospice care, consistent with applicable standards of hospice medical care....Responsible for the oversight and direction of the medical aspect of their assigned hospice programs...Essential duties and responsibilities- All duties and responsibilities are to be performed in accordance with...governmental regulations...Advise in recruitment and selection of program medical directors...Participate in assuring that program medical directors have appropriate competencies...participate in yearly evaluation of the program medical directors they work with. Establish and maintain direct communication with program medical directors as assigned by the Chief Medical Officer. Consult with and advise these program medical directors regarding certification and recertification standards.... Oversee and mentor program medical directors...Assist each program medical director...Assist in professional development of program medical directors...Assist and guild program medical directors...."
 
Review of the Chief Medical Director job description effective 6/1/18, read, ";Responsible for the leadership, and oversight of physician practices in the interdisciplinary delivery of hospice care consistent with applicable standards of hospice medical care...Responsible for the oversight and direction of the medical aspect of hospice care program, the credentialing process, the establishment of patient care protocols....Essential duties and responsibilities....Oversees the regional medical directors...Ensures all clinical programs are in compliance...."

Upon patient record review, 5 of 19 (Patient #4, 8, 12, 15, & 16) did not have evidence in the patient record that a review was completed of all prescription and non-prescription medications, including herbal remedies that could affect drug therapy. This review includes, but is not limited to:
• Effectiveness of drug therapy
• Drug side effects
• Actual or potential drug interactions
• Duplicate drug therapy
• Drug therapy currently associated with laboratory monitoring
Patient 4 & 16: Colace 100mg daily PRN "bowel care" on medication list with no further instructions to further explain "bowel care" or indications for use of medication.
Patient 8: SN documentation reveals report from patient on 4/24/24 of use of Milk of Magnesia for relief of constipation. There is no evidence the medication list was updated to include this medication at that time.
Patient 12: Medication list reflects Lorazepam 0.5mg tablets every 4 hours as needed anxiety. Lorazepam 2mg/ml oral concentrate 0.25ml every 4 hours as needed agitation is also present. There are no further instructions on when it is appropriate to administer which medication related to pill versus liquid, to prevent overdose, or whether they can or cannot be utilized in conjunction with each other. 
Patient 15: Medication list contains both Hydrocodone 5-325 every four hours as needed "pain" and Tylenol 325mg 2 tablets every 6 hours as needed "pain or fever". There are no further indications on when to administer one medication versus the other for pain.

Upon patient record review, 8 of 19 (Patient #2, 4, 8, 9, 12, 13, 15, & 16) did not have evidence the plan of care must include all services necessary for the palliation and management of the terminal illness and related conditions, including medications and treatments.
Patient 2: Nursing documentation 5/23/24 indicates "wounds" under integument assessment with DTI to left heel with hydrocolloid in place. No evidence found of any wound care treatment/orders present on medication/treatment record.
Patient 4 &16 : MD order for Colace 100mg 1-2 capsules daily PRN "bowel care" with no further instructions to further explain "bowel care" or indications for use of medication.
Patient 8: SN documentation reveals report from patient on 4/24/24 of use of Milk of Magnesia for relief of constipation. There is no evidence of an MD order to include this medication on the plan of care at that time. 
Patient 9: Wound care orders on 4/29/24 & 5/8/24 are incomplete and do not contain method for securing dressing or any PRN change/indications, only stating for the nurse to change at each visit. Also, wound inactivated at 6/3/24 visit but no evidence of order found to discontinue wound care. 
Patient 12: MD orders reflect Lorazepam 0.5mg tablets every 4 hours as needed anxiety. Lorazepam 2mg/ml oral concentrate 0.25ml every 4 hours as needed agitation is also present. There are no further instructions on when it is appropriate to administer which medication related to pill versus liquid, to prevent overdose, or whether they can or cannot be utilized in conjunction with each other. 
Patient 13: MD order 5/21/24 is incomplete. Buttocks wound care lacks indication for PRN application and does not specify who is to perform care. Right Heel order lacks the frequency of wound care and any PRN change order or indications. Left Heel fluid blister order states, "Cover with foam. Monitor for open skin." it lacks when foam is to be removed, who is to monitor for open skin and if foam is to be removed to monitor site is it to be reapplied and at what frequency. 5/30/24 MD order states, "Skin tear to right heel. Clean and dry, apply Silvasorb gel and cover with foam, wound care to be provided by RN until resolved." Order lacks what agent to cleanse with, method for drying, how foam is to be secured or if it is a bordered foam dressing, how often wound care is to be performed and any prn indication for change. These wounds were inactivated 6/12/24 with no orders found to discontinue wound care.
Patient 15: Medication list contains both Hydrocodone 5-325 every four hours as needed "pain" and Tylenol 325mg 2 tablets every 6 hours as needed "pain or fever". There are no max dose instructions or further indications on when to administer one medication versus the other for pain.

Upon patient record review, 2 of 13 (Patient #5, 7) did not have evidence in the patient record that the hospice has developed an individualized written plan of care for each patient that reflects all problems identified in the initial and comprehensive assessments. 
Patient 5: On the comprehensive initial assessment, dated 09.16.2021, it was noted that the patient had difficulty swallowing; nectar thick liquids were ordered and a commercial thickener appeared on the patient's medication list for use. The SN note dated 10.27.2021 indicated the patient had developed aspiration pneumonia; the patient was treated with Levaquin and prednisone. There is no evidence of a care plan related to aspiration risk or swallowing status. (corrected on site)
Patient 7: On the comprehensive initial assessment, dated 10.08.2021, it was noted that the patient was an elopement risk; the patient was transferred from an acute care hospital to an ALF, where he was then admitted for hospice services, largely due to previous elopements from his private home. SN note dated 10.26.2021 indicates the patient escaped the ALF twice during the previous week. There is no evidence of a care plan related to elopement risk. (corrected on site)

It is required that the written Patient Bill of Rights includes the right to voice grievances to the hospice, CHAP, or a state entity without fear of discrimination or reprisal and voice grievances regarding treatment or care that is—or fails to be—provided. 

This standard was not met as evidenced by document review, clinical record review, and interview. In 3 of 3 (100%) clinical records reviewed, the hospice did not ensure the Patient Bill of Rights included information to voice grievances when it did not include contact information for the hospice, CHAP, or the state agency. 

The admission folder provided to patients at the start of care included a paper titled “Patient Care Information.” The paper stated, if we are not meeting your expectations of our service, please feel free to contact us first or one of the following: (HOSPICE) and a phone number and included the name and phone number of another accrediting organization, not CHAP. The Patient Care Information paper did not include the name of the hospice caring for the patient and did not include the CHAP name and phone number for reporting grievances. 

Clinical Record 1: The patient elected the hospice benefit on 10/10/2023. Clinical record review revealed no documented evidence that the patient was informed of the process to report a grievance. There was no documented evidence that contact information including name and phone number for the hospice agency, CHAP or the state entity was provided to the patient.
 
Clinical Record 2: The patient elected the hospice benefit on 09/19/2023. Clinical record review revealed no documented evidence that the patient was informed of the process to report a grievance. There was no documented evidence that contact information including name and phone number for the hospice agency, CHAP or the state entity was provided to the patient.

Clinical Record 3: The patient elected the hospice benefit on 10/25/2023. Clinical record review revealed no documented evidence that the patient was informed of the process to report a grievance. There was no documented evidence that contact information including name and phone number for the hospice agency, CHAP or the state entity was provided to the patient. 
 
During an interview on 10/26/2023, the Executive Director/Clinical Director/Registered Nurse stated, "We have the Patient Care Information paper we give the patients on admission, but we do not have a copy for the clinical record. What we give the patient does not include the name of our hospice if the patient wants to report a complaint. The paper we give the patient does not include the grievance process to notify CHAP, and it only includes the name of another accrediting organization, not CHAP. We got the "Patient Care Information" paper from someone in (another state).” During interview 10/26/23, the Executive Director/Clinical Director/RN stated, "We have the "Patient Care Information" paper we give the patients on admission but we do not have a copy for the clinical record", "What we give the patient does not include the name of our hospice if the patient wants to report a complaint", "The paper we give the patient does not include the grievance process to notify CHAP, and it only includes the name of another accreditation agency, not CHAP", and "We got the "Patient Care Information" paper from someone in (another state)".

It is required that licensed professionals participate in hospice-sponsored in-service training.

This standard was not met as evidenced by document review, interview, and personnel record review. In 10 of 10 (100%) personnel records reviewed, the agency did not ensure that the employees completed the required annual in-services as required by agency policy. 

DOCUMENT 4: Agency Policy, Staff Education, HR.S55, stated in part, "Non-direct personnel have a minimum of 8 hours of ongoing education per year. Direct Care Personnel must have a minimum of 12 hours of ongoing education during each 12-month period. Yearly in-service requirements include, but are not limited to: Infection Control, HIPAA, Medical Device Act/Reporting, Emergency Management/Disaster Training, Ethics, Methods for coping with work-related issues of grief, loss, and change, Compliance Plan, Patient Rights and Responsibilities, Communication Barriers and Cultural Diversity, and How to handle complaints/grievances. The Director of Nursing maintains a written description of in-service training provided during the previous 12 months."

PERSONNEL RECORD 1: The Administrator/Director of Nursing/Registered Nurse/Volunteer Coordinator was hired on 05/24/2022 and completed in-service education in November 2022. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2023, 2024, 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

PERSONNEL RECORD 2: The Alternate Administrator/Alternate Director of Nursing/Registered Nurse was hired on 05/24/2022. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2023, 2024, 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

PERSONNEL RECORD 3: The Hospice Medical Director was hired on 01/03/2024. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2025 through 03/16/2026. 

PERSONNEL RECORD 4: The Alternate Medical Director was hired on 11/02/2022. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2023, 2024, 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

PERSONNEL RECORD 5: The Hospice Aide (CNA) was hired on 12/21/2022. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2023, 2024, 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

PERSONNEL RECORD 6: The Chaplain was hired on 07/21/2023. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2024, 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

PERSONNEL RECORD 7: The Master Social Worker/Bereavement Coordinator was hired on 05/30/2023. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2024, 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

PERSONNEL RECORD 8: The Nurse Practitioner was hired on 10/07/2024. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

PERSONNEL RECORD 9: The Registered Nurse was hired on 01/30/2023. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2024, 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

 
PERSONNEL RECORD 10: The Volunteer was hired on 10/03/2023. There was no documented evidence that the required in-services were completed annually in 2024, 2025, and through 03/16/2026. 

During a joint record review and interview on 03/18/2026, the Administrator (Personnel Record 1) agreed that there was no documented evidence that the employees completed the required annual in-services as required by agency policy. Additionally, the Administrator stated, "I was in the field a lot providing patient care until I hired another nurse. These administrative items fell to the wayside. I was busy with CMS audits, and a lot of paperwork didn't get done. I was wearing too many hats."

It is required that the written Patient Bill of Rights includes the right to: voice grievances regarding treatment or care that is—or fails to be—provided; 

This standard was not met as evidenced by clinical record review, document review, and interview. Agency policy #HOS-C_06A "Complaints and Grievances Procedure" (effective 01/24/2021) (revised 07/07/2025) stated in relevant part(s): "Purpose: Provide prompt investigation and resolution to patient and/or family complaints or grievances. Procedure: A) Complaint or grievance-a concern expressed by anyone about the quality of care, care delivery, services, colleagues, or any area under the influence or responsibility of the XXXXXX program, if from a patient or family member. 4. The Director of Clinical Services or designee will be responsible for the following actions: a. Complete the top portion of the written complaint report...g. Complete the complaint log."

In 1 of 19 (5%) clinical records reviewed, the agency did not ensure that a concern expressed by the patient or family was documented in a complaint log for investigation and resolution in accordance with the agency's policy. 

CLINICAL RECORD 19: The patient elected hospice care on 08/13/2025 with a diagnosis of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. A clinical record review revealed a Social Worker note dated 10/07/2025 documenting: "Son was frustrated that patient was on morphine and declining so fast. He would like updates after each visit. He would like a nurse to call and explain the morphine because he is concerned he is overmedicated and would like the morphine stopped. SW relayed the message to DCS (Director of Clinical Services) in person." A clinical record review revealed no documented evidence that a nurse called the patient's son to discuss the medication concern.

During an interview, joint clinical record review, and review of the complaint log on 01/30/2026, the Administrator explained she was "the acting DCS on the date in question, and the son was out of town and wanted his father to sign some financial paperwork, and it was believed he was too medicated to do so." The Administrator stated that "It was not documented as a concern or complaint at the time, but reading the policy now, it should have been."

Based on policy review, grievance file review, and interview, the agency failed to document the investigation of all alleged violations in accordance with established procedures in one (Complaint #1) of three complaint records reviewed. This deficient practice has the potential to affect the investigation of complaints and/or grievances of all patients served by the agency. 

Findings included: 

Review of the agency's undated policy titled, "Patient Rights and Responsibilities," showed in part that the patient had the right to receive an investigation by the organization of complaints made by the patient or the patient's family or guardian regarding treatment or care and that the organization will document the existence of the complaint and the resolution of the complaint.

Complaint #1: 
Review of complaint #1 with report date of 07/08/2022 showed the complaint form failed to contain documentation of: 
- The description of the complaint; 
- Resolution of the complaint (action taken);
- Follow up needed; and 
- Signature, title and date of person reviewing and ensuring the implementation related to this complaint including any follow up that was needed. 

During an interview on 07/14/2022 at 12:40 PM, the administrator stated that the complaint form should have been completed. That he/she is busy and wears many hats and it just got missed. She did investigate via calling other patient's the staff member was caring for at that time and there was no other patients with problems with that staff member.

Based on policy review, record review, and interview, the hospice provider failed to document the investigation of an alleged violation of possible abuse and immediately take action to prevent further potential violations in accordance with established procedures in one of three records reviewed (Record/Patient #1). This deficient practice has the potential to affect the investigation of complaints and/or grievances of all patients served by the provider.

 
 
Findings included: 
 
Review of the providers policy titled, "Abuse, Neglect, Mistreatment and Exploitation," dated 2021, showed in part, that the administrator immediately (as soon as possible and not more than 24 hours after discovery of the incident) investigates alleged violations involving persons providing services on behalf of the hospice and immediately takes action to prevent further violation(s) during the investigation. If necessary, the Administrator will seek consultation to ensure an alleged violation is thoroughly investigated in order to verify whether or not it occurred and that it constituted abuse, neglect, mistreatment, or exploitation.
 
RECORD/PATIENT #1:
Review of the registered nurse (RN A) supervisory visit note, dated 12/26/2023 at 3:35 PM, showed the following:
- Primary diagnosis was senile degeneration of the brain;
-Alert to person and place and confused;
-"The social worker and clinical director were notified of concerns of possible abuse as evidenced by recurring bruising to forearms and reports of tying patient to bed"; 
-The patients left forearm was bruised ";though" caregiver states the patient was scratching at his/her dry skin; and
-The documentation failed to include any further information about the bruising or tying the patient to the bed and if this included staff or caregiver.
 
During an interview on 01/03/2024 at 10:08 AM, RN A stated that he/she told the administrator, medical director, and social worker on 12/27/2023 about the patient. Failure to ensure the patient is informed of all components of the procedures for submitting a complaint/grievance inhibits the patient's ability to exercise their rights with the potential to result in negative patient outcomes.

This standard was not met as evidenced by document review, clinical record review, and interview. Based on interview, record review, and review of agency policy, the hospice agency failed to identify, document, and act upon verbal grievances from the caregivers for one of one patient (Patient (P) 7) reviewed for grievances out of a total sample of 19. This had the potential to cause patient and caregiver concerns to be unaddressed.
Findings include:
Review of P7's "Patient Information Report," provided by the agency, revealed P7 was admitted to hospice services on 09/27/24 with a terminal diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.
Review of P7's "Visit Note Report," dated 10/08/24 at 2:38 PM, provided by the agency, and written by Registered Nurse (RN)1, revealed, ". . . Pt [patient] sitting awake in . . . recliner . . . is alert and pleasant. Oriented x 4 . . . c/o [complained of] SOB [shortness of breath] . . . started on [oxygen] . . . education on concentrator given . . . "
Review of P7's "Client Coordination Report," dated 10/08/24 and written by RN4, revealed, ". . . Received phone call from [Family Member (F) 7] at 5:09 PM . . . was getting [P7] up to the bathroom and it appeared [P7] had a stroke. [F7] wanted to know what to do. [F7] had some friends over and they were going to help get [P7] into bed. And I will come and do a visit to assess [him/her] . . ."
Review of P7's "Client Coordination Report," dated 10/08/24, untimed, and written by RN4, revealed, ". . . Called [F7] at 5:30 PM to let [him/her] know I was going to a death visit and asked her how [P7] was doing. [F7] said they had gotten [P7] back into bed. [P7] did appear a little agitated and was responsive. [F7] put her friend on the phone and I suggested that they give [P7] a Lorazepam [anti-anxiety medication] . . . and if not effective give another one in 20 minutes. I said I would be there as soon as I could. I said I would be there after my other visit . . ."
Review of P7's "Visit Note Report," dated 10/08/24 at 7:11 PM and provided by the agency, revealed, ". . . Death was quick and was a surprise for the family as [he/she] had been doing well over the weekend . . ." Review of the Visit Note Report revealed no documented evidence the caregiver had voiced any grievance related to the delay in the nurse's arrival for the visit. The arrival time of 7:11 PM for this visit was over two hours after the time of the call requesting assistance at 5:09 PM.
During an interview on 01/13/25 at 1:00 PM, the Director of Clinical Services (DCS) stated the agency serviced all of Cochise County, and there were different cities that they visited within the county. The DCS stated the staff had one hour to make it to a patient home after a call was placed requesting a visit.
During an interview on 01/14/25 at 10:39 AM, F7 stated on the day that P7 died, the nurse had made a visit to check P7, and about an hour later, P7 went to the bathroom and collapsed. F7 stated the hospice agency was called, and he/she was told that they would try to get someone out. F7 stated he/she knew he/she had talked to a man to begin with and then had talked to a woman. F7 stated the woman told him/her she was on another call and said it would probably be another hour. F7 stated, "I guess I was thinking in my head that they would have someone else." F7 stated it was close to two hours before the nurse arrived and P7 had passed by that time. F7 stated, "I never received any follow-up calls. I got a form letter [bereavement letter] from the Chaplain – fill name in here, fill name in there. You have our condolences." F7 stated, "You could have at least filled in our name." F7 stated, "The chaplain stopped by the house two or three weeks later to say I'm sorry and that [he/she] blamed [himself/herself] for it. [He/she] came one other time, and I didn't even answer the door. I was so done with it." F7 stated, "Even the signature [on the form letter] was fill in the blank here." F7 was asked if he/she had verbalized his/her frustration to anyone with the hospice agency. F7 stated he/she had expressed his/her displeasure about the time it took for the nurse to arrive with the nurse the night P7 passed, with the chaplain two to three weeks after P7 had passed, and another family had "verbalized it to the director up in Tucson and told the director everything that happened." F7 stated, "No one has called me." F7 stated there was nothing that could be done now, but he/she did not want anyone else to have to experience these things.
During an interview on 01/14/25 at 12;16 PM, the Bereavement Coordinator (BC), who was the chaplain for P7, stated, "My understanding was that there was a complication and [P7] died unexpectedly. The nurse on call had two deaths at the same time." The BC stated P7's family was annoyed because they thought the bereavement letter the agency sent was "too generic." The BC stated he/she believed F7 expressed dissatisfaction with the length of time it took for the nurse to arrive the night P7 passed. The BC stated, "I went as sort of a peacemaker and told him/her we dropped the ball." The BC stated the former Administrator and the present Director of Clinical Services (DCS) had instructed him/her to take a plant to F7.
Review of the agency's grievance log for 2024 revealed only one grievance for the year. The grievance listed was logged in January 2024. There was no documented evidence of F7's verbal grievances to RN4, the BC, or any Valor Hospice employee.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 1:12 PM, Human Resources (HR) stated he/she was the agency's grievance coordinator. HR stated that clinical grievances were handled by the DCS or Clinical Coordinator (CC). HR stated the DCS and CC were supposed to notify him/her of any grievances so they could be logged. HR stated he/she had no knowledge of any grievance related to P7.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 4:12 PM, the DCS and CC were asked about the circumstances surrounding P7's passing. The DCS stated P7 had a change in condition, the family called, and RN4 said he/she would go to their house. The DCS stated while RN4 was in route to P7, RN4 received a call that someone had died. The DCS stated RN4 called the family of P7 and was told they had gotten P7 into bed. The DCS stated RN4 had completed the death visit, and approximately one and one-half hours later, arrived at P7's home. The DCS stated P7 had passed prior to the nurse arriving. The DCS stated, "It was an abrupt death. There was just no idea [P7] was going to die like that. We felt bad about it." The CC stated, "The case manager was shocked he/she had passed." The CC stated, "There was no sign he/she was actively dying; otherwise, [RN4] would have asked one of us to back him/her up." The DCS was asked if he/she was aware of the family's dissatisfaction with the bereavement letter. The DCS stated he/she was aware the family thought it was too generic but did not have knowledge the letter sent had been a copy of the template used for bereavement letters. The DCS was asked what the agency's policy was on identifying, documenting, and acting upon grievance. The DCS stated, "I was aware it was not an optimal situation. We did not get a formal complaint." The DCS was asked if per the policy, grievances had to be formally written. The DCS reviewed the policy and stated no.
During an interview on 01/15/25 at 5:50 PM, RN4 stated while he/she was completing the death visit on 10/08/24, he/she must have received a call from P7's family that was missed. RN4 stated he/she called the family back and they stated P7 had passed, and they were wondering why he/she was not there. RN4 stated the family was upset that he/she did not come right away. RN4 stated he/she prepared P7's body for the funeral home, and F7 had shown he/she some pictures. RN4 stated he/she thought the family was okay then. RN4 stated, "I knew they were upset that I hadn't gotten there in time and then the unexpected death." RN4 was asked if he/she had reported to the DCS that the family was upset. RN4 stated she had told the DCS about it in conversation but had not reported it as a grievance.

The Complainant stated that they, as the primary caregiver and surrogate decision-maker for the patient, met with a nurse, who reviewed the patients medications with the Complainant. The Complainant noted at the time that the patients medications had been ";pared down to the essentials" but otherwise no changes had been made. The Complainant stated that on July 4, 2024, Latanoprost was ordered for the patient but was not delivered for the patient until a stat order was placed and the medication received on July 12, 2024. The Complainant stated they reported this issue to Hospice of the West and stated the responsiveness on this issue was ";very appropriate."
On July 4, 2024, the patient began taking all other medications ordered, including Metoprolol. The Complainant reported that the Complainant was made aware by staff at the facility where the patient resided that the patient had been prescribed ";ten times the amount" of Metoprolol than the patient was intended to be prescribed. The Complainant reported this to the hospice nurse who came to see the patient and stated the hospice nurse told the Complainant this was ";not possible" and that what the Complainant read on the MAR (medication administration sheet) ";must be a typo."
The patient continued to receive 200mg of Metoprolol from July 4 to July 25, 2024 according to the Complainant. The Complainant reported to the nurse that the patient had a heart rate in the 40s, was shaking and had not been responsive for weeks. The Complainant stated the hospice nurse told the Complainant this was a normal part of the dying process.
The Complainant stated that the nursing home sent the Complainant a photograph of the prescription bottle to provide the hospice and the hospice finally agreed there was a medication error. But the Complainant stated that the hospice was not apologetic and instead ";tried to deflect blame" onto the nursing home. The Complainant stated the Complainant contacted Hospice of the West. The Complainant stated, ";I wanted to know, what are you going to do?" The Complainant stated they were ignored by the first person they spoke to. Interviews were conducted with Employees #1 and #3 on August 21 and August 22. Employee #3 stated that patients who are unhappy with the medication service provided by the hospice can instead pick up their medications at the pharmacy of their choice at no additional cost. But when asked how this right is communicated to patients, Employee #3 could not direct Compliance Officers to specific information provided to patients. This right did not appear to be clearly communicated in the admission materials provided by Hospice of the West to patients. 
Both Employees #1 and #3 acknowledged and agreed that adverse trends affecting patient care should be identified, a root cause analysis performed and actions to improve agency performance should be taken in accordance with policies and procedures; however, Employee #1 was asked to provide all performance improvement plans initiated by HOW in 2023 and 2024 related to the provision of patient care and related to pharmaceutical services. The two PIPs initiated, one initiated in March 27, 2023 regarding live discharge rates, and the other initiated March 1, 2024 regarding the transition to OnePoint Pharmacy as a subcontracted provider, did not appear to address the complaints and grievances reported by patients.

Based on record review, policy review, and interview, the Hospice Agency (HA) failed to ensure the immediate investigation of alleged violations and immediate action to prevent further potential violation for 1 (Patient 1) of 1 patient allegation that required immediate investigation. The hospice's failure to immediately investigate alleged complaints had the potential to place all patients at risk for compromised preservation of individual patient rights, compromised patient safety and inadequate management of the hospice patient's rights in the home.

Findings Include:
Review of the HA policy titled, ";Nondiscrimination Policy and Grievance Process," revised February 2017, showed, ";Any person who believes she or he has been subjected to discrimination or who believes he or she has witnessed discrimination, in contradiction of the policy stated above, may file a grievance under this procedure. It is against the law for Home Health of Kansas, LLC to retaliate against anyone who files a grievance or cooperates in the investigation of a grievance. ... Grievances must be submitted to the Section 504 Coordinator within 30 days of the date the person filing the grievance becomes aware of the alleged discriminatory action. ... A complaint may be filed in writing, or verbally, containing the name and address of the person filing it ("the grievant"). The complaint must state the problem or action alleged to be discriminatory and the remedy or relief sought by the grievant. ... The Section 504 Coordinator (or her/his representative) will conduct an investigation of the complaint to determine its validity. This investigation may be informal, but it must be thorough, affording all interested persons an opportunity to submit evidence relevant to the complaint. The Section 504 Coordinator will issue a written decision on the grievance no later than 30 days after its filing."

Findings included:

Policy Grievances/Complaints, revised 10/20/21, was received from the agency director on 05/17/22 at 2:11 PM. This policy revealed, " ...Upon receipt of the complaint, the departmental manager (or designee) shall take the following steps: Contact the individual voicing the complaint of the status of the complaint/grievance within 24 hours. During the contact, the departmental supervisor will obtain all additional necessary information on the nature of the complaint. He or she will also assure the client that the complaint will be reviewed, and further contact will be forthcoming ...Speak with involved employees, as appropriate, to obtain further clarification, and to allow the employee an opportunity to respond to allegations. If required, discuss ways to prevent future similar incidents with involved employee. Plan corrective action plans with employee to address behavior and implement. If required, initiate the disciplinary process. Document all activities on the Complaint/Grievance form. The Supervisor will report status of activities to client/responsible party within three (3) business days following receipt of complaint. Once the investigation of the complaint is completed, the Supervisor will notify the client/responsible party and review the findings..."

It is required that the written Patient Bill of Rights includes the right to voice grievances to the hospice, CHAP, or a state entity without fear of discrimination or reprisal and voice grievances regarding treatment or care that is—or fails to be—provided. 

This standard was not met as evidenced by document review, clinical record review, and interview. In 3 of 3 (100%) clinical records reviewed, the hospice did not ensure the Patient Bill of Rights included information to voice grievances when it did not include contact information for the hospice, CHAP, or the state agency. 

The admission folder provided to patients at the start of care included a paper titled “Patient Care Information.” The paper stated, if we are not meeting your expectations of our service, please feel free to contact us first or one of the following: (HOSPICE) and a phone number and included the name and phone number of another accrediting organization, not CHAP. The Patient Care Information paper did not include the name of the hospice caring for the patient and did not include the CHAP name and phone number for reporting grievances.

Based on interview and record review, the Hospice agency failed to meet the Condition of Participation (CoP) for L500 Patient's Right when they failed to 1.) comply with mandatory reporting requirements to immediately report suspicions of neglect to Adult Protective Services (APS) for one of 19 patients (Patient (P) 15) whose records were reviewed out of a total sample of 19. P15 was noted to be a vulnerable adult on 09/11/24, and the case was not filed with APS until 11/26/24. Additionally, local law enforcement was not notified. These failures had the potential to place P15 at risk of serious injury, harm, or impairment, up to and including death, and 2.) identify, document, and act upon a verbal grievance from the caregivers for one of one patient (P7) reviewed for grievances out of a total sample of 19. This had the potential to cause patient and caregiver concerns to be unaddressed.
The agency was notified of the Immediate Jeopardy (IJ) at L517which was related to the failure to comply with mandatory reporting requirements on 01/15/25 at 5:30 PM. In concurrence with Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) review, the removal plan was approved on 01/16/25 at 10:07 AM. The survey team verified implementation of the facility's IJ removal plan on 01/16/25 at 2:36 PM.
Findings include:
1. The agency failed to immediately notify APS of suspicions of neglect for one of 14 active patients (P15) when the patient was first assessed to be vulnerable and unsafe living in his home without caregivers present. (Refer to L517)
2. The agency failed to identify, document, and act upon a verbal grievance from the caregivers of P7. (Refer to L505)
